en: The Sutra of the Collection of One Hundred Karmic Causes and Conditions, Volume One, translated by the Wu-period Yuezhi layman Zhi Qian.
Chapter One: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon the Bodhisattva. Chapter One: The Bestowal of Prophecy upon the Bodhisattva.
1. The Story of the Brahmin Pūrṇa Inviting the Buddha from Afar (I). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a brahmin in the south named Pūrṇabhadra, whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation, resembling the god Vaiśravaṇa. He was virtuous and upright in his conduct, possessed a gentle and compliant nature, and benefited both himself and others; he felt compassion for all sentient beings, loving them as a mother loves her child.

At the assembly of non-Buddhist teachers, he prepared various kinds of delicacies and constantly made offerings to hundreds of thousands of externalists, hoping and desiring to be reborn in the Brahma Heaven.

At that time, Pūrṇa had a close friend who came from Rājagṛha to that country. Upon arriving at Pūrṇa’s residence, he extolled the merits of the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṃgha, saying: "His fame and renown have spread far and wide; his threefold knowledge perceives all things with distant clarity. He is called the Bhagavat. He is currently at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha, where gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans, as well as kings, elders, and the common people, all together make offerings to him, revere him, and praise him."
The practice he cultivated was of such exquisite flavor that it pervaded the entire world, and there was none who did not revere it.

At that time, the brahmin, hearing his close friend extol the Buddha’s merits, conceived deep faith and respect. He immediately ascended a high tower, holding fragrant flowers in his hands; kneeling long with palms joined, he invited the World-Honored One from afar, speaking these words:

"The Tathāgata truly possesses such merit that the fragrance I have burned shall spread throughout the city of Rājagṛha, and the flowers I scatter shall transform into a floral canopy in the air above the Buddha’s head."

Having made this vow, incense and flowers arrived immediately; they transformed above the Buddha’s head into a flower canopy, and the smoke from the incense spread throughout the entirety of Rājagṛha.
At that time, having witnessed this transformation, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying,
"From where does such a fragrant cloud come?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“In the south there is a country named Suvarṇabhūmi; there dwells an elder named Pūrṇabhadra, who has sent a distant invitation to me and the community of bhikṣus.”
"I shall go there to receive their offerings; you all should each, by means of your supernatural powers, go to accept their invitation.

When the bhikṣus had received the Buddha's command, they traveled through the air to that place. Not far from the sacrificial site, the Buddha used his supernormal power to conceal the thousand bhikṣus and manifested only himself, holding his alms bowl, as he arrived at the residence of Pūrṇa.
At that time, when the elder heard that the Buddha had arrived, he led his five hundred followers, each carrying food and drink of a hundred flavors, to welcome the Tathāgata.

He beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining brilliantly like a hundred thousand suns; with a serene and elegant gait, his majestic deportment was most worthy of contemplation, as he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet.
“Welcome, World-Honored One!
Out of compassion and pity, please now accept our offering of food.
The Buddha told the elder:
"If you wish to give, place it in this bowl.
Then the five hundred followers each took the food and drink they had brought and personally placed it into the Buddha’s bowl with their own hands, yet they were unable to fill it.
"How marvelous, World-Honored One!
You possess such supernormal power.
His mind was immediately subdued.
A community of a thousand bhikṣus, their almsbowls likewise filled, suddenly appeared before him and circumambulated the World-Honored One.
At that time, the elder marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; he immediately prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground and made this great vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this gift of food, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages."
For those without a refuge, they act as a refuge;
for those without protection, they act as a protector;
for those not yet liberated, they act as a liberator.
"May those who have not yet attained peace find peace;
may those who have not yet entered Nirvana enter Nirvana.

Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued rays of five-colored light that illuminated the world in all its various hues. The light circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see the householder Purna making offerings to me?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen him."

“In a future age, after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, you shall fulfill the bodhisattva practices, cultivate the mind of great compassion, and bring the six pāramitās to completion; you shall then attain buddhahood, named Pūrṇabhadra, and deliver immeasurable sentient beings—it is for this reason that I smile.”

When the Buddha had spoken this account of Pūrṇa, there were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; there were those who resolved to attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, and there were those who resolved upon unexcelled Bodhicitta.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
2. The Story of Yaśodharā Inviting the Buddha (II) The Story of Yaśodharā Inviting the Buddha: The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Kūṭāgāraśālā on the bank of the Monkey River.
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city with his bhikṣus to beg for food, arriving at the house of the elder Siṃha.

At that moment, the elder had a daughter-in-law named Yaśodharā; seeing the Buddha’s majestic countenance and his body adorned with various marks and signs of excellence, she went before her mother-in-law and said:
"Is it possible to obtain a body such as this?"
The aunt then replied:
"If you can now cultivate all manner of meritorious virtues and give rise to the unsurpassed, vast, and great resolve, you too shall obtain all the marks and signs of excellence."
When the son’s wife heard these words, she followed her mother-in-law’s request to seek out wealth and provisions to prepare a feast and invite the Buddha.

Once the meal was finished, she took various kinds of flowers and scattered them over the Buddha’s head; in mid-air, they transformed into a flower canopy that moved and stayed in accordance with the Buddha’s walking and standing.
Having witnessed this transformation, he was overcome with joy and prostrated himself on the ground with his five limbs. He made this great vow:
"By the merit created through this offering, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
For those without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberation;
for those without peace, he acts as their peace.
"For those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa, I shall bring about their nirvāṇa.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the woman had given rise to such a vast and noble mind, immediately smiled. From his mouth issued rays of five-colored light that illuminated the entire world, manifesting in various hues. They circled the Buddha three times and then re-entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see this woman of renown making an offering to me?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen her."

“Now, this Yaśaskāma has given rise to a vast mind; through the merit of his roots of goodness, after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he will fulfill the bodhisattva practices, cultivate the mind of great compassion, and complete the six pāramitās. He shall attain buddhahood with the name Ratnamati, extensively delivering immeasurable sentient beings. This is why I smile.”

When the Buddha spoke this account of the causes and conditions for the name, there were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; there were those who resolved their minds on Pratyekabuddhahood, and there were those who resolved their minds on unexcelled bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(3) The Story of the Lazy Son Nanda Seeing the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation. He had an only son named Nanda, who was extremely indolent and always delighted in sleep; he would neither walk nor sit, yet he was exceptionally intelligent and far surpassed his peers. Even while lying in bed, he listened to and studied the sūtras and śāstras, becoming profoundly learned in their meanings and essences.
At that time, the elder father, seeing that his son was intelligent and well-versed in the sūtras and śāstras, had this thought:
"I shall now invite the six heretical teachers, such as Pūraṇa and others, to come to my home and instruct my son."
Having had this thought, he prepared various delicacies and immediately invited them, saying:
"The meal is finished.
He then addressed the six teachers, saying:

"My only son is extremely indolent; he refuses to rise from his sleep. I only pray that the Great Master will instruct him, so that he may cultivate his family business as well as the sūtras and śāstras."
Then the six teachers and their followers went together to where the son was;
yet he lay there without rising, let alone offering them a seat or pleading for his life on their behalf.
When the father, the elder, saw his son in such a state, he rested his cheek in his hand, overcome with great distress, sorrow, and unhappiness.

At that time, the World-Honored One, constantly moved by great compassion, observed sentient beings throughout the six periods of the day and night. Whenever he saw anyone suffering, he would immediately go to them and preach the Dharma to bring them understanding and liberation. He then beheld the elder, distressed by his son, sitting with his cheek propped up, and led the bhikṣus to the elder’s house.
At that moment, the son of the indolent man suddenly sprang up, prepared a seat for the Buddha, prostrated before the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit at one side.
The Buddha then preached various teachings to him, rebuking his slothfulness and pointing out its many faults.
He immediately repented and reproached himself, developing deep faith and reverence.
The Buddha then gave him a sandalwood staff and said to that lazy man:

"If you can now apply even a little effort toward diligent practice and strike this staff, the sound it produces will be most delightful. Upon hearing this sound, you will be able to see all the hidden treasures beneath the earth."

At that time, the indolent son immediately took up his staff and struck it until it made a sound; he then beheld all the hidden treasures within the earth. Overjoyed beyond measure, he thought to himself:

"If, through this diligent effort, by applying only a small amount of mental focus, I have already obtained such great benefit, how much more so if I apply myself with even greater diligence, exerting my body and strength? In future lives, I shall certainly obtain unsurpassed and supreme benefit."
"I shall now exert myself with diligent effort to enter the sea and gather jewels.
Having formed this thought, he immediately issued a proclamation, addressing the multitude:
"Who wishes to enter the sea to gather great treasures?"
"I am the caravan leader.

The multitude gathered together in competition and made a solemn vow to enter the great ocean; each obtained precious treasures and all returned in safety. They prepared various delicacies to invite the Buddha and the Sangha, and having completed the offerings, the Buddha immediately preached the Dharma to them in various ways. Their minds were opened and their intentions understood, whereupon they cast their five limbs upon the ground and made this great vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages."
For those without refuge, he acts as their refuge;
for those without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberation.
"To those who lack peace and security, I shall provide peace and security;
to those who have not attained *nirvāṇa*, I shall cause them to attain *nirvāṇa*.
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued rays of five-colored light that circled the Buddha three times before re-entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Can you now see this lazy son who entered the sea to gather treasures and prepared various delicacies to provide for me?
Ānanda replied,
“Indeed, I have seen him.”

“This indolent son, in a future age after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood under the name Vīryabala. He will deliver immeasurable sentient beings; for this reason, I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
4. The Story of Five Hundred Merchant Caravans Entering the Sea to Seek Jewels (IV) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a merchant leader in that city who, taking five hundred traders, entered the great ocean together. Their ship was wrecked, and they returned; day and night they diligently prostrated before various deities, seeking blessings and protection.
A second and a third time they entered the sea again, yet their ships were destroyed as before.
At that time, by the power of his merit, the merchant leader did not drown and returned safely to his native land. There, he was overcome with great anguish and thought to himself:

"I have often heard that there is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who has attained all-knowledge; none among gods or men can equal him. Out of compassion for sentient beings, he brings benefit to both himself and others."
"I shall now invoke the name of that Buddha and enter the great ocean;
if I return in safety, I shall offer half of the precious jewels I have obtained as a gift to that Buddha."

Having formed this thought, he immediately gathered the merchants and entered the great ocean together; by invoking the name of the Buddha, they obtained a vast quantity of precious treasures and returned safely.
Upon arriving home, he gazed upon his treasures with longing and greed; unwilling to give them to the Buddha, he thought to himself:
"If I were to diminish these treasures and give half of them, I would have nothing left for myself."

"I shall now take these precious items and give them all to my wife; from her, I will borrow a small amount of money to purchase incense, which I will then carry to the Jetavana to burn as an offering."
Having formed this thought, he acted according to his plan; having obtained two coins, he purchased incense and went to the Jetavana to burn it as an offering.
By the Buddha’s supernormal power, the incense smoke was made to hang down in dense, billowing clouds, completely covering the Jeta Grove.
At that time, seeing this incense smoke, the merchant leader deeply repented before the Buddha, reproaching himself:
"How could I have been so stingy with this treasure toward the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and failed to offer it as a gift?"
"The Tathāgata truly possesses supernatural power, for he has caused these fragrant fumes to pervade and cover the Jetavana; this is most rare!
I shall now prepare various delicacies and food and drink, and invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha to my residence to receive my offerings."
Having formed this thought, he immediately knelt down and invited the Buddha, the World-Honored One.
The Buddha granted his consent by remaining silent.
He returned to his home, prepared the food and drink, and when the time arrived the following day, sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is prepared; may the Holy One know the time.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and accompanied by the bhikṣus, went to that house.

Having accepted that offering, the Buddha preached the Dharma on the faults and evils of stinginess and greed; their minds were opened and their understanding awakened. They further took up precious jewels and scattered them over the Buddha’s head, which in mid-air transformed into a jeweled canopy that followed the Buddha wherever he walked or stayed.
Having seen this transformation, he immediately cast his five limbs upon the ground and made a great vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
To those without protection, he provides protection;
to those without liberation, he provides liberation;
to those without peace, he provides peace.
"May those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa be led to attain it.
Having made this vow, the Buddha immediately smiled, and from his face issued light of five colors that circled the Buddha three times before returning to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what conditions do you now smile?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see this merchant leader making offerings to me with a heart of shame and remorse?
Ānanda replied to the Buddha,
"Indeed, I have seen him."

“Because this merchant leader has made offerings to me, he shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; instead, he will be born among gods and humans, constantly experiencing happiness. After three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he shall attain Buddhahood, named Ratnasaṃbhava, and deliver sentient beings in numbers beyond measure. It is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(5) The Story of the Poor Man Sumati Offering Thread to the Buddha The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a weaver in that city named Suma, who was impoverished and suffering; his household possessed not even a peck or a pint of grain, and he constantly worked as a traveling weaver to sustain himself.
Furthermore, on one day, he had this thought:
"Because I failed to practice giving in my previous lives, I have now encountered such poverty and suffering;
if I do not practice giving again now, my poverty will surely become even more severe in future lives."

Having formed this thought, he reflected: "I should now exert myself even more diligently to seek out some small thing to offer as a gift; perhaps in a future life I might obtain such a reward. Thereupon, he went searching and obtained a small amount of thread.
On his way home, he reached a certain lane and saw from afar the World-Honored One, wearing his robes and holding his alms bowl, entering the city with a company of bhikṣus to beg for food.
He went before the Buddha and immediately took this thread to offer it to the World-Honored One.
Having accepted it, the World-Honored One manifested a torn garment and immediately used it to sew the robe.

At that time, Sumana saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, mending a tattered robe. With a heart full of joy, he approached and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, making a great vow and speaking these verses before the Buddha:
"Though my gift is small and slight, I encounter a great and excellent field of merit.
Having offered it to the World-Honored One, I vow to attain Buddhahood in the future."
"The multitude of living beings is excessive, their number beyond measure;
may the World-Honored One of Great Majestic Virtue bear witness to this matter.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
“Because you have now encountered me, you have returned with sincerity and given rise to faith and generosity;
in the future you shall attain Buddhahood, and your name shall be Daśa-vastra.
Your fame shall pervade the ten directions, and you shall deliver and liberate beings beyond measure.”

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Sumā gave rise to profound faith and reverence. Prostrating herself with her five limbs touching the ground, she made this great vow:
"By all the merit from this gift of thread, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
For those without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberation;
for those without peace, he acts as their peace.
"May those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa be led to attain it.
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this poor man, Suma, who has given me a thread with a heart full of joy and made a great vow?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it."

“Because that Suma, with a heart of profound sincerity, gave me this thread, he shall in a future age attain Buddhahood under the name Daśasūtra (Ten Threads). He will extensively deliver immeasurable sentient beings; it is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(6) The Account of the Illness of Baddhika (Sixth) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Bhaṭika, who was extremely ill-tempered and prone to anger; he had no one with whom he shared intimacy or friendship, yet he felt faith and reverence toward the six classes of beings.
At a later time, he encountered a severe illness and was so afflicted that no one attended to him for food, drink, or medicine; with but little life remaining, he thought to himself:
"I am now in such extreme suffering and distress; who can rescue and sustain my life?"
"I shall serve him with devotion for the rest of my life.
Having reflected thus, [he thought], "Only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can save my life.
Thereupon, he conceived a heart of profound reverence toward the Buddha and yearned with thirsty longing to behold him.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with constant great compassion, observed sentient beings throughout the six periods of day and night, thinking: "Who is suffering and afflicted? I shall go to them to deliver them; I shall speak the Dharma with gentle words to gladden their hearts.
If they have fallen into the evil realms, I shall employ skillful means to rescue them, establishing them in the human or heavenly realms so that they may attain the fruits of the Path."

At that time, the Tathāgata immediately observed him and saw that the elder was beset by illness, emaciated and beyond hope of recovery, with no one to attend to his needs. He then emitted a radiance that shone upon the sick man’s body, bringing him refreshing coolness.
His mind was immediately awakened, and he was overcome with joy; prostrating himself on the ground, he took refuge in the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the roots of goodness of Vāśiṣṭha had matured and that he was ready to receive his transformation, immediately went to the house of that elder.
Suddenly starting up in alarm, he joined his palms in reverent greeting:
"Welcome, World-Honored One!
He prepared a seat and sat down.
The Buddha asked Vatsagotra,
"Regarding your current illness and suffering, which is the most severe?
He replied:
"I am now suffering both physically and mentally.
The Buddha thought to himself:
"Throughout kalpas past, I have cultivated compassion, vowing to heal the physical and mental ailments of sentient beings."
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the Buddha’s thoughts, immediately went to Mount Gandhamādana, gathered medicinal herbs called "White Milk," and offered them to the World-Honored One.
The Buddha obtained this medicine and gave it to Bhaṭika, instructing him to take it all until it was finished. His illnesses were entirely cured, and his body and mind became joyful and at ease.

Thereupon, he conceived redoubled faith and reverence toward the Buddha; he immediately prepared various delicacies for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. Having completed the offerings, he further presented the Buddha and the Saṅgha with exquisite robes worth one hundred thousand taels of gold, making this great vow:

"By the roots of goodness and merit from these offerings, just as the World-Honored One has now healed my body and mind so that I am free from all ailments and have attained swift peace and happiness, may I, in future lives, heal the physical and mental illnesses of all sentient beings, enabling them to attain peace and happiness."
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued forth light of five colors, which circled the Buddha three times and re-entered through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see that son of a householder who, having recovered from his illness, has prepared an offering and invited me and the community of bhikṣus?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have already seen him."
“In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood and be named Śākyamuni; you will extensively deliver sentient beings beyond measure. It is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
7. The Story of the Royal Pond-keeper Scattering Flowers upon the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, King Prasenajit had not yet heard of the Buddha; day and night, during the six periods, he carried incense and flowers to serve the heavenly deities.

When the Buddha appeared in the world and attained perfect enlightenment, he intended to convert King Prasenajit; therefore, he donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and went to the king's residence.

At that time, King Prasenajit saw the Buddha approaching; his radiance was brilliant and dazzling, illuminating heaven and earth, and his majestic demeanor was composed and dignified, standing out preeminent among men. With a heart full of joy, the king invited him to sit and prepared various delicacies for him.

When the offerings were completed, the Buddha preached various teachings for the king; thereupon, the king conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Buddha, abandoned his service to celestial deities, and no longer paid them homage with his heart.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit went three times each day, carrying fragrant flowers to make offerings to the Tathāgata.

Once, after the flower-bearer had presented the flowers to the king and was holding one flower for himself, intending to go to the marketplace, he encountered a non-Buddhist (tīrthika) on the road who asked him:
"Do you intend to sell this flower?"
He replied,
"I wish to sell it.
At that time, the elder Sudatta came to his side again and asked the man once more:
"Take these flowers; do you wish to sell them?
They both replied that they wished to sell.
Then these two masters vied with one another, each doubling the price until it reached a hundred thousand taels of gold, yet they still refused to stop.
At that time, the person carrying the flowers asked the non-Buddhist practitioner,
"For what purpose do you wish to buy these flowers?
The non-Buddhist practitioner replied:
"I shall offer these to Nārāyaṇa to seek his blessings.
He then asked the elder Sudatta,
"For what purpose do you wish to purchase these flowers?"
Sudatta replied,
"To make an offering to the Buddha.
The person carrying the flowers said:
"What is meant by 'Buddha'?
Sudatta replied, "Looking forward, there is no end;
looking back, there is no limit. He is the Honored One within the three realms, whom all devas and people of the world alike revere and honor."
When the flower-seller heard these words, he secretly harbored great joy and thought to himself:

"The Elder Sudatta is composed, discerning, and not impulsive; yet today, for the sake of this single flower, he is willing to pay a price amounting to as much as hundreds of thousands of taels of gold to take it away."
"Now there must be a matter of great benefit; regardless of whether it is noble or lowly, you must certainly obtain it.
At that time, the person carrying the flowers replied to the two masters:
"I am not selling these flowers; I wish to take them myself to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha."

Having heard this, Sudatta was overcome with joy beyond measure. He immediately led the man to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One, whose thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs radiated a brilliance like that of a hundred thousand suns. With profound faith and reverence, he took the flowers he held and scattered them over the Buddha; in mid-air, they transformed into a flower canopy that followed the Buddha wherever he went or stayed.
Having witnessed this transformation, he immediately cast his body down, prostrating with his five limbs touching the ground, and made this great vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from scattering these flowers, may I, in future lives, serve as eyes for sentient beings who are blind and dark;
may I serve as a refuge for those who have no refuge."
For those without protection, he acts as their protector;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberator;
and for those who have not attained nirvāṇa, he causes them to attain nirvāṇa.
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this gardener?

Because he took this single flower and scattered it over me, in a future age, after three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas have passed, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name Puṣpasaṃpanna. He will deliver and liberate immeasurable sentient beings; for this reason, I smile."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
(8) The Story of Two Brahmins Each Vying for Superiority over the Tathāgata The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were two brahmins in that city. One had deep faith in the Buddha-dharma and constantly spoke of all the merits of the Tathāgata, saying that he was the most honored and supreme among the three realms;
the second was deeply attached to false views and claimed that the disciples of the six heretical teachers were likewise the most supreme and without equal.
Thus, amidst such turmoil, they began to contend with one another without ceasing, until the matter reached the ears of King Prasenajit.
The king summoned the two brahmins and asked them the cause of this dispute.
Those who believe in the non-Buddhist teachers say:
"The spiritual powers of those whom we serve, such as Pūraṇa and others, are truly real and superior to those of the śramaṇa Gautama."
The king again asked that follower of the Buddha:
"What supernormal powers does this Śramaṇa Gautama, whom you now serve, possess?
The brahmin replied:
"The śramaṇa Gautama whom I serve possesses extraordinary supernormal powers; there is no one who can equal him.
When King Prasenajit heard these words from the two great brahmins, he addressed them, saying:
"Now you both praise the celestial deity you each serve as being the most supreme."
I shall now wait for you until the seventh day, at which time I will assemble a multitude of hundreds of thousands of people in a level and spacious place to test their spiritual efficacy.
You two, each burn incense, scatter flowers, and sprinkle water, inviting your masters to come to this assembly; we shall together offer them worship.
When the two brahmins had heard the king’s words, they agreed with one another.
On the seventh day, when the king had commanded the populace and they had all assembled, the two brahmins stood before the great multitude and each made a solemn vow.
Those who placed their faith in Pūraṇa immediately took fragrant flowers and pure water, and before the great assembly made this solemn vow:

"If those whom we have honored, such as Pūraṇa and the others, possess supernatural power, let these fragrant flowers and pure water travel through the air to where our Teacher is, so that he may know my heart and come to this assembly;
if they possess no supernatural power, let these fragrant flowers and pure water remain here and not depart."
Having made this vow, they immediately scattered incense, flowers, and pure water; yet these all remained suspended and did not fall to the ground.
When the great assembly witnessed this, seeing that there was no divine efficacy, they said to one another:
"Now Pūraṇa and the others truly possess no supernormal powers; they have falsely accepted our offerings from within the kingdom."
Having spoken these words, those who believed in the Buddha once again took fragrant flowers and pure water before the great assembly and scattered them into the air, making this vow:
"The Tathāgata truly possesses supernormal power; may these scattered flowers and pure water reach the presence of the Tathāgata, and may he know that I have come to this assembly with my own mind."
Having made this vow, he immediately scattered [the offerings] from afar; clouds of smoke and mist spread downward, covering Śrāvastī entirely.
The various flowers thus scattered transformed into floral canopies in mid-air, following the Tathāgata wherever he walked or stayed as they reached above him.
Furthermore, pure water like lapis lazuli was sprinkled from afar upon the ground before the Buddha, arriving there instantly.

At that time, when the great assembly witnessed this transformation, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence; they conceived a profound sense of faith and reverence toward the Buddha and abandoned their service to the various non-Buddhist practitioners.
At that time, having attained his aspiration, the brahmin immediately cast his five limbs upon the ground and made this great vow:
"By the merit of these scattered flowers and sprinkled water, may I become the eyes for sentient beings who are blind and ignorant in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
For those without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberation;
for those without peace, he acts as their peace.
"May those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa be led to attain it.
Having made this vow, the Buddha immediately smiled; from his face, five-colored rays of light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what conditions do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see how that great brahmin has offered me incense, flowers,
and pure water? Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it."

"That great brahmin, in a future age after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, shall attain Buddhahood and be named Acala. He will deliver and liberate immeasurable sentient beings; for this reason, I smile."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
9. The Account of the Buddha Preaching the Dharma and Ordaining Two Kings (IX). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were two kings who were constantly at odds and in conflict with one another, causing much harm to the populace. They plotted against each other day and night without ceasing.
King Prasenajit observed those two kings as they wandered through the cycle of birth and death, fearing it would be difficult to rescue them from within that cycle.
Desiring liberation, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and said:
“World-Honored One!

Now the Tathāgata, the unsurpassed Dharma King, observes those among all sentient beings who suffer from calamities and provides them with protection; amidst strife and contention, he is able to bring about reconciliation.”

Now these two kings are constantly at war with one another, causing much injury and harm; they have harbored enmity for a long time and cannot be reconciled. We only pray that the World-Honored One will harmonize those two kings and cause them to cease their strife.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
Then, on a subsequent day, the Tathāgata donned his robes, took up his bowl, and, surrounded by the bhikṣus, proceeded to the Deer Park in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī.

At that time, those two kings each assembled their armies and were about to engage in battle; however, one was timid and weak, becoming greatly terrified, so he retreated to the place where the Buddha was, went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then spoke these verses on impermanence for the king:
"Even that which is high shall fall; That which is eternal shall come to an end.
All who are born must die; In meeting there is separation."

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the king’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna* and immediately sought ordination before the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His hair and beard fell away naturally, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.

When that second king heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had already delivered his former king and caused him to leave the household life, his mind became serene and he was no longer afraid.

He then came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and listened to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma. Filled with great joy, he immediately requested the World-Honored One [to ordain him], and the Buddha granted his consent.
Returning to his own country, he prepared various delicacies and invited the Buddha and the Sangha. When the meal was finished, he made a great vow before the Buddha:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
To those without protection, he acts as their protection;
to those without liberation, he acts as their liberation;
to those without peace, he acts as their peace.
"For those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa, I shall bring about their nirvāṇa.
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled; from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
“Do you see this King Pañcāla making offerings to me?
Ānanda replied,
“Indeed, I have seen it.”

“Because you have made offerings to me, you shall not fall into the evil realms; you will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans. After three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you shall attain Buddhahood, named Anabhibhūta (Unconquerable), and extensively deliver immeasurable sentient beings. It is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 10.
The Story of the Householder Who Reigned as King for Seven Days. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit and Ajātaśatru were constantly at odds and contending with one another; each assembled the fourfold army—elephant troops, cavalry, chariot troops, and infantry—and they engaged in battle, whereupon King Prasenajit’s entire host was utterly defeated.

Thus, after three battles, his army was utterly defeated; the king alone entered the city, filled with profound sorrow and distress, prostrating himself in shame upon the ground, forgetting both sleep and food.
At that time, there was an elder who possessed immeasurable wealth and treasures beyond calculation. Hearing that the king was distressed, he came to address the king, saying:

"My household has abundant gold, silver, and precious jewels at your disposal; you may use them as you wish to purchase elephants and horses and recruit brave warriors, so that we may go out to battle and defeat those enemies."
"For what reason are you now so sorrowful and distressed?
The king immediately agreed.
He then brought forth a great quantity of precious treasures and presented them to the king, commissioning strong men to travel throughout all lands in search of strategic counsel.
There was a strong man who came to respond to the recruitment; upon arriving at the gate of the Jetavana, he saw two officers discussing military tactics.
One officer said:
"At the vanguard of the formation, station the strongest men first, followed by those of middling strength, and place the weakest last."
Having heard these words, he returned and informed the king, recounting in detail the military strategies discussed by the generals and soldiers.

Upon hearing this, the king immediately assembled his fourfold army; following their counsel, he placed the bravest at the front and the weaker behind. They soon engaged in battle and defeated the enemy host, seizing their elephants and horses. He then captured King Ajātaśatru and, filled with great joy, had him ride together in a carriage adorned with precious feathers and gems. Leading him to the Buddha’s dwelling, he addressed the World-Honored One, saying: “World-Honored One!”
Throughout the long night of time, I have never harbored resentment or envy toward that king, yet he has instead conceived enmity toward me.
However, King Ajātaśatru’s father, the former king, was my close friend; unable to bear taking his life, I now wish to release him so that he may return to his own kingdom.
At that time, the Buddha praised King Prasenajit:
"Excellent, excellent!
To maintain a mind of constant equanimity toward both kin and non-kin is praised by the noble and holy ones."
He then spoke this verse for the king:
"To lose brings grief and fear; to win brings joy and celebration.
If you now release that king, both will experience delight."
"If one can bring an end to victory and defeat, / That is the most wondrous and supreme joy.

When King Prasenajit heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he immediately released Ajātaśatru to return to his own country and returned himself to Śrāvastī, thinking to himself:
"The reason I have achieved victory in this battle is due to that elder who provided me with precious treasures to reward and recruit my generals and soldiers; it is because of this that I have won."
Having formed this thought, he immediately summoned the elder and addressed him, saying:
"It is because of you that I have been provided with precious treasures to reward the brave and strong, and thus achieved victory in battle."
"I shall now repay your kindness; let your wishes be granted as you desire.
At that time, the elder knelt and said to the king, "Grant me fearlessness, and I shall venture to speak what is on my mind."
The king replied immediately,
"I grant you leave to speak.
The elder addressed him, saying:
"I now wish to act on behalf of the King and govern the realm for seven days.
The King immediately granted his permission, fulfilling the Elder's wish; he then had the drum beaten and installed him as king.
He beat the drums and proclaimed the decree so that all within his realm might hear and know it, granting them all freedom.
He then immediately dispatched messengers with an edict to the various minor kings:
"Each of you shall suspend your royal duties for seven days, come to pay court and prostrate before me, take refuge in the Triple Gem, and invite the Buddha to receive offerings."
When the seven days had passed, he was filled with great joy and immediately cast his body prostrate upon the ground, making this great vow:
"By the merit of having served as king for these seven days, may I become eyes for sentient beings who are blind and in darkness in future ages;
may I become a refuge for those who have no refuge."
For those without protection, he acts as their protection;
for those without peace, he acts as their peace;
for those without liberation, he acts as their liberation.
"Those who have not yet attained nirvāṇa, may they be led to attain it.
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled; from his face, five-colored rays of light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Can you now see that great elder acting as king for seven days?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it."

"Because that great elder invited me, in a future age, after three asaṃkhyeya kalpas have passed, he shall attain Buddhahood under the name Most Victorious (Vijaya). He will extensively deliver sentient beings in immeasurable numbers; it is for this reason that I smile."

When the Buddha spoke of this causal account of the elder becoming a king, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some the stage of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some the stage of *anāgāmin*, and some the stage of *arhat*; some conceived the aspiration for *pratyekabuddhahood*, and some conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed *bodhi*.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Chapter Two: Receiving Offerings as a Result of Retribution. 11.
The Story of the Boatman Inviting the Buddha to Cross the Water. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
On the banks of the Airāvatī River there were various boatmen who lived by the river’s edge.
At that time, the Tathāgata, accompanied by his bhikṣus, went to that village, intending to cross the water in order to transform those boatmen.
When these people saw the Buddha arrive, each felt great joy; they boarded their boats to cross the water and went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, saying:
“World-Honored One!
"Tomorrow, you shall deign to board a boat and cross the water.
The Buddha immediately consented.

[The king] then adorned the vessels, leveled the roads, and removed all tiles, stones, filth, and impurities. He erected banners and streamers, sprinkled fragrant water upon the ground, and scattered various exquisite flowers, thus decorating the boats while awaiting the arrival of the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

Then, when the time had come for the following day, the World-Honored One, taking his bhikṣus with him, went to the riverbank, crossed the water by boat, and arrived at that village, where he spread out his seat and sat down.

When the boatmen observed that the assembly was seated, they personally served the various delicacies and food with their own hands; having completed the offerings, they all sat before the Buddha, thirsting for and yearning to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One accordingly preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for them; their minds were opened and their intentions were resolved, such that some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, and some of Anāgāmin, while others even gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, seeing this offering and the crossing of the water, marveled at such an unprecedented event and came forward to address the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did the Tathāgata plant in previous lives?"
"Now there has arisen such spontaneous offerings as well as this crossing of the water.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!"
I shall now explain this to you in detail for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Vipaśyin. Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, he traveled through other lands, teaching and transforming sentient beings.

Upon reaching the bank of a river, there were several merchants carrying precious treasures who had come from another land. Arriving at that riverbank, they saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, together with a multitude of sixty-two thousand arhats; they conceived deep faith and reverence, and approaching the Buddha, they said:
"Do you wish to cross the water?"
The Buddha immediately consented.
Having prepared various delicacies and made offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha, [the king said]:
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will cross ahead; should there be bandits who might seize the robes, bowls, or other necessities of the bhikṣus."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately crossed the water and preached the Dharma in various ways to the merchants. Each of them felt great joy and resolved their minds upon Bodhicitta. He then bestowed a prediction upon the caravan leader:
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood, named Śākyamuni; you will extensively deliver sentient beings beyond all measure."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that caravan leader was at that time, it was I myself.
Those merchants at that time are now these sixty-two thousand arhats."

All this is due to having made offerings to the Buddha at that time; for immeasurable lifetimes, I did not fall into the evil realms, but constantly experienced happiness among devas and humans, until now I have personally attained Buddhahood, and thus devas and humans come to make offerings to me.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
12. The Story of King Mūrdhaja’s Invitation to the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by sixty-two thousand arhats, traveled to the kingdom of Kuvilva.
The people there were by nature virtuous, kind, compassionate, and filial; they were broad-minded and magnanimous. Then the Tathāgata thought to himself:
"I shall now construct a multi-storied lecture hall of ox-head sandalwood to transform these people."

Having formed this thought, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, knowing the Buddha’s mental intention, immediately joined with the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others, each bringing a tree of gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood to present to the World-Honored One. For the sake of the Tathāgata, they constructed a great lecture hall; celestial couches, beds, bedding, and quilts, as well as celestial *sūdā* food, were spontaneously provided to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.
At that time, when the people saw this matter, they marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and each said:
"Now the Tathāgata possesses such great merit and benefit as to have moved the various devas to establish these offerings."
They immediately went together to the place where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for them; their minds were opened and their understanding awakened, such that some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some *sakṛdāgāmin*, and some *anāgāmin*, while others even gave rise to the mind set on unsurpassed *bodhi*.
At that time, the bhikṣus, seeing these offerings presented by the devas as well as the couches and seats, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not know what merit the Tathāgata planted in past lives that has caused the devas to arrange such offerings?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Brahmācarya. Leading a company of bhikṣus, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings until he arrived at the palace of King Dr̥ḍhacūḍa.
Hearing that the Buddha had arrived, he went out of the city to welcome him, prostrating at the Buddha’s feet and requesting of the Buddha and the Sangha:
"Please deign to visit me and accept my offerings of the four requisites for three months. The Buddha immediately consented.
He immediately established a multi-storied lecture hall, providing beds, bedding, and various delicacies, making offerings for three months; he further bestowed a fine robe upon each person.
The Buddha then preached various teachings for the king; with a heart full of joy, the king resolved to attain bodhicitta, whereupon the Buddha bestowed upon him this prediction:
"In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni, delivering immeasurable numbers of sentient beings."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If you wish to know who that King Cūḍābandha was at that time, it was myself. Those ministers at that time are now these sixty-two thousand arhats. Because they all made offerings to the Buddha at that time, they did not fall into the evil realms for immeasurable ages; instead, they constantly experienced happiness among devas and humans until now, when I have personally attained Buddhahood, and thus devas and humans come to make offerings to me."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
13. The Account of King Dharmapāla Inviting the Buddha to Bathe (Thirteen) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were five hundred merchants in that city who traveled to another land to trade and seek profit. As they proceeded along the road, they entered a vast wilderness and lost their way, not knowing where to go.

Encountering the heat of the day, they were so parched with thirst that they were on the verge of death; each knelt and prostrated before the various celestial deities, seeking their blessings, yet none received any response.
At that time, among the merchants, there was one upāsaka who addressed the crowd, saying:

"The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, constantly observes sentient beings through the great compassion of his six periods of the day and night, seeing who is suffering in distress and going to deliver them."
"We now all together, with sincere hearts, invoke 'Namo Buddhāya' to rescue us from this suffering and distress.
When the merchants heard these words, they each raised their voices in unison, invoking "Namo Buddhāya," praying for deliverance from this parching heat and thirst.

At that time, the Tathāgata heard from afar the merchants invoking the name of the Buddha; together with Śakra, Lord of Devas, he immediately went to where the merchants were and sent down a great, sweet rain. Their heat and thirst were dispelled, and filled with joy, they reached their own country, where they invited the Buddha and the Saṅgha. The Buddha then granted his consent.

They erected banners and streamers, hung various precious bells, sprinkled the ground with scented water, scattered exquisite flowers, burned diverse incenses, and prepared a variety of delicacies; then they went to inform the World-Honored One:
"O Sage, please know that the time has come; the meal is ready."
At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and accompanied by the bhikṣus, went to their home and accepted their offerings.

Then, as the merchants thirsted for and yearned to hear the Dharma, the Buddha preached various teachings to them. Their minds were opened and their intentions understood; some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, and some anāgāmin, while others even gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, plant in past lives,
such that these merchants have been moved to provide such offerings and have further attained the fruits of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
In the distant past, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Candanagandha; he, leading a company of bhikṣus, traveled to the kingdom of King Dharmapāla.
At a time when the heavens were parched with drought and the crops had failed, the King, hearing that the Buddha had arrived, led his ministers to welcome the World-Honored One, saying:
"Please accept from me for three months the fourfold offerings."
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
Within that city, he further had a bathing pool constructed for the Buddha and the Sangha to bathe. He then made a great vow:
"By the merit of this act, may Śakra, Lord of the Devas, send down a great rain of sweet nectar throughout Jambudvīpa, nourishing the crops and providing relief to all living beings."
Having made this vow, the heavens immediately sent down rain, and there was no one who did not rely upon its benefits.

He then fashioned eighty-four thousand precious jars to hold the water used for the Buddha’s ablution, bestowing one jar upon each of the eighty-four thousand cities throughout Jambudvīpa, and commanded that stupas be built to enshrine and honor them.
Because he had resolved to attain unsurpassed bodhicitta, Candana Buddha immediately bestowed a prediction upon the king, saying:
"In a future age, you shall attain buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, and you will extensively deliver sentient beings beyond measure."

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: "If you wish to know who that King Dharmapāla was at that time, it was I myself. Those who were his ministers at that time are now these bhikṣus. Because they all made offerings to the Buddha at that time, throughout immeasurable lifetimes they did not fall into the evil realms; instead, they constantly experienced happiness among devas and humans. For this reason, I have now attained Buddhahood, and thus devas and humans come to make offerings to me."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
14. The Circumstances of the Buddha’s Rescue and Deliverance from Illness (14). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, in the village of Nāla, many pestilential spirits were killing the populace; everyone vied with one another to petition the celestial benevolent deities, hoping that the epidemic would gradually be dispelled.
Thus they knelt repeatedly, yet the illness did not subside or heal.
At that time, there was a lay follower (*upāsaka*) in the village who said to the crowd:
"The Tathāgata remains in the world for the benefit and peace of sentient beings; we should together with one mind invoke 'Namo Buddhāya' to seek relief from the affliction of this illness."
When the people there had heard these words, they all simultaneously cried out, “Namo Buddhāya!”:
“We pray only that the World-Honored One, out of great compassion and pity, will shield us from the suffering of this pestilential plague.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, ever moved by great compassion, observed sentient beings throughout the six periods of the day and night. Seeing who was suffering from calamity and distress, he would immediately go to transform and deliver them, causing them to cultivate wholesome dharmas so that they might forever uproot all sufferings.

Seeing that all these people afflicted by the pestilence were simultaneously single-minded in invoking the name of the Buddha to seek relief from the plague, the Tathāgata then led his bhikṣus to that village.

With great compassion, he permeated the populace with his influence and exhorted them to cultivate goodness; thereupon, the pestilential spirits all retreated and dispersed at once, and the multitude was no longer plagued by afflictions.
At that time, the people of the village, seeing that the Tathāgata had brought benefit and peace to the populace, each said:
"We have now received the Buddha's gracious favor and our lives have been saved; tomorrow we shall prepare a feast and invite the Buddha, the World-Honored One."
Having spoken these words, they each went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at his feet, and knelt with their right knees on the ground to entreat him:
"We pray only that the World-Honored One will accept our invitation."

Knowing that the Buddha had granted permission, the multitude returned to their homes, leveled the roads, and removed tiles, stones, filth, and impurities. At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his bowl, and accompanied by the bhikṣus, entered the village.

After receiving their offerings, the multitude of people thirsted for and yearned to hear the Dharma. The Buddha then preached various teachings to them; their minds were opened and their intentions were resolved, such that some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, and some anāgāmin, while others even gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
What merit did you plant in your past lives?"
Thereupon, the people were moved to establish this offering and to eliminate pestilence.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the assembly of bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

In the distant past, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Candrasūryaprabha. He led a company of bhikṣus to the kingdom of King Brahmā, and after receiving the king’s offerings, he knelt for a long time and addressed the Buddha:
"I pray that you will rescue and deliver these masses of people from calamities, epidemics, and illnesses."

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately took the saṃghāṭī robe he was wearing and bestowed it upon the king. The king tied it to the top of a banner, and as they all made offerings together, the pestilence spirits naturally dispersed at once, and no further calamities occurred.
The King was filled with great joy and resolved his mind upon Bodhi; the Buddha then bestowed a prediction upon him, saying:

The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “If you wish to know who that King Brahmā was at that time, it was myself. Those who were his ministers at that time are now these bhikṣus. For this reason, I have now attained Buddhahood, and thus devas and humans come to make offerings to me.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 15.

At that time, Devadatta was extremely foolish, arrogant, and envious; he instructed King Ajātaśatru to establish unlawful regulations and beat the drum to proclaim:
"The common people shall not be permitted to bring offerings to the presence of Gautama."

At that time, there were those within the city who had faith in the Buddha; hearing of this restriction, they were filled with sorrow and wept, their grief and distress so profound that even the celestial palaces trembled and became unsteady.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"By what cause and condition does this palace of mine shake so violently?

He immediately examined himself and saw that King Ajātaśatru had established unlawful regulations, causing the people of that city to grieve and weep, which moved his palace to shake in such a manner.
He immediately came down and cried out in a loud voice,
"I myself shall now provide offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha.
Having spoken thus, he went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the Buddha’s feet, and knelt for a long time to entreat him:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus will accept my offerings for as long as my life lasts.
The Buddha did not grant his request.
He spoke to the Buddha again, saying:
"If you will not accept my lifelong offerings, then please accept them for five years.
The Buddha still did not grant permission.
He spoke to the Buddha once more:
"If we do not accept five years, we shall accept five months.
The Buddha did not permit this either.
Again, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"If you do not accept [the offering] for five months, you should accept it for five days.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.

He then transformed the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove into the Vaijayanta Palace; the beds, couches, and bedding were provided, along with divine *sūdhā* food served in golden vessels. He personally distributed the offerings to the assembly of devas, making offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

At that time, King Ajātaśatru was atop a high tower and saw from afar that the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove resembled a celestial palace; he saw the heavenly Sudhā food served in precious vessels, and saw Śakra, Lord of the Devas, together with the hosts of devas, personally distributing and offering it to the Buddha and the Saṅgha.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, having witnessed this event, immediately reproached himself and, filled with extreme rage, reviled Devadatta:

Having spoken these words, he immediately conceived deep faith and reverence for the Buddha.
At that time, the various ministers came forward and addressed the king, saying:

He immediately commanded the officials to beat the drums and proclaim:

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached various teachings for them; their minds were opened and their intentions were resolved, such that some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some Sakṛdāgāmin, and some Anāgāmin, while others even gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.

Among gods and humans, they constantly experienced happiness, until now they have personally attained Buddhahood; therefore, there are gods and humans who make offerings to me."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The Story of the Gandharvas Playing Music and Praising the Buddha (17). The Story of the Gandharvas Playing Music and Praising the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there were five hundred gandharvas within that city who were skilled at lute-playing; they provided offerings to the Tathāgata through music, song, and dance, never departing for day or night. Their fame spread far and wide, reaching the four quarters.

At that time, in the southern city, there was a gandharva king named Sunanda, who was also skilled at playing the lute and performing music, song, and dance. Within that land, he had no rival; he was arrogant and conceited, with none to equal him.

I have heard that in the north there are gandharvas who are skilled at lute-playing, performing music, singing, and dancing; therefore, I have come from there, traversing various lands and passing through sixteen great kingdoms. Playing a single-stringed lute, they are able to produce seven kinds of musical tones, each of which has twenty-one variations.

At that time, the people, having heard of his lute-playing, music, singing, and dancing, were filled with joy and merriment; intoxicated by their own indulgence and unable to restrain themselves, they followed one another to Śrāvastī, desiring to see the king, pay their respects, and compete in their various skills.
At that time, the deities of the city and the gandharvas addressed the king, saying:

"In the southern lands there is a gandharva king named Sundara, who is exceptionally skilled at playing the lute and performing music and merriment. He is now outside the gate, sending his greetings."

He said, "I have been there for some time and heard from afar that near the King there is a gandharva who is skilled at playing the lute and performing songs, dances, and mirthful plays; therefore, I have come from afar to seek a contest to test our respective skills in lute-playing."
"I pray that Your Majesty will now deign to hear what I have to report.
At that time, King Prasenajit told the gatekeeper to summon him quickly to enter.
They met with the king, each harboring great joy.

The king replied, "I do not fear you;
not far from here, let us go there together now and compete as you wish."

Upon arriving at the World-Honored One’s dwelling, the Buddha, knowing the King’s thoughts, immediately transformed his body, manifesting as the Gandharva King and leading the celestial musician Pañcaśikha; seven thousand in number, each holding a lapis lazuli lute in hand, they attended him on the left and right.

Thereupon, King Sumanā took up a single-stringed lute and played it, capable of producing seven kinds of musical tones. These sounds possessed twenty-one variations, and his playing was so perfectly attuned to the rhythm that it was most pleasing to hear. He caused the great multitude to rejoice, dance, and frolic, becoming so intoxicated and heedless that they could not control themselves.

At that time, the Tathāgata again took up the lapis lazuli lute of Pañcaśikha and plucked a single string; it was able to produce tens of millions of varieties of sounds. Their tones were elegant, wondrous, clear, and lovely; those who heard them danced and laughed, filled with joy and delight, their happiness beyond measure.

At that time, King Śubhavyūha, having heard this sound, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He felt self-reproach and shame for the sounds previously produced by his lute-playing, and immediately submitted himself. Kneeling with palms joined, he said:
"I request you to become my great teacher and further instruct me in the methods of the lute."
At that time, the Tathāgata, seeing that King Subhavyūha had cast off his pride and that his mind was already subdued, resumed his original form, while the assembly of bhikṣus sat in silence.

His heart was struck with awe and his hair stood on end; he immediately conceived deep faith and reverence before the Buddha, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and requested to enter the stages of the Path.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:

His beard and hair fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa; through diligent and earnest practice, before long he attained the fruit of arhatship.

At that time, King Prasenajit, having seen King Subāhu with his mind already tamed and having further attained the fruits of the Path, felt great joy in his heart; he knelt for a long time and invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus.

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Samyaksaṃbuddha. From afar, he beheld the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus sitting cross-legged beneath a tree; their radiance was magnificent, illuminating heaven and earth like hundreds of thousands of suns. Because they all made offerings to the Buddha at that time, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, they did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; instead, they constantly experienced happiness among gods and humans, until now, when I have personally attained Buddhahood, they have offered me this music and have never been separated from it.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
18. The Story of Yathāpraṇihita, Who Sought Ordination from the Buddha While Facing Execution (18). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in that city, there was a foolish man named Yathābhiprāya (As He Wishes), who delighted in killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. “Out of great compassion and pity, please petition the King on my behalf to allow me to leave the household life; then even in death I shall have no regrets.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately granted his consent and addressed Ānanda, saying:

Along the way, he encountered a rishi who, upon seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One—adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns—felt great joy in his heart. When that rishi heard the Buddha’s words, he immediately resolved upon unexcelled bodhicitta in the presence of the Buddha, whereupon the Buddha bestowed a prediction of his future enlightenment upon him.
"In a future age, you shall attain Buddhahood; your name shall be Śākyamuni, and you shall extensively deliver sentient beings beyond measure.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If you wish to know who that rishi was at that time, it was I myself. Because I showed reverence and compliance toward the Buddhas in the past, my words are now received with faith and acceptance; thus I saved those sinners from losing their lives and enabled them to obtain the fruits of the Path."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

The dragon king Elāpattra held up a banner and canopy, covering the crown of the Buddha’s head.

"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Pūrṇamanoratha. Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings until he arrived at the kingdom of King Brahmadatta.
Hearing that the Buddha had arrived, he led his ministers out of the city to welcome him; they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and knelt for a long time, entreating him:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will accept our offerings."
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.

He commanded his ministers to prepare various foods and drinks of a hundred flavors; once the offerings were completed, the Buddha preached the Dharma to the king in various ways, causing him to resolve upon the Bodhicitta.
He then bestowed a prophecy upon the king: "In a future age, you shall become a Buddha named Śākyamuni, extensively delivering sentient beings beyond measure."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

“If you wish to know who that King Brahmadatta was at that time, it was I myself. Because I made offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha at that time, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, I did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. I constantly experienced happiness among devas and humans, until now, when I have personally attained Buddhahood; therefore, humans and devas come to make offerings to me.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

*The Compendium of One Hundred Avadānas*, Fascicle Three.
