Chapter Three: The Prophecy Concerning Pratyekabuddhas. Chapter Three: The Prophecy Concerning Pratyekabuddhas.

(21) The Story of Prince Huasheng Becoming a Pratyekabuddha. The Buddha was in the kingdom of Magadha. Accompanied by his bhikṣus, he traveled by stages until he reached the banks of the Ganges River. There he saw an ancient stūpa that was dilapidated, collapsed, and ruined, with no one to maintain it.
At that time, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What stūpa is this?"
"It has become so dilapidated that no one comes to repair it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now explain this for you in detail.

During this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Brahmadatta who ruled according to the True Dharma. The population was flourishing, and the land was exceedingly prosperous and joyful. There were no wars, military expeditions, strife, calamities, pestilence, or disease; it abounded in elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and other livestock, as well as various precious treasures.
The king alone had no offspring; he prayed and made offerings to the gods and spirits, seeking to obtain a son, yet he could not find one.

At that time, in the king’s garden there was a pond where beautiful lotuses grew. One of these flowers blossomed, and within it sat a small boy in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), endowed with the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics. From his mouth issued the fragrance of the *utpala* lotus, and from all the pores of his body emanated the scent of sandalwood.

At that time, the keeper of the pond reported the matter to the king, who was filled with great joy. He took his queen and concubines to the garden; upon seeing this boy, he could not contain his delight and wished to go forward and embrace him.
The boy then became king and spoke this verse:
“The Great King has always sought [an heir]; Thus I have come to fulfill the wish for kingship.
Because he saw that there were no children, I have now come to be his prince.”

At that time, when the great king, his queen, and the court ladies heard this account, there was none among them who did not rejoice; they immediately took up the young child and returned to the palace to raise him.

As he gradually grew older, wherever he went, lotuses sprang up; from the pores of his body, sandalwood fragrance issued forth. Consequently, they gave him a name, calling him Candanagandha (Sandalwood Fragrance).

At that time, the boy immediately observed the places where his footprints had been and the lotus flowers they produced; seeing that they were fresh and beautiful at first, but soon withered and fell away, he reflected:
"This body of mine shall likewise surely come to such an end."
Realizing in his heart that all things are impermanent, he became a Pratyekabuddha. His body ascended into the void, performing the eighteen transformations, and he soon entered nirvana.

At that time, the great king, his queen, and the palace ladies wailed to the heavens and wept bitterly; they collected his remains, cremated them with perfumed incense, gathered the relics, and erected a stupa to make offerings.
"Therefore, what we see here now is merely that stupa.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did this pratyekabuddha plant in his past lives to receive such a karmic retribution?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Krakucchanda.”
Within that community, there was a householder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation.
When his father passed away, the son and his mother lived separately from one another.

At that time, the son of a wealthy man was deeply addicted to sensual pleasures. Upon seeing a courtesan, he found her most agreeable to his heart; for one night's stay, she required him to pay one hundred pieces of gold. As many years passed, his wealth was completely exhausted and he had nothing left to give. She barred him and would not allow him to stay overnight. He entreated her with great earnestness, praying that he might stay for a single night.
The courtesan said,
"If you can obtain a beautiful flower and bring it to me, I will allow you to stay for one night.
At that time, the son of the elder reflected to himself:
"I have no wealth in my home now with which to buy flowers to give to the courtesan.
Having reflected thus, he thought, "There must be fine flowers within the King’s stupa; I shall steal some and give them to her, so that I may stay the night."

However, the gate of that stupa was guarded by people, so he had no way to approach it directly; instead, he entered the interior of the stupa through a hidden drain, stole some fine flowers to give to the courtesan, and she then permitted him to stay the night.

When daybreak arrived, the man’s body broke out with various malignant sores; he suffered such intense affliction and distress that the pain was beyond description. He summoned skilled physicians to attend to his treatment, who said that *gośīrṣa-candana* must be used to apply over the sores for them to be healed.
At that time, the son of the elder reflected deeply to himself:
"My family has no wealth.
He immediately sold his house and residence, obtaining six hundred thousand gold coins, which he promptly used to purchase ox-head sandalwood.
He obtained exactly six *liang* and immediately applied it to his sores, saying to the skilled physician:
"The ailment I now suffer from is a disease of the mind; can it possibly be cured by treating only the exterior?"
Having spoken these words, he immediately took the six *liang* of powdered gośīrṣa-candana sandalwood he had purchased and entered the stūpa, making this great vow:

"In the past, the Tathāgata practiced various ascetic austerities and vowed to deliver all sentient beings according to their hardships and calamities. Now that my present body has fallen into the count of one more birth, I pray only that the World-Honored One [grant me his protection]!"
“Out of compassion and pity, please remove this affliction of mine.

Having made this vow, he immediately took two *liang* of powdered Gośīrṣa sandalwood—using two *liang* to pay for the price of the flowers and two *liang* as a sincere offering—and sought mercy through repentance. His wound was instantly healed, and from all the pores of his body, the fragrance of sandalwood issued forth.
Having smelled this fragrance, they could not contain their joy and made a vow to depart.

By virtue of this merit, they do not fall into the evil realms; wherever they are born among gods or humans according to their karma, beautiful lotuses arise, and a constant fragrance emanates from all the pores of their bodies.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that son of a householder was at that time who anointed the stūpa with sandalwood, it is this very pratyekabuddha here.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

22. The Story of the Children Offering Flowers to the Buddha (22). The Story of the Children Offering Flowers to the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the bhikṣus, donned his robes and took up his alms bowl to enter the city for alms. Upon reaching a certain alleyway, he saw a woman sitting on the ground in the lane, holding a small child in her arms.
At that time, the young boy saw the World-Honored One from afar and felt great joy in his heart. He asked his mother for flowers, and she immediately bought them for him.
Having received them, the boy went to where the Buddha was and scattered them over the Buddha; in mid-air, they transformed into a flower canopy that followed the Buddha wherever he walked or stayed.
Upon seeing this, the child was filled with great joy and made a solemn vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and deliver sentient beings no differently than a Buddha."

At that time, when the World-Honored One saw this child having made such a vow, the Buddha immediately smiled. From his face, five-colored rays of light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what conditions do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this child here scattering flowers over me?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen him."

“This child has scattered flowers upon me; in a future age, he shall not fall into the evil realms, but will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans. After three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, he will attain Buddhahood under the name Puṣpasaṃpanna (Flower-Abundance), extensively delivering immeasurable sentient beings. It is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
23. The Account of a Woman Throwing a Golden Wheel at the Buddha (23). The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, in that country, there was a merchant leader named Floating Ocean, who, together with various merchants, entered the great ocean to gather precious treasures.

His wife was young and of beautiful appearance; longing for her husband, she brooded in sorrow day and night, wishing for his swift return home. She then went to the abode of the god Nārāyaṇa and uttered this incantation:
"If the god possesses divine power and does not disregard human wishes, let my husband return safely and swiftly. I shall now fashion a necklace of gold and silver to repay the god’s grace;
if he does not return, I shall defile the god’s body with excrement, filth, and foul odors."

Having made this vow, before long, it was fulfilled exactly as he had wished; he returned home in safety and felt profound joy. He immediately commissioned gold and silver necklaces and bracelets, and taking his attendants with him, went to the celestial shrine.
On the road, he encountered the Tathāgata, who was leading a company of bhikṣus into the city of Rājagṛha.

At that time, the woman saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns. Her heart was filled with joy, and she wished to scatter necklaces of gold and silver over the Buddha;
her attendants said to her, "This is not Nārāyaṇa."
He forbade her and would not allow it.

At that time, the woman did not follow his instruction; she instead took her jeweled necklace and threw it over the Buddha. In mid-air, it transformed into a precious canopy that followed the Buddha wherever he went or stayed.
Having witnessed this transformation, he conceived deep faith and reverence; prostrating himself with his five limbs touching the ground, he made this great vow:

"By the roots of goodness and merit from these flower garlands scattered for the Buddha, may I, in a future life, attain perfect enlightenment and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha."
Having made this vow, the Buddha immediately smiled; from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you see this woman now scattering gold and silver necklaces over me?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen her."

"This woman, in a future age, shall not fall into the evil realms; she will experience various joys among gods and humans, and after thirteen kalpas have passed, she will attain Buddhahood under the name Suvarṇacakrāvalambinī (Golden Wheel Necklace). She will extensively deliver sentient beings in immeasurable numbers; it is for this reason that I smile."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 24.
The Story of the Old Woman Suppiyā’s Miserliness (Twenty-four) The Story of the Old Woman Suppiyā’s Miserliness. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in that city, King Prasenajit had a lady of the inner palace named Śyāmāvatī; she was advanced in years, extremely stingy and greedy, took no pleasure in giving, and sat back while eating and drinking.

At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana, wishing to transform her, put on his robes and took up his bowl; by means of his supernormal powers, he leaped forth from the ground and stood before the old woman to beg for alms, but the old woman, filled with anger, refused to give.
When the meal was finished, there remained a single leftover fruit and water from the washing of the vessels; because it smelled foul, she would not eat it.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately begged for it, and the old woman, filled with indignation, promptly gave it to him.
Having attained this, Maudgalyāyana leaped into the air and performed the eighteen miraculous transformations.

When the old woman saw these transformations, her heart was filled with faith and reverence; she returned to the truth and repented. That very night, she passed away and was reborn in the wilderness beneath a tree, where she sustained herself by eating fruit and drinking water.

After some time had passed, King Prasenajit, accompanied by his various ministers, was engaged in the sport of hunting and archery, pursuing a herd of deer. Becoming parched with thirst to the point of death, he saw that tree from afar; hoping for water, he galloped toward it.
Not far from the tree, a flame burst forth, barring them and not allowing them to approach; they could only see a person sitting beneath the tree from a distance.
The king immediately asked from afar, "Who are you?"
"I am beneath this tree.
She then replied, "I was a palace lady of King Prasenajit;

now advanced in years, my name is Shan-ai (Sundarī). Because I did not delight in giving, I have been reborn here at the end of my life. I only pray that the Great King will take pity and compassion on me, provide an offering for me by inviting the Buddha and the Sangha, so that I may escape this wretched and evil body."
The king then asked,
"Can you know whether merit has been generated for you by making offerings?
That person replied:
"If merit is established, it will surely be obtained; Your Majesty shall see this for yourself.
When King Prasenajit heard these words, he commanded his troops:
"Place one man every hundred paces so that their voices may carry to one another, and return to the city to prepare offerings for the Buddha and the Sangha."
"If he obtains this merit, let each of his troops hear my voice; in an instant they shall hear me and know the truth of the matter.
He immediately made the arrangements and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
When the incantation and aspiration were completed, a hundred-flavored meal appeared spontaneously before the person beneath that tree.

King Prasenajit, realizing this was indeed true, immediately conceived deep faith and reverence in the presence of the Buddha. The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 25.
The Story of the Elder Sugandha Inviting the Buddha (25). The Story of the Elder Sugandha Inviting the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Kṣemadhūpa, who possessed immeasurable wealth and treasures beyond calculation; by nature he was virtuous and gentle, and he revered and placed his faith in the Triple Gem.
I constantly reflect to myself:
"This body of mine, as well as all my wealth and treasures, are false and unreal; they are like the moon reflected in water or a mirage in the heat of the sun, incapable of being preserved for long."
Having formed this thought, he went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I wish to provide an offering for the Buddha and the Sangha; I pray only that you will grant me your consent.”
The Buddha immediately gave his consent.
[The householder] returned home, prepared various delicacies, and sent a messenger to inform the Buddha:
"The meal is ready; may the Holy One know the time."

At that time, the World-Honored One donned his robes, took up his alms bowl, and accompanied by the bhikṣus, proceeded to her home. Having accepted her offerings, he departed; she, filled with joy, took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, thirsting for and yearning to hear the Dharma.
The Buddha then preached various teachings for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, whereupon he made this vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha."
After he had made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued rays of five-colored light that circled the Buddha three times before re-entering through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause. I only pray, World-Honored One, [to explain the reason for this smile]."
"Expound and explain this.
The Buddha said to Ānanda:
"Do you now see this Elder Hānxiang (Containing Fragrance) preparing various delicacies to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṃgha?"
Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
“Indeed, I have seen it. “The Buddha said:

‘This great householder, by virtue of the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts for ninety kalpas in future ages. He will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans, and in his final body, he shall attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha named Kṣepagandha (Containing Fragrance). He will extensively deliver sentient beings in immeasurable numbers; it is for this reason that I smiled.’”
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 26.

The Story of the Boatman Ferrying the Buddha and the Saṅgha Across the Water (26) The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Magadha. Accompanied by his bhikṣus, he traveled by stages until he reached the banks of the Ganges River.
At that time, there was a boatman living by the riverbank.
The Buddha said to the boatman,
"Now, for my sake, ferry the assembly of monks across."
The boatman replied,
"Give me the fare, and then I shall ferry you across.
The Buddha told the boatman:
"I am also a boatman; within the three realms, we ferry one another across to emerge from the sea of birth and death—is this not a source of joy?
Just as Aṅgulimāla was once consumed by blazing anger and slaughtered the people, I too have delivered him across to emerge from the sea of birth and death."
Just as with Maṇḍavya, who was extremely arrogant and looked down upon others, I have likewise delivered him across the ocean of birth and death.
Just as with Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, who was excessively foolish and devoid of wisdom, I have likewise delivered him across the ocean of birth and death.
In this manner, I have likewise delivered immeasurable sentient beings across the ocean of birth and death, never once seeking any recompense.
Why is it that you now specifically demand payment from me before delivering others?
At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to him in various ways; however, his mind became even more resolute, and he was unwilling to cross.
Downstream from there, there was another boatman who, upon hearing what the Buddha had said, felt great joy in his heart and came forward to say:
"I shall now ferry the Buddha and the assembly of monks across."
The Buddha immediately consented.
He adorned the boats and summoned the monks to board them.
At that time, some bhikṣus were in the air, some were in midstream, and some were on the opposite shore.

At that time, the boatmen, seeing the Buddha and the Saṃgha manifesting such various supernatural transformations, conceived profound faith and reverence. Exclaiming that it was unprecedented, they paid homage to the Buddha and the Saṃgha. The Buddha then preached the Dharma to them in various ways; their minds were opened and their understanding clarified, and they attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.

At that time, the former boatman who had demanded a high price, seeing that the latter boatman had successfully ferried the Buddha and the Sangha across and witnessing his miraculous transformations, felt deep shame and remorse. He immediately prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground, sought refuge in the Buddha with sincere devotion, repented with all his heart, and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.

[The king] returned home, prepared various delicacies and food of a hundred flavors, and personally served them to the Buddha and the Sangha. Having made the offerings, he took a small seat and sat before the Buddha, thirsting for and yearning to hear the Dharma.
The Buddha then preached various teachings for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, whereupon he made this vow:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from this offering, may I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha."
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued rays of five-colored light that circled the Buddha three times before returning to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see this boatman feeling ashamed and self-reproachful as he prepares an offering and performs repentance?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it."

“That boatman, by virtue of this merit from his repentance and the offering he made, shall for thirteen kalpas in future ages not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. He will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans, and upon receiving his final body, he will attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha named ‘Crossing the Sea of Birth and Death. He will extensively deliver sentient beings beyond measure; it is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
27. The Story of the Maidservant Who Anointed the Buddha’s Feet with Sandalwood Incense (27) The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, in that city, there was a great elder who had a maidservant of a naturally virtuous and kind disposition, who held deep faith and reverence for the Triple Gem.
On one occasion, she went outside the gate for a short while to grind sandalwood paste for her mistress.

Seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, wearing his robes and holding his alms bowl, entering the city with his bhikṣus to beg for food, he felt great joy in his heart. He immediately returned inside, took some sandalwood, and anointed it upon the Buddha’s feet;
by the Buddha’s supernatural power, this fragrant cloud was made to billow and spread, covering the entirety of Rājagṛha.
At that time, having witnessed this transformation, the woman’s faith and reverence redoubled. She immediately prostrated herself with her five limbs touching the ground and made this vow:

"By the merit of this offering of fragrant incense, may I in future lives forever be free from poverty and lowly birth; may I swiftly attain perfect enlightenment and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha himself."
Having made this vow, the Buddha smiled, and from his face issued forth light of five colors, which circled the Buddha three times and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see this elder’s servant girl anointing my feet with sandalwood incense?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen it."

"This servant of the householder has applied sandalwood incense to my feet; by the roots of goodness and merit from this act, for ninety kalpas in a future age, her body shall be fragrant and pure. She shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts, but will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans. Upon receiving her final body, she shall attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha named Candanagandha (Sandalwood Fragrance), extensively delivering immeasurable sentient beings. It is for this reason that I smile."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
28. The Story of the Poor Man Balipratigrāhaka Offering Charred Wood to the Buddha (28). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was a poor man in that city named Badhrika, who sustained himself by working as a gardener for others.
Every day, he would carry a piece of charred wood into the city intending to sell it.
At the city gate, he encountered a manifested person who said to the poor man:
"If you can now take this piece of charred wood and give it to me, I shall bestow upon you food and drink of a hundred flavors."
At that time, the poor man, hearing the words of the transformed person, felt great joy in his heart and immediately gave the wood to him.
The transformed person replied, "Take this wood and follow me as we go; let us go together to the Jetavana Monastery, and I shall give you food."

At that time, the poor man followed him into the Jeta Grove, where he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns. With a heart full of joy, he went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and immediately offered a piece of charred wood to the World-Honored One.

Having accepted it, the World-Honored One planted it in the ground. By means of his supernatural power, he caused this withered wood, in a mere moment, to sprout branches and grow leaves, its flowers and fruits flourishing so luxuriantly and its form so perfectly lovely that it resembled a nyagrodha tree.
The World-Honored One was seated below in the full lotus posture, expounding the sublime Dharma for an assembly of hundreds of thousands of millions of humans and devas.
Upon seeing this, the poor man felt great joy; he immediately cast his body prostrate upon the ground with its five limbs and made this great vow:
"By the merit of this gift of withered wood to the Buddha, may I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha."
Having made this vow, the Buddha immediately smiled; from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see this poor park-keeper who gave me these withered logs?
Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen him."

"That poor man, through the root of goodness and merit from offering me these charred logs with a heart of faith and reverence, shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts for thirteen kalpas throughout future ages. He will constantly experience happiness among gods and humans, and in his final body, he will attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha named Vimala (Stainless). He will extensively deliver immeasurable sentient beings; it is for this reason that I smile."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
29. The Story of Making Musical Offerings to Attain Pratyekabuddhahood (29) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the wealthy and noble elders of that country each adorned themselves, wearing fine garments, necklaces, bracelets, and armlets; carrying fragrant flowers and performing music, they all set out together, wishing to go outside the city to enjoy themselves.
Upon reaching the city gate, they encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who, accompanied by his bhikṣus, had put on his robes and taken up his bowl to enter the city for alms.

At that time, those people, seeing the Tathāgata with his radiant halo, his thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, and his brilliant light shining like a hundred thousand suns, each felt great joy. They came forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, performed music and dance as offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, and each scattered various kinds of flowers they held upon the Buddha; these transformed in mid-air into a canopy of flowers.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he completely covered Śrāvastī.
When the people there saw this transformation, they marveled at such an unprecedented event; they immediately prostrated themselves on the ground with all five limbs and made this vow:

"By the roots of goodness and merit from these performances of music and dance, may we attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and extensively deliver sentient beings, no different from the Buddha."
Having made this vow, the Buddha immediately smiled; from his face, rays of five-colored light issued forth, circled the Buddha three times, and returned to enter through the crown of his head.
At that time, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"The Tathāgata is revered and does not smile without cause.
For what reason and by what condition do you now smile?"
“I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Do you now see these people? Ānanda replied,
"Indeed, I have seen them."

“Because these people have performed the roots of merit through the offering of music and scattered flowers, for one hundred kalpas in future ages they shall not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; they will constantly experience happiness among devas and humans, and in their final bodies they will attain the state of a Pratyekabuddha, all bearing the same name, ‘Wondrous Voice. They shall extensively deliver sentient beings beyond measure; it is for this reason that I smile.”
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
30. The Story of the Robber and the Wicked Slave (30). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in that city, there was a foolish man named Evil Servant (Duṣṭadāsa), who constantly delighted in hiding and lurking in various places to plunder the property of others for his own livelihood.

At that time, there was a bhikṣu dwelling among the burial mounds who sat in meditation and practiced the Path. When the time for the meal approached, he put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

At that moment, an elder saw that the bhikṣu’s deportment was dignified and orderly; faith and reverence arose in his heart, and he immediately went inside his house, took a piece of fine cotton cloth, and offered it to the bhikṣu.
He returned to the cemetery and encountered those thieves; seeing that the bhikṣu was coming with cotton cloth, they demanded it from him, and the bhikṣu gave it to them immediately.
On the following day, they came again and demanded woolen blankets, which he likewise gave to them in turn.
On the third day, the bhikṣu went out to beg for alms and returned to his cell, where he again asked for his bowl.
At that time, the bhikṣu thought to himself:

"I have only this one bowl, which I must use for begging alms to sustain my life; yet this thief demands it without end. Now I shall devise a plan to grant him the Three Refuges and discipline this thief so that he will not come back."
Having had this thought, he spoke to the robbers, saying:
"Wait for me a moment; after I have rested for a short while, I shall give you my bowl.
When the robbers heard these words, they immediately sat down and waited.
The bhikṣu took a rope, spread out a snare, and positioned it facing inward;
he then said to the thief, "I am now utterly exhausted and cannot rise; you yourself must reach your hand in and place it within this opening, and I shall give you the bowl."
Upon hearing these words, the bandit immediately reached his hand inside. The bhikṣu pulled the rope and caught his hand, binding it to the leg of the bed.
The bhikṣu went outside, seized a staff, and beat him while shouting:
"With one blow, you shall take refuge in the Buddha!"
The pain was beyond words, and only after a long time did he revive.
He was rebuked in various ways and further subjected to flogging, [being told]: "For the second strike, you shall take refuge in the Dharma."
The pain redoubled, and he was on the verge of death; after a long while, he revived.
He rebuked himself even more, saying, "For the third time, I shall take refuge in the Saṃgha."
The bandits thought to themselves:
"Now this examination of us reaches to our very marrow; the pain is beyond description. If we do not submit and receive the Four Refuges, we shall surely die."
Having had this thought, he immediately submitted.
The bhikṣu released him, and he ran to where the Buddha was, crying out in a loud voice:

"Now, World-Honored One, you are truly great in compassion! You have commanded the bhikṣus to grant me the Three Refuges; thus I have escaped death. Had I received the Four Refuges, I would certainly have died without a doubt, having no one left to turn to for refuge."

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the hearts of those bandits were ready for subduing, immediately preached the Dharma for them. Their minds opened and their understanding was clarified; they attained the fruit of Srotāpanna and sought ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and dharma robes appeared upon his body; he immediately became a śramaṇa. Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernatural powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations. He was revered and honored by all devas and people of the world.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

Chapter Four: The Birth of the Bodhisattva.
Story Thirty-One: The Circumstances of King Padma Sacrificing His Body to Become a Red Fish. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, when the autumn fruits were ripe, the World-Honored One, accompanied by his bhikṣus, traveled through the villages. They ate various fruits and gourds, which they could not digest; consequently, many suffered from malaria and various other ailments arose, such that they were unable to practice dhyāna, recite the scriptures, or cultivate the Path.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha,
saying: “What merit did the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, cultivate in the past,
such that whatever he consumes is able to be digested without causing any internal ailments or suffering, and his majestic countenance is now even more radiant and lustrous?”
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"I recall that in past lives, I practiced loving-kindness and compassion, prepared medicinal decoctions, and gave them to sentient beings. For this reason, I have obtained the retribution of being free from illness."
"Whatever they eat or consume is all completely digested, and they experience no suffering or distress.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!"
"What were the events of that past life?
We pray that you will explain them for us.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"Listen attentively now! I shall explain this to you in detail.

In the distant past, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Padma. He governed the world with justice; the people were numerous and flourishing, enjoying boundless prosperity and happiness. There were no weapons of war, and no mutual attacks or punishments. Abundant were the elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and other domestic animals, as well as sugarcane, grapes, and various fruits and melons, all of which were sweet and delicious."

At that time, because those people ate excessively out of greed, they were unable to digest their food; various diseases arose, and supporting one another, they came to the king’s presence to seek medicine.

At that time, King Padma saw these sick people and gave rise to a heart of great compassion. He summoned a multitude of physicians and commanded them to compound medicines to bestow upon the populace.
However, the number of the sick became so great that he was unable to provide healing for all.
At that time, King Padma rebuked the physicians, saying:
"For what reason do you now fail to treat the common people, causing them to come to me?
The physicians replied to the king:
"Because our medicinal decoctions were not complete, we did not treat ourselves.
We who are now still afflicted by the suffering of illness cannot even cure ourselves; how much less so others who are ill?"
At that time, King Padma, having heard these words, was deeply distressed and asked the physicians,
"What is lacking?
The physicians replied:
"It must be the flesh and blood of a red fish that can cure this illness.
Although I have now sought them from every physician, none at all can obtain them; for this reason, those who are ill are many, and those who die are numerous."
At that time, King Padma thought to himself:
"Now this red fish cannot be caught with a hook; I shall make a vow to take the form of a red fish in order to treat all the diseases within the bodies of sentient beings."
Having had this thought, he summoned the crown prince and his various ministers, saying:
"I entrust this kingdom to you; govern and transform it well together, and do not oppress the people."

At that time, having heard these words, the crown prince and the various ministers were overcome with grief and choked with emotion; weeping and shedding tears, they were so moved by sorrow that they could not speak, and they stepped forward to address the Great King:
"What lawlessness have we ministers and the crown prince committed that the Great King should utter such words of resentment?"
Then King Padma replied to his crown prince and his ministers:
"Do you not see any grounds for reproach in yourselves at this time?"

However, all the people within this kingdom are suffering from many ailments, and those who die are numerous; it is necessary for them to consume the flesh and blood of the red fish in order for their illnesses to be cured.
Therefore, I now wish to relinquish this body and take the form of a red fish to cure the diseases of the people.
For this reason, I have summoned you all here today to entrust the kingdom to you.

At that time, the Crown Prince and the various ministers, hearing these words from the King, cried out to heaven and wept; overcome with grief and choking with sobs, they stepped forward and clasped the King’s feet, saying:
"By the grace of Your Majesty's compassionate protection, our land has been abundant and joyful, and the people have flourished, allowing us all to survive."
"Why do you suddenly wish to abandon us and depart alone?
At that time, King Padma replied to the princes, "What I am now doing is also for the sake of the people; why do you all so stubbornly obstruct me?"
At that time, the crown prince and the various ministers offered many kinds of admonitions to the king, but they could not make him desist.
Then King Padma took fragrant flowers, ascended a high tower, prostrated toward the four quarters, and made this great vow:
"May I, upon casting off this body, be reborn in the great river of the kingdom of Vārāṇasī as a large red fish; may all those who eat me be cured of their many ailments."
Having made this vow, he threw himself from the top of the tower and immediately passed away, being reborn in that river as a large red fish.

At that time, when the people heard that there was a large red fish in the river, they each brought axes and hatchets, vying with one another to come and butcher it for its flesh and blood; by eating them, their illnesses were all cured.
Wherever he was cut, the flesh immediately grew back again.
In this manner, continuing for twelve years, he gave to sentient beings without a single hair’s breadth of regret or resentment in his heart.
Thereupon, his life ended and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who the King Padma was at that time, it was I myself."

Because he sacrificed his own body and life at that time to sustain sentient beings, throughout immeasurable lifetimes he never suffered from illness, even until now when he has personally attained Buddhahood to deliver and liberate all beings.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
32. The Story of King Brahmadatta Giving Grain to a Brāhmaṇa (Thirty-two) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
Then the bhikṣus came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata now constantly praise the merit of giving as being immeasurable?”
I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What is the matter?
I wish most earnestly to hear it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

I recall that in the past, during immeasurable eons, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta who ruled his kingdom with justice. The population was flourishing and its prosperity was boundless; it abounded in elephants and horses, and cattle, sheep, and other livestock were also exceedingly numerous.
At that time, there was a brahmin in that country who was skilled in physiognomy and divination; he bowed and addressed the king, saying:
"Now, within these borders, a fire-star has appeared. Heaven shall suffer a great drought for twelve full years; the crops will not ripen, and the people will suffer from hunger."
When King Brahmadatta heard these words, he was filled with profound sorrow and thought to himself:
"How shall I sustain these people?"
He immediately commanded the mathematicians:
"Calculate the grain in the granaries and the number of the people; how much does each person receive?
At that time, the mathematicians, having received the king's command, quickly completed their calculations together and found that each person received one *sheng*.
The provisions were sufficient for six years, yet many had died; of the king’s own portion of grain, only two *śī* remained.
A brāhmaṇa arrived later and addressed the king, saying:
"I alone have received no grain and my life hangs by a thread. I pray that Your Majesty will now grant me a small portion of the grain you intend to distribute."
At that time, King Brahmadatta, having heard these words, reflected thus:
"I cannot even endure this slight hunger and thirst now; how much less so in a future life?"
"Throughout immeasurable lifetimes, for the sake of sentient beings, I have endured all manner of sufferings—hunger, thirst, cold, and heat.
Having reflected thus, he immediately reduced his grain by half and gave it as alms to a brahmin.
The sincerity of their response moved the celestial palaces so that they could not remain at rest.
At that time, Śakra, the Lord of Devas, had this thought:
"For what cause and condition are these palaces of mine shaking in such a manner?"
"Could it be that my life is now coming to an end, that such a portent as this has occurred?

Having had this thought, he immediately observed and saw that King Brahmadatta, for the sake of sentient beings during a famine, was able to renounce what is difficult to renounce, thereby causing my palace to shake and tremble in such a manner.
"I shall now go to test whether his virtuous mind is genuine or hypocritical.
He then transformed himself into a brahmin, leaning on a staff, emaciated and with but little life remaining, and approached the palace gate to beg from the king.
The king thought to himself:
"Whether I give this body of mine away or not, it will inevitably return to death.
Having formed this thought, he resolved: "It would be better to proceed with generous giving to benefit sentient beings, so that at death I may have no regrets."
He had only one measure of grain remaining for his own consumption, which he gave to the brahmin.
Having received this grain, the brahmin asked the Great King:
"In the midst of such a famine, you have been able to renounce what is so difficult to renounce; is it for the sake of seeking the state of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin king?"
"Worldly glory and pleasure?
The King immediately replied:

"By the merit of these gifts I now bestow, I do not seek the status of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin, nor worldly glory and pleasure; my wish is that in the future I may attain Perfect Enlightenment and rescue sentient beings from hunger, thirst, cold, and heat."
Having made this vow, the brahmin then praised him, saying:
"Excellent! This is truly unprecedented!"
Returning once more to his form as Śakra, he said: "I pray that Your Majesty now issue a command to the people to prepare the fields for sowing; seven days from now, I shall send down rain."
When King Brahmadatta heard these words, his heart was filled with great joy, and he commanded the people:
"Plow and sow your fields at once; within seven days, rain will surely fall."
At that time, having heard the king’s command, the people each and all together attended to their cultivation of the fields.
When the seventh day arrived, a great and sweet rain fell; all the crops reached full maturity, and the population flourished with boundless abundance and joy.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that King Brahmadatta was at that time, it was none other than myself.
For this reason, I always praise the fruit and retribution of giving as being beyond measure."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
33. The Story of King Śibi’s Plucking Out His Eyes and Giving Them to a Vulture (Thirty-three) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, as the rainy season retreat (varṣā) was drawing to a close and the time for the invitation ceremony (pravāraṇā) had arrived, the bhikṣus gathered regularly during both the spring and autumn seasons to listen to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma.
Among them, some were washing their robes, fumigating their alms bowls, beating, dyeing, and mending their garments; thus, each was occupied with his own affairs.
At that time, among the assembly, there was a bhikṣu named Śiva who was elderly and blind; sitting on the ground sewing his robes, he could not see the needle as he threaded it, and so he cried out:
"Who desires merit?"
"Please sew with a needle for me.
At that time, having heard the bhikṣu’s words, the World-Honored One immediately went to him, took the bhikṣu’s hand, and asked for the needle, wishing to thread it.
At that time, the elderly bhikṣu recognized the voice of the Buddha and addressed him, saying:
“World-Honored One, Tathāgata!

In the past, throughout three asaṃkhyeya kalpas, you cultivated great kindness and compassion, fulfilled the six pāramitās, perfected the bodhisattva practices, severed all fetters and afflictions, and became fully endowed with merit, thereby attaining Buddhahood by yourself.”
"Why do you still seek to acquire merit from me now?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu,
"Because I have not forgotten the habitual practices cultivated since the past, I still cultivate merit through you."
When the bhikṣus heard these words from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What merit did the Tathāgata cultivate in the past under those elder bhikṣus?"
"I pray that you will explain this for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Śibi. He ruled his realm with justice, and the people were numerous, flourishing, and enjoyed boundless prosperity and happiness.

At that time, King Śibi was always fond of giving charity and providing relief to those in want; regarding all manner of wealth and treasures—even his own head, eyes, marrow, and brain—he never begrudged them to anyone who came to beg.
The sincerity of their devotion produced a resonance that shook the celestial palaces, making them unstable in their places.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, had this thought:
"For what cause and condition is my palace shaking so violently?"
"Could it be that my life is now coming to an end?

Having had this thought, he immediately observed himself and saw that King Śibi, being unrelenting toward wealth and treasures, gave everything away to those who came to beg; through the resonance of such pure sincerity, his palace was shaken and all things were unsettled in their places.
"I shall now go to test whether his virtuous mind is empty or real.
He immediately transformed himself into the body of a great vulture and flew to the king, addressing him thus:
"I have heard, Great King, that you delight in giving and do not oppose sentient beings."
"I have now come for this very purpose, seeking something; I only pray, Great King, that you will fulfill my heart's wish.
When the king heard this, he was filled with great joy and immediately replied to the vulture:
"I shall never begrudge you whatever you seek.

The vulture addressed the king, saying, "I have no need for gold, silver, precious jewels, or any other wealth; I require only the king's eyes as my fine meal. I pray that the king will now grant me his two eyes."

When King Śibi heard the words of the vulture, he was filled with great joy; taking a sharp blade in his hand, he gouged out both his eyes to give them to the vulture, enduring the pain without so much as a hair’s breadth of regret.
At that time, the heavens and earth shook in six ways and celestial flowers rained down. The vulture said to the King:
"Now that you have gouged out your eyes to give them to me, do you feel no regret?"
The king replied to the vulture, saying, "I give you my eyes; I truly have no heart of regret.
The vulture said to the king:
"If you have no remorse, what serves as proof?
The king replied to the vulture,
"If I have no remorse in giving my eyes to you now, may my eyes be restored to their former state."
Having made this vow, the king’s two eyes were restored exactly as they had been before.
The vulture then resumed his human form and praised him, saying:
“How marvelous! How extraordinary!”
"It is truly unprecedented!
Do you now intend to renounce what is so difficult to renounce for the sake of seeking the status of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin King, and for the sake of worldly glory and pleasure?
The King replied to Śakra:

"I now do not seek the status of Śakra, Brahmā, or a Cakravartin, nor the worldly glory and pleasures; by the roots of goodness and merit from this gift of my eyes, may I attain perfect enlightenment in a future life and deliver all sentient beings."
Having made this vow, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, returned to his celestial palace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that King Śibi was at that time, it was I myself; and who that vulture was, he is now this aged bhikṣu."
Because at that time he gave his eyes without any reluctance, he attained Buddhahood for himself; therefore, even now, he still cultivates merit upon you and remains without satiety.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
34. The Story of King Sumukha Seeking the Dharma (34). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, with a heart permeated by great compassion, took the unsurpassed, sublime Dharma of the ambrosia attained through all-knowledge and extensively preached it for the sake of the eight classes of celestial and human beings throughout the long night; he never grew weary or fatigued, nor did he give rise to indolence.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the bhikṣus immediately addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do you now proclaim the essentials of the Dharma through the long night without ceasing, yet the Buddha’s body and mind remain entirely free from weariness?"
"How is this so? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Listen well!
I shall explain this for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a kingdom named Vārāṇasī and a king named Sumukha. The king’s crown prince was named Sundarī; that country was prosperous and joyful, and its population was flourishing.

At that time, King Sumukha was intelligent and wise, deeply delighting in the Way and its virtue, and constantly seeking the sublime Dharma. He placed various rare treasures at the crossroads and made this proclamation:
"Whoever possesses the sublime Dharma and will preach it to me, I shall bestow these rare treasures upon them."
Because of his utmost sincerity, the celestial palaces were moved to tremble.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra immediately observed and realized that King Sumukha, out of a profound devotion to the Dharma, had invoked such a response through his refined integrity that it caused this shaking.

He immediately transformed his body into the form of a rākṣasa, with fangs protruding from both jaws and sharp, long claws; famished and terrified, he was most fearsome to behold. He came to the palace gate and cried out:
"I possess a wondrous Dharma!"
When the king heard this, he immediately went out to welcome him and sought to hear the Dharma.
Then the rākṣasa said to the king:
"Although I possess the Dharma, I am currently afflicted by hunger and thirst and cannot preach it."
Upon hearing this, the king immediately prepared various kinds of food and drink and gave them to the rākṣasa.
The rākṣasa replied, "What I eat consists only of warm blood and fresh meat; these hundred flavors are not what I eat."
At that time, the Crown Prince Sūndarī, having heard these words, addressed his father the King, saying:

"The sound of the Dharma is extremely difficult to hear. I now offer my own body to the rākṣasa to be eaten at his will, so that my father the King may be granted the opportunity to hear the sublime Dharma."
When the king heard that the prince had resolved upon such a vast mind as to not spare even his own body or life, he immediately reflected:
"For kalpas beyond measure, I have been bound by affection and wandered through birth and death without end;
now, it would be better for me to hear the Dharma than to hold onto my beloved son."
Having reflected thus, he immediately consented.
At that time, the Prince, having received permission, gave his own body to the rākṣasa.
Having obtained him, the rākṣasa immediately tore the prince apart before the king, leaving him mangled on the ground; he drank the blood and devoured the flesh.
Even after eating it all, he still said it was not enough.

At that time, the king’s consort, seeing her son sacrifice his body to the rākṣasa, and hearing that the rākṣasa had finished eating yet still said he was not satiated, immediately thought to herself:
"If my son can even give up this life and body, how could I not likewise give up my own?"
He then reported everything exactly as he had thought to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king immediately gave his consent.
Thereupon, the king’s consort offered her own body to the rākṣasa.
Having obtained him, the rākṣasa devoured him as before; yet even after he had finished eating, he still spoke of hunger and thirst.
At that time, the rākṣasa then said to the king:
"Now you must offer your own body for my food."
The king replied immediately:
"I do not begrudge this body of mine at all; however, once my life has ended, I shall no longer be able to hear the Dharma.
Therefore, you should first preach it for me now, and only after that will I sacrifice my body to provide food for you."
At that time, the rākṣasa, knowing his sincerity and faith, immediately spoke this verse for the king:
"From craving arises sorrow; from craving arises fear.
One who can detach from affection and love Will forever sever [the bonds] and be without dread."
At that time, after the rākṣasa had spoken these verses, he returned to his form as a Śakra-deva, and the Prince’s wife suddenly appeared before him.

Having heard the Dharma, the King’s faith and reverence redoubled; seeing again that both his wife and the Prince were still alive, his heart was filled with such joy that he could not contain himself.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the King of Fine Face was at that time, it was myself; the prince was the present Ānanda, and the king’s consort was the present Yaśodharā."
In the past, when I was practicing the bodhisattva path, for the sake of seeking the Dharma, I did not begrudge even my most cherished wife and children; how much less could I feel weary today?
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
35. The Story of Prince Brahmadatta Seeking the Dharma (35). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Sudatta, who was by nature benevolent and virtuous, and who revered and placed his faith in the Triple Gem. Day after day he went to the monastic quarters and the vihāra to sweep and clean the stūpas and temples.
Furthermore, on another occasion, as the World-Honored One was occupied with various affairs and happened to be away, he had not swept that stupa and temple.

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by Mahāmaudgalyāyana, Śāriputra, Mahākāśyapa, and others, entered the stupa. Having finished sweeping, he withdrew to sit at one side and, for the sake of the bhikṣus, spoke of the five merits gained from sweeping the ground:

first, one removes the defilements of one's own mind; second, one also removes the defilements of others; third, one eliminates arrogance; fourth, one tames the mind; and fifth, one increases merit and attains rebirth in a favorable realm.

At that time, the elder Sudatta, returning from his journey, arrived at the vihāra and heard the Buddha, the World-Honored One, preaching to the bhikṣus on the merits obtained from sweeping the ground. With a heart full of joy, he stepped forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I have now heard the Buddha speak of these five kinds of merit from sweeping the ground; wherever one practices this, it is as if a worthy sage were present before my very eyes."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Sudatta:
"All wholesome dharmas that I love and revere are likewise so.
Listen now attentively!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta who ruled and transformed his realm through the True Dharma; the people were flourishing and enjoyed boundless abundance and happiness.
At that time, the King’s consort perceived that she was pregnant; naturally, a precious canopy appeared above her head, following her wherever she walked or sat.
The King summoned a physiognomist to examine the consort's features.
The physiognomist, having observed him, said:
"Once this child is born, he will possess great merit and virtue; he shall surely seek the Dharma by traveling in all four directions.

Thereupon, when the lady’s ten months were complete, she gave birth to a crown prince who was exceptionally handsome and rare in the world; they therefore established a name for him, calling him Dharmaparyeṣin (Seeker of the Dharma).

As he gradually grew older, his heart took delight in the Way and its teachings; he immediately sent men again, carrying precious jewels to search in all directions, yet they were utterly unable to find it.
He wept and wailed in distress, unable to find peace for himself.
The response of his sincerity caused the palace of Śakra to tremble, making it unstable in its place.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of Devas, thought to himself:
"For what cause and condition does this palace of mine shake so violently?"

He then observed for himself and saw that the Prince was seeking the Dharma with such distress that he could not attain it at all; for this reason, he wept and wailed, moving my palace until it shook in such a manner.
"I shall now go to test whether his virtuous mind is genuine or not.
He then immediately manifested as a brahmin, went to the palace gate, and proclaimed:
"I possess a sublime Dharma; whoever wishes to hear it with joy, I shall explain it for them."

At that time, the Crown Prince, hearing the messenger’s words, was overcome with joy beyond measure; he immediately went out to welcome him, prostrated at his feet in greeting, and led him to the palace hall. There he prepared an excellent seat and invited the messenger to sit, then joined his palms and said:
"I pray only that the Great Master..."
"Out of compassion and pity, please explain this for me.
Then the brahmin replied to the prince:
"The study of the Dharma is extremely difficult; one can only come to know it by following a teacher for a long time."
"Now, how can you simply wish to hear it?
Such a principle is not possible.
Then the Prince addressed the Master, saying:

"If you have any needs, please inform me; as for myself, my wife and children, elephants, horses, and precious treasures—all are fully provided, and I shall never be stingy, but will surely supply them to you."
The brāhmaṇa said:

"As you have stated, I do not require any of it at all; however, if you can now dig a great pit ten fathoms deep, fill it with fire, and cast your own body into it, only then shall I grant you the Dharma."
At that time, having heard these words, the Prince felt great joy in his heart; he immediately had a large pit dug and filled it with fire, intending to throw himself into it.
At that time, the king’s consort and the various ministers came quickly to embrace him, advising and consoling the prince, and addressing the brahmin:
"We pray only that you, Great Master!..."
Out of compassion and pity, for our sake, do not cause the Prince to throw himself into this fire pit.
Whatever you may require—whether the kingdom, cities, precious treasures, or even his wife and children—we shall provide them all to you.
The brāhmaṇa said:
"I do not coerce you; it shall be according to the prince's own will. If you can act in this manner, I shall preach the Dharma for you.
When the prince heard these words, he spoke as follows:
"Throughout kalpas of vast eons, I have squandered my body and life in vain; never before has anyone been willing to preach such a sublime Dharma for my sake.
Thinking this, he immediately wished to throw himself down.

At that time, the king’s consort and the various ministers, observing his sincere resolve that he must surely throw himself [into the pit], immediately dispatched a messenger riding an eight-thousand-li elephant to proclaim throughout all of Jambudvīpa: "Let all the great ministers assemble quickly and go to the prince's location; with palms joined, they shall admonish and entreat him:
'For our sake, do not throw yourself into this pit! Do not now, for the sake of one person, abandon us all.'"
Then the Crown Prince replied to the ministers, saying:

"Throughout countless cycles of birth and death, whether in the realms of hell-beings, animals, or hungry ghosts, we have repeatedly slaughtered one another, been burned by fire and boiled in cauldrons, and suffered the hardships of hunger and thirst beyond measure in a single day. The pain was unspeakable, and we have squandered our lives and bodies without ever having benefited the Dharma."
"How can you all now offer me such counsel?
For the sake of seeking the path to unsurpassed bodhi, I shall cast away this foul body and life, vowing to deliver sentient beings from the sea of birth and death."
Having spoken these words, he was determined to throw himself [into the fire] and addressed the brahmin, saying:
"I only pray, Great Master!
First explain the Dharma for me; if my life should end, I will not have the opportunity to hear the teaching."
At that time, the brahmin spoke this verse for the crown prince:
"Always practice a heart of loving-kindness, Eliminating thoughts of anger and malice;
With great compassion and pity for sentient beings, You shed tears of sympathetic sorrow."
"One who practices great compassion, sharing with others the Dharma they have attained themselves to rescue and protect all living beings, truly accords with the conduct of a Bodhisattva.
At that time, having heard these verses, the Prince was overcome with joy beyond measure and immediately cast himself down.

The great pit of fire was transformed into a pond of lotuses; the Prince sat upon a lotus flower therein, while the earth shook violently and a rain of celestial flowers fell, accumulating up to his knees.
At that time, the brahmin returned to his original form as a Śākya and praised the prince, saying:
"In the midst of this fire calamity, you have not spared your own life for the sake of this single verse; what vow do you seek to fulfill?"
The Prince replied,
"I seek the Great Way of Unsurpassed Bodhi to deliver sentient beings and enable them to emerge from the sea of birth and death.
When Śakra heard these words, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and returned to the heavens.

At that time, King Brahmadatta and his ministers, seeing such extraordinary wonders in the crown prince, marveled at this unprecedented occurrence; there was none among them who did not rejoice, and they escorted the prince back to the palace.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"If you wish to know who that King Brahmadatta was at that time, he is now King Śuddhodana; she who was his mother at that time is now Queen Māyā; and the prince of that time was none other than my own self."

When the Buddha spoke of these causes and conditions for seeking the Dharma, there were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; there were those who resolved to become Pratyekabuddhas, and there were those who resolved upon unsurpassed Bodhicitta.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 36.

The Story of the Brahmin Who Demanded a Debt from the Buddha (36) The Story of the Brahmin Who Demanded a Debt from the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by his bhikṣus, entered the city to beg for food. Upon reaching a certain alleyway, he encountered a brahmin who drew lines on the ground with his finger, blocking their path and refusing to let them pass, saying:
"You must now give me five hundred gold coins; only then will I allow you to pass.
If you do not give them, I will not permit the Buddha to pass."
At that time, the World-Honored One and the bhikṣus remained silent and stood still, unable to proceed further.

This report reached the ears of the sovereign King Bimbisāra, as well as King Prasenajit, the Śākyas of Vaiśālī, Pūrṇa, and others; each brought various precious gems and diverse wealth to offer to the brāhmaṇa, yet he refused to accept them.

At that time, the elder Sudatta heard that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, had been hindered by a brahmin who stood in his way and would not depart. He immediately took five hundred gold coins and gave them to the brahmin, whereupon the brahmin allowed the Buddha to pass.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed these events, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions have such obstacles and hindrances arisen, preventing the Buddha from passing through?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.”

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta. At that time, the king’s crown prince, whose name was Sujāta, was out enjoying himself with his kinsmen and friends on an excursion.
On the road, he encountered a man who was gambling with the son of a minister at *chupuru* (backgammon), wagering five hundred gold coins.
At that time, the minister’s son had lost five hundred gold coins to the gambler; when the man immediately demanded repayment of the debt, the son refused to pay it.
At that time, the Crown Prince said to the jester,
"If he does not give it back, I shall pay it in his stead.
Later, however, the minister's son, relying on his own power and influence, ultimately did not repay the debt.
"From that time onward, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, this man has constantly been a gambler who has sought debts from me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the prince was at that time, it was I myself. The son of the prime minister at that time is the present Elder Sudatta. The gambler at that time is the present brāhmaṇa."
"Therefore, you who owe a debt must not act with insolence or presumption and fail to repay it; even until you attain Buddhahood, you shall not escape this difficulty.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

37. The Circumstances of the Buddha’s Passing into Parinirvāṇa and His Delivering of the Five Hundred Mallas (37). The Buddha was staying between the twin śāla trees at Kuśinagara, on the verge of entering parinirvāṇa.

At that time, Subhadra, hearing that the Buddha, the World-Honored One, was about to enter nirvana, led five hundred strongmen to the place where the Buddha was. He prostrated before the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to stand to one side, and requested to enter the Path.
The Buddha then addressed him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma to them in various ways; their minds were opened and their understanding clarified, and each attained the fruit of the Path.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having witnessed these events, addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What merit did these five hundred followers of Subhadra plant in their past lives,
that amidst such urgent distress they were able to receive deliverance when the Buddha was about to enter parinirvāṇa?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only now that he has received deliverance amidst calamity and distress; in past lives as well, I delivered him and freed him from all such misfortunes.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!"
"In past lives, how did you deliver them?
We pray that you will explain this for us.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain this to you in detail.
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta. He took his subjects out of the city to hunt."
Arriving at a mountain valley, there was a great river where I encountered a herd of five hundred deer and intended to hunt and shoot them.
At that time, I was the king of those deer.
As the encirclement drew near, the deer were on the riverbanks; panic-stricken and terrified, they fled toward the river.
At that time, the river water was deep and bottomless, impossible to cross by leaping. As the encirclement closed in further, their lives hung by a thread.
Then that deer king said to the deer:
"For your sake, I shall extend my four legs and place them on both banks of the river; you deer may step upon my back and cross over to the other shore."
At that time, having heard these words, the deer rushed forward together to cross; they trampled upon the back of the Deer King until it was completely broken, causing pain beyond description.
At that time, when all the deer had finished crossing, there was only one doe leading a fawn who, wandering in agitation and filled with terror, was at the very rear.
Seeing her behind him, the Deer King endured his exhaustion and suffering, waiting for her to cross; he then passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"At that time, while I was among the animals, I still gave rise to compassion and, undaunted by weariness or suffering, delivered sentient beings;
how much more so now that I have transcended the three realms and am sovereign and unimpeded—could I possibly feel any fatigue?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who the king of deer was at that time, it was I myself; those who were the herd of deer at that time are now the five hundred bhikṣus, including Subhadra."
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What merit did Subhadra and the other five hundred bhikṣus plant in their past lives,
such that they encountered the World-Honored One and each attained the fruit of the Path?”
The Buddha addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you.”
In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa.
At that time, there were five hundred bhikṣus dwelling in mountain forests, practicing meditation and cultivating the Path, yet they had not yet attained the fruits of the Way.
At that time, when Kāśyapa Buddha had completed his work of transformation and his conditions for teaching were exhausted, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
Yet, the bhikṣu did not perceive this at all.
The tree spirits, knowing that the Buddha was about to enter nirvāṇa that very day, felt deep distress; they wept and shed tears, which fell upon the crown of the bhikṣu’s head beneath the trees.
At that time, the bhikṣus each asked the tree deity,
"For what reason are you now weeping so profusely?
The tree deity replied:
“World-Honored One Kāśyapa!
You are now about to enter nirvana.
For this reason, my heart is filled with anguish, and I weep in this manner.”

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard the words of the tree spirit, their hearts were struck with alarm and their hair stood on end; filled with anxiety and fear, they addressed the tree spirit, saying:
"By what means may we now obtain the opportunity to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One?"
"We must cross over first; we cannot bear to see the Buddha enter parinirvāṇa before us.
The tree deity replied, "If you wish to go now, each of you should close your eyes; we, the tree deities, can lead you to the presence of the World-Honored One."

When the bhikṣus heard these words, they immediately closed their eyes; before they knew it, they had suddenly arrived at the place where the World-Honored One was. They repented of their transgressions and each attained nirvāṇa.
"This was entirely because they left the household life and maintained the precepts at that time; thus, they have now encountered me and attained the realization of the fruits of the Path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who those five hundred bhikṣus were at that time, they are these very five hundred Malla bhikṣus, including Subhadra and the others."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
38. The Story of the Hare Who Offered His Body as Fuel for an Ascetic (38) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Bhadrika who left the household life to enter the path; however, his mind always delighted in the affairs of lay life, and thus he neglected all three karmas.
At that time, the Tathāgata, observing that the roots of merit of this Bhaṭṭika were already matured and that he was ready to be transformed by him, addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Go and summon that bhikṣu Bhaṭṭika; let him come to where I am."
He immediately went to summon him.
The Buddha instructed Bāḍhi:
"You should go to the mountain forests and among the trees to practice the wholesome Dharma."
He immediately accepted the Buddha’s teaching and went into the mountain forests, where he sat in meditation and practiced the Path. Before long, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
When the bhikṣus witnessed this event, they came forward and said to the Buddha:
“What merit did this bhikṣu Utpala plant in his past lives?”
"Although he has left the household life, he constantly delights in worldly attachments;
yet, having encountered the World-Honored One, he has attained the fruits of the Path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"It is not only today that I have been able to transform him;
in past lives as well, I transformed him.
At that time, the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“I do not understand, Blessed One!
What was the matter in a past life?
At that time, the Blessed One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain this to you in detail.

In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a rishi who dwelt among the mountain forests, subsisting on fruit and drinking water as he practiced the way of the rishis. After many years had passed, he encountered a severe drought during which fruits and flowers did not flourish; driven by hunger and thirst, he intended to enter a village to beg for food so that he might sustain his life."

At that time, there was a hare-king who was a bodhisattva; accompanied by his fellow hares, he followed the course of water and grass. As they traveled together, they saw this long-bearded rishi, who, driven by hunger and thirst, was about to enter a village to beg for food so as to sustain himself. The hare-king then stepped forward and said to him:
