"Please accept from me tomorrow a small, humble offering, along with an excellent Dharma which you may listen to and receive."
Having heard this, the seer thought to himself:
"Perhaps that rabbit king will encounter a bird or beast whose life has come to an end and provide it as food for me."
He immediately granted his permission.

Then, the hare-king, knowing that the rishi had consented, gathered all the hares along with the rishi and proclaimed the sublime Dharma. He then took up firewood with his own hands, piled it upon the ground, lit the fire himself, and cast his body into the great flames.
Then that rishi immediately went forward and embraced him;
his impermanent life had already passed into the next world.
The rishi cried out:
"Upādhyāya, Great Master!
Why have you suddenly turned your back on me today and abandoned me?
I shall no longer hear the Dharma."
Overcome with grief and choking with sobs, he cried out to heaven and wept; fainting and collapsing to the ground, his sorrow was such that he could not speak.
At that moment, the earth shook violently, and the heavens rained down exquisite flowers that covered the hare king.
At that time, the seer, seeing that the rabbit king had cultivated great compassion, did not dare to eat him; he gathered his remains, erected a stupa, and made offerings to them.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that Bodhisattva rabbit king was at that time, it was I myself. The seer of that time is now the bhikṣu Udayin."
"All this is because at that time they followed my words and came to listen to the Dharma; thus, they have now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
39. The Story of Prince Dharmapāla Being Killed by His Mother (39). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, Devadatta was foolish and lacked wisdom; constantly harboring jealousy, he directed anger and verbal abuse toward the World-Honored One, yet the Tathāgata never harbored a heart of resentment toward Devadatta.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen this matter, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What is the meaning of this?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
“It is not only today that I have been reviled by him; in past lives as well, he constantly abused me with foul language, yet I always endured it.”
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We wish and desire to hear an exposition and explanation concerning the past.
At that time, the World-Honored One told the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you.
In this Bhadrakalpa, there was a king in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī named Brahmadatta. He ruled with the True Dharma; the people were flourishing, and their prosperity and joy were boundless.”
He had two consorts: the first was named Bhadrayāśas and the second was named Subhadrayāśas.
The senior consort was of a gentle and compliant nature, who was exceedingly well-suited to the king’s heart, yet she had no offspring.

The second queen had but one son, who was intelligent, compassionate, and kind, and was filial toward his parents; the king loved him dearly and sent him to the schoolhouse to study and recite the scriptures.
The Senior Queen went out of the city for recreation and amusement, enjoying herself with delight; she took some wine and food and sent them to the Second Queen within the city.
The Second Queen became enraged and reviled her with harsh words:
"I would rather pierce your son, the Prince, in the throat and drink his blood than ever drink the wine sent by the King."
The messenger returned in haste and reported the situation to the king.
Upon hearing these words, the king again gave rise to anger; he immediately dispatched someone to deliver the prince to him, testing whether he was capable or not.
When the lady had received it, she immediately intended to stab her throat. The prince returned home and, with palms joined toward his mother, said:
"I am without fault or transgression; why do you treat me thus?"
The mother replied to her son, "Your father commanded that you be killed; it was not my fault.
Having heard these words, he immediately turned toward his mother and repented for his transgressions.
His mother would not listen and immediately stabbed him to death.
By virtue of this wholesome mind, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
At that time, I was still an ordinary person; though I was killed by my mother and subjected to her insults, I harbored no resentment in my heart.
"How much more so now that I have transcended the three realms—how could I not give rise to compassion for Devadatta?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know, the king's one son at that time was none other than myself; the mother at that time is now Devadatta."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus were filled with a mixture of sorrow and joy; they paid their respects and withdrew.
40. The Story of the Robber Lūḍha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a bandit in that city named Raudra, who wore a sharp sword at his waist and carried a bow and arrows in his hands; he waylaid people along the road to plunder their property for his own livelihood.
After several days had passed, driven by hunger and thirst, he saw from afar a bhikṣu walking with his alms-bowl toward the foot of a tree. He thought to himself:
"There must surely be food and drink in that man's bowl; I shall go there now and seize it to eat.
If he has finished eating, I shall slit open his belly and devour him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately hurried toward them; when they were not far away, he paused for a moment.

At that time, the bhikṣu perceived the thieves' intention and thought: "If I do not call out now, they will surely kill me, thereby increasing their karmic guilt and causing them to fall into the three miserable realms;
it would be better to call out first and offer them food and drink."
Having formed this thought, he immediately called out from afar:
"Come quickly! I shall give you food.
The thief thought to himself:
"This bhikṣu, knowing from afar that I was hungry, called me to give me food.
He immediately came forward; having eaten that rice, I was fully satisfied and my heart was filled with joy.

At that time, the bhikṣu immediately expounded various sublime dharmas for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of srotāpanna. He then sought ordination, practicing with diligent application, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and endowed with the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
Compiled Avadāna Sūtra, Volume Four;
Compiled Avadāna Sūtra, Volume Five.
Translated by the Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Yuezhi during the Wu Dynasty.
Chapter Five: The Chapter on Hungry Ghosts (5).
Story Forty-one: The Circumstances of Pūrṇika’s Fall into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts. The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, when the Venerable Śāriputra and Mahāmaudgalyāyana were about to take their meal, they first surveyed the realms of hell, animals, and hungry ghosts, and only then did they eat.
The reason for this was that he wished to cause sentient beings to feel weary of and detached from birth and death, and to seek after nirvana.

At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw a hungry ghost whose body was like a charred pillar, its belly like a great mountain, and its throat like a fine needle. Its hair was like awls and knives, piercing and entangling its body; from all its joints and limbs, flames issued forth. It groaned and cried out loudly, running in the four directions, seeking excrement and urine as food and drink, yet it exhausted itself all day long without being able to obtain any.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw this hungry ghost and went forward to ask him,
"What karma did you create to undergo such suffering?
The hungry ghost replied:
"Where there is the sun, there is no need for lamps or candles; since the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is currently present in the world, you may ask him yourself.
I am now hungry and thirsty, and cannot answer you."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately went to where the Buddha was, wishing to ask the Tathāgata about the karmic actions he had committed to receive such suffering.
At that moment, the World-Honored One was in the midst of the great assembly, expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of devas and humans; seeing Maudgalyāyana enter, he immediately asked him:
"What extraordinary matter have you seen today?"
Maudgalyāyana replied,
“I saw a hungry ghost with a body completely scorched, running back and forth from east to west.
He then related the matter in full detail to the Buddha.
"What evil karma did he create to undergo such suffering?
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Maudgalyāyana:
"Listen well now!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

During this Bhadrakalpa, in the city of Śrāvastī, there was a householder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he would constantly have his servants press sugarcane juice to deliver to his master.
There was a pratyekabuddha who suffered greatly from a disease of thirst; a skilled physician prescribed medicine, saying that by drinking sugarcane juice his illness would be cured.

At that time, the pratyekabuddha went to the house of a householder to beg for sugarcane juice. When the householder saw his dignified demeanor and noble bearing, he conceived deep faith and reverence, and asked him:
"What do you require?"
The Pratyekabuddha said, "I am suffering greatly from thirst and require sugarcane juice; that is why I have come to inform you.
Upon hearing this, the elder’s heart was filled with joy, and he immediately commanded his wife, Punnāgī:
"I have an urgent matter and must certainly go out.
You remain here for now and prepare sugarcane juice to offer to the Pratyekabuddha.
At that time, the wife replied:
"Simply go out; I shall give it to you later.
After her husband had gone out, she took the Pratyekabuddha’s bowl and, in a secluded place, urinated into it, covering the bowl with sugarcane juice before giving it to the Pratyekabuddha.
Having received it, the Pratyekabuddha immediately realized it was not [proper food], threw it away on the ground, and returned with his bowl empty.
Later, when his life ended, he fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*), where he was constantly tormented by hunger and thirst.
"Due to these karmic conditions, he undergoes such suffering.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"If you wish to know who that householder’s wife was at that time, she is now this hungry ghost Pūrṇaka."

When the Buddha had spoken this account of the hungry ghosts, the bhikṣus abandoned stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhat; some conceived the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some conceived the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 42.

The Story of the Wife of the Householder Bhadra Falling into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts (42). The Story of the Wife of the Householder Bhadra Falling into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts. The Buddha was staying on Vulture Peak Mountain near Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was sitting cross-legged beneath a tree, contemplating and observing. He saw a hungry ghost whose body was like a scorched pillar, its belly like a great mountain, and its throat like a fine needle. Its hair was like awls and knives, entangling its body; from all its joints and limbs, flames blazed forth. It groaned and cried out loudly, running in the four directions, seeking filth and excrement. Day and night it suffered until it was utterly exhausted, yet it could never find any.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana saw this hungry ghost and asked him,
"In your previous life, what karmic actions did you perform to undergo such suffering?"
The hungry ghost replied:
“There is a Tathāgata in the world; you may ask him yourself.
I am now hungry and thirsty and cannot answer you.”
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling and asked about the cause of his situation:
"What karmic actions did he perform to undergo such suffering?
Thereupon, the World-Honored One told Maudgalyāyana:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain this for you.

In the distant past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a land named Vārāṇasī; its territory was prosperous and joyful, its people were numerous and flourishing, and there were no weapons of war or mutual strife."
At that time, there was an elder named Bhadra, whose nature was gentle and mild; he revered and had faith in the Triple Gem, always delighted in giving charity, and his fame was widely renowned.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu who, having put on his robes and taken up his bowl, went to that house to beg for food.
At that moment, the elder had some minor urgent business and did not personally offer anything; he immediately departed, earnestly instructing his wife:
"While you remain behind, take good care to provide that bhikṣu with food and drink."
His wife replied, "Do not worry;
I shall give it to you later.
At that time, a spirit of stinginess and greed arose in the householder’s wife, and she thought to herself:
"If I give them food now, they will come again the following day.
These people are truly loathsome to behold.
He immediately summoned the bhikṣus, brought them into his house, and locked them in an empty room, ensuring that they would not receive food that evening.
"Due to these karmic conditions, for immeasurable lifetimes, she fell among the hungry ghosts and underwent such suffering.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"If you wish to know who that householder’s wife was at that time, it is this very hungry ghost here."
"Therefore, you all should diligently practice giving; do not be attached to stinginess or greed, and you should train yourselves in this way.

When the Buddha had spoken these words concerning the karmic conditions of the hungry ghosts, those present in the assembly abandoned stinginess and greed and grew weary of birth and death. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat. Some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 43.
The Story of Falling into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts Due to Holding Evil Views and Refusing to Give Water (43). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana was beneath a tree when he saw a hungry ghost (preta). Its body was like a charred pillar, its belly like a great mountain, and its throat like a fine needle. Its hair was like awls and knives, piercing and lacerating its body; all the joints of its limbs were ablaze with fire. Emaciated by thirst and on the verge of death, its lips and mouth were parched and withered as it rushed toward rivers and springs, only for the waters to dry up before it. Even if sweet rain were to fall from the heavens, once it touched its body, it would all turn into fire.
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana stepped forward and asked,
"In a previous life, what karmic actions did you perform to undergo such suffering?
Thereupon, that hungry ghost replied to Maudgalyāyana:
"I am now parched with thirst and suffering from hardships beyond reckoning; I cannot answer you, so you should ask the Buddha yourself.
Thereupon, Mahāmaudgalyāyana went at once to the place where the Buddha was, wishing to inquire about this matter.

At that time, as the World-Honored One was expounding the sublime Dharma for the great assembly, he saw Maudgalyāyana approaching. Anticipating his arrival, he greeted him with words of affection and gentleness, asking:
"What extraordinary thing have you seen?"
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha,
“Just now, beneath a tree, I saw a hungry ghost whose body was scorched and who was running in all directions.
He then related the preceding events in detail to the Buddha.
"What karma did he create in his previous life to undergo such suffering and distress?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Listen attentively now!"
I shall now explain this to you in detail.
During this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha named Kāśyapa. At that time, there was a śramaṇa traveling along a road who suffered greatly from heat and thirst.
At that time, there was a woman named Duṣṭadṛṣṭi who went to a well to draw water and begged for some.
The woman replied to her, "Even if you die of thirst, I can never give you any water; it would cause my own supply to diminish, and I cannot take it away from myself."
At that time, the śramaṇa, having failed to obtain water, departed by the same path he had come.
Then that woman became even more stingy and greedy; whenever anyone came to beg, she never gave anything away.
Thereafter, when her life ended, she fell among the hungry ghosts; due to these karmic conditions, she undergoes such suffering.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
“If you wish to know who that woman was who did not give water at that time, it is this very hungry ghost.”

When the Buddha had spoken these conditions regarding evil views, the bhikṣus abandoned stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhat; some gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
44. The Story of Paṇḍara Falling into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts Due to the Stench of His Body (44) The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, when the hour for eating had arrived, the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana put on his robes, took up his bowl, entered the city to beg for food, and returned to his dwelling.
Having finished his meal and set aside his robes and bowl, he sat cross-legged beneath a tree and entered into samādhi.
He saw a hungry ghost whose body was so extremely foul-smelling that it was absolutely impossible to approach.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately asked him:
"What karma did you create to receive this physical form, which is so foul as to be unapproachable?"
The hungry ghost replied, "You should ask the Buddha yourself; he will explain it for you.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
“World-Honored One!
It is the constant law of all Buddhas to first inquire with kind intent:
“What extraordinary matter have you seen this day?”
Maudgalyāyana said to the Buddha:

"Just now, while I was beneath a tree, I entered into samādhi and saw a hungry ghost whose body emitted an extreme stench worse than human excrement. It ran in all four directions, seeking out feces and urine to use as its sweet food."
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
How can such a retribution be received?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Do you now wish to know the causes and conditions for this?
Maudgalyāyana addressed the Buddha, saying,
"I wish most earnestly to hear them."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Maudgalyāyana, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the distant past, immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared in the world a Pratyekabuddha. He dwelt in a secluded place, using grass as his mat, sitting in meditation with his mindfulness firmly fixed.
When his body was afflicted by illness, a skilled physician prescribed medicine that required the consumption of meat for the disease to be cured.
Upon hearing these words, the Pratyekabuddha immediately entered the city and, seeing an elder named Kṣema, requested meat from him.
At that time, the elder commanded his wife, Pāṇḍarā:
"I have an urgent matter and must now go outside; you should properly prepare medicinal treatments according to the illness for that Pratyekabuddha."
Then the wife replied, "You need only be careful regarding what precedes; do not worry about what follows. As for the food for the Pratyekabuddha, I shall provide it myself.
Thereupon, the elder departed immediately.
At that time, Bandhula gave rise to thoughts of stinginess and greed, and he thought to himself:
"If I give food to him today, he will surely come again tomorrow; it would be truly loathsome to behold him."
Having formed this thought, he immediately asked for his alms-bowl; in a secluded place, he defecated into the bowl and covered it with rice, then gave it to the Pratyekabuddha.
Perceiving it as foul and loathsome, he threw it onto the ground and departed.

Due to these karmic conditions, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he constantly fell among the hungry ghosts (*preta*); his body was foul-smelling and unbearable to approach, and he constantly used human excrement as his food.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"If you wish to know who that householder’s wife was at that time who gave alms from her chamber-pot to the pratyekabuddha, she is this very hungry ghost."

When the Buddha had spoken this account of the hungry ghosts, the bhikṣus abandoned stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhat; some conceived the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some conceived the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 45.
The Story of Maudgalyāyana Entering the City and Seeing Five Hundred Pretas (45). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
At that time, when it was time for almsround, Maudgalyāyana put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.
At a certain gate, he encountered five hundred hungry ghosts coming in from outside; upon seeing Maudgalyāyana, they felt great joy and addressed him, saying:
"We pray only that the Venerable One..."
Out of compassion and pity, they call my name and say to the close relatives in my household:
"We, because we did not cultivate goodness nor take pleasure in giving, have now received these forms and fallen among the hungry ghosts."
"I only pray, Venerable One!
Please seek wealth and goods from my kinsmen to prepare a feast and invite the Buddha and the Saṃgha;
if the resources are insufficient, please exhort and convert various donors on my behalf so that they may join in providing this assembly, thereby enabling us to escape our bodies as hungry ghosts."
At that time, Maudgalyāyana immediately granted his consent.
He then asked the hungry ghosts:
"In your previous lives, what karmic actions did you perform to receive this retribution of suffering?"
At that time, all the hungry ghosts raised their voices in unison and said to Maudgalyāyana:

"In our past lives, we were all sons of elders here in this city of Rājagṛha. We were arrogant and heedless, taking no pleasure in giving, being greedily attached to worldly pleasures, and having no faith in the unsurpassed teaching of the Triple Gem."
Seeing various śramaṇas entering the city to beg for alms, he neither gave anything himself nor stopped others, saying:
"These practitioners!
They do not support themselves but merely rely on the common people; if you give to them now, they will come again tomorrow, and there will never be an end to it."
"By reason of these karmic conditions, when his life later came to an end, he fell among the hungry ghosts (preta) and underwent this retribution for his sins.
At that time, Maudgalyāyana said to the hungry ghost:
"I shall now speak to your relatives on your behalf, and with their assistance, we shall jointly arrange a great assembly."
"At that time, you all must come together of your own accord to this assembly.
Then all the hungry ghosts, with one voice, addressed the Venerable One, saying:

"Now, due to our past transgressions, although we have received physical forms, our bodies are like charred pillars, our bellies are like great mountains, our throats are like fine needles, and our hair is like awls and knives that pierce and prick our bodies; every joint and limb is ablaze with fire."

They ran in all four directions, searching for food and drink, yet were utterly unable to find any; even when they saw sweet delicacies, as they rushed toward them, the food turned into pus and blood. How, then, could they sustain this physical body and proceed to the assembly?
Then Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately spoke to the kinsmen of those hungry ghosts on their behalf, recounting the matter in detail.
Having heard this, all the relatives were filled with distress; they gathered together and wished to establish a memorial assembly for them.
At that time, Mahāmaudgalyāyana immediately entered meditative concentration to observe where the hungry ghosts were located. He searched throughout the sixteen great nations but did not see them.
Next, he went from Jambudvīpa through the four continents, up to a thousand worlds, and even as far as the trichiliocosm, yet he could not see them anywhere.
Wondering at the reason for this, he went to where the Buddha was and said:
“World-Honored One!
I have now exhorted various people, along with their relatives, on behalf of those hungry ghosts, to establish a great assembly and perform meritorious deeds for them.”
I have searched throughout the world, yet I could not see them at all.
I wonder, World-Honored One!
Where do these hungry ghosts dwell?
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"Those hungry ghosts have all been blown away by the winds of karma; this is not something you, a śrāvaka, are able to know or see."

"However, at this moment, those hungry ghosts have had their karmic defilements removed by virtue of your establishment of this assembly; I myself shall cause them to come to the place of the gathering.
Thereupon, Maudgalyāyana immediately prepared various delicacies for the hungry ghosts and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.

By the Buddha’s supernatural power, he caused all the hungry ghosts to come to the assembly, so that the brahmins, kṣatriyas, and householders of Rājagṛha all beheld the ghosts’ hideous and wretched appearances, which were most terrifying. Consequently, they all abandoned their hearts of stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and their minds were opened and liberated. Among them, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some of *anāgāmin*, and some of *arhat*; some resolved to attain the mind of a *pratyekabuddha*, and some resolved to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately preached various teachings on the faults and evils of stinginess and greed for those hungry ghosts.
They conceived deep faith and reverence; that very night, their lives came to an end, and they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Thereupon, they thought to themselves:
"By what meritorious karma did we come to be born here in this Trāyastriṃśa Heaven?"

He immediately observed himself and knew he was a hungry ghost, [thinking]: "It is because the Venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana has established this assembly and invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus for our sake that we have been able to be born here."
"We shall go together to repay his kindness.

Having spoken these words, they immediately descended from heaven; wearing celestial crowns upon their heads and adorning their bodies with various necklaces and ornaments, each carrying fragrant flowers, they came to make offerings to the Buddha and Mahāmaudgalyāyana.

Having completed their offerings, they withdrew to sit on one side to listen to the Buddha’s preaching. Their minds were opened and their understanding clarified; each attained the fruit of the Path. They circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the heavens.
The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana:
"If you wish to know who those five hundred hungry ghosts were at that time, they are these five hundred devaputras here now.
When the great assembly heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
46. The Story of Mātṛ Udārā’s Fall into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts (46). The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, in that country, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman from a noble family to be his wife, and provided her with performances and music to entertain her.
When his wife’s pregnancy reached full term, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and rare in the world; his parents were filled with joy and thus bestowed upon him the name Uttara.
As he gradually grew older, his father passed away. The son thought to himself:
"Since my late father's time, we have engaged in trade to manage our livelihood and established this family estate; should I not now follow in his footsteps?"
"However, I harbor deep faith and reverence for the Buddha's teachings and now wish to leave the household life.
He then went before his mother and requested to go forth.
At that time, his mother replied:
“Your father has already passed away, and now I am your only remaining support; you have but this one son.
Why do you now wish to abandon me and leave the home life?
As long as I am alive, I will never permit you to renounce the world and enter the path.”
"After I have passed away, you may go as you please.
At that time, the son, his wish unfulfilled, felt deep distress in his heart and immediately said to his mother,
"If you do not permit me, I shall now surely throw myself from a cliff or drink poison to death."
Then the mother replied:
"Do not speak such words!
For what reason do you say this now?"
"If you are determined to leave the household life,
from this day forward, should you wish to invite various śramaṇas, brāhmaṇas, and others, I shall provide the offerings so that you may make your donations accordingly."
Upon hearing these words, the boy felt reassured; he invited various śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas and repeatedly brought them to his home to provide offerings.

At that time, the boy’s mother, seeing the many ascetics coming and going frequently, became deeply distressed and gave rise to a sense of aversion. She then uttered harsh words, reviling the śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas:
"They have no desire for a livelihood and rely solely on the common people; they are truly loathsome to behold."
At that time, the son was not at home; his mother merely sprinkled food, drink, and water upon the ground and cast them away.
When the son returned from his journey, she said to him:
"After you had gone out, I prepared various delicacies and invited śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas to offer them sustenance."
He then immediately took his son and showed him the place where the leftover rice and gruel had been discarded, saying, "I have just made this offering and have now departed.
Upon hearing this, the boy was filled with great joy.
At a later time, the mother passed away and fell among the hungry ghosts (preta).
The son then went forth into homelessness; through diligent application and vigor, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

While he was sitting in meditation in a cave by the riverbank, there was a hungry ghost whose mouth was parched and who was tormented by hunger, thirst, and heat; it came to where the son was and said to the bhikṣu, "I am your mother."
The bhikṣu spoke in astonishment:
"When your mother was alive, she always delighted in giving alms; how is it that now, on the contrary, she has fallen into the realm of hungry ghosts to undergo such retribution?"
The hungry ghost replied:

"Because of my stinginess and greed, I was unable to make offerings to śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas; for this reason, I have received the body of a hungry ghost, and for twenty years I have never once obtained food or even water."
Whenever I go toward rivers, springs, or ponds, the water has completely dried up; whenever I go toward fruit trees, the trees have withered away.
I am now tormented by hunger, thirst, and the distress of heat, beyond all description.
The bhikṣu asked,
"By what cause have you come to this?
The hungry ghost replied:

"Although I practiced giving, my mind was always characterized by stinginess; toward śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas, I lacked a heart of respect and instead insulted them with groundless abuse. Now I am receiving this retribution."
"If you can now provide an offering for me, giving alms to the Buddha and the Sangha, and perform repentance on my behalf, I shall surely be able to escape this hungry ghost body.
When the son-monk heard these words, he was moved by deep compassion; he immediately exhorted [the ghost] to prepare a meal and invited the Buddha and the Sangha.
When the offerings had been completed, that hungry ghost immediately manifested its body within the assembly and confessed its transgressions.

At that time, the World-Honored One preached the Dharma to this hungry ghost in various ways. With a heart filled with shame and remorse, the ghost passed away that very night and was reborn with a new body among the flying hungry ghosts. Adorned with a celestial crown upon its head and various necklaces, it beautified its form and came to where the bhikṣu was, speaking again:

"I have not yet escaped the body of a hungry ghost; you must once more exhort and transform those in my place, providing abundant offerings along with bedding and mats, and bestowing them upon the Sangha of the four quarters, so that I may finally escape the body of a hungry ghost."
When the novice monk heard these words, he again exhorted others to provide food, drink, bedding, and mats, which he then offered to the Sangha of the four directions.

When the offerings were completed, the hungry ghost again manifested his body before the great assembly and immediately repented. That very night, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. He then thought to himself:
"What merit have I created that I have been able to be born here?"

He then reflected to himself: "Because of my son, the bhikṣu, who prepared various delicacies to invite the Buddha and the Saṅgha on my behalf, I have escaped the body of a hungry ghost and attained rebirth in heaven. I must now repay the kindness of the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and the bhikṣu."
Wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorning his body with various necklaces and ornaments, he brought fragrant flowers and came to make offerings to the Buddha and his son, the bhikṣu.

Having finished making the offerings, he withdrew to sit on one side to listen to the Buddha’s teaching. His mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his celestial palace.

When the Buddha had spoken this account of Udāra, the bhikṣus abandoned stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and some attained the fruit of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhatship; some resolved their minds toward pratyekabuddhahood, and some resolved their minds toward unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
47. The Story of the Hungry Ghost Born Blind (47). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, Ānanda put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the city to beg for food.

He saw a hungry ghost whose body was like a scorched pillar, whose belly was like a great mountain, and whose throat was like a fine needle; moreover, it was born blind and was being pecked by crows, vultures, kites, and owls. It rolled about and threw itself down, crying out at the top of its voice without ceasing.
At that time, Ānanda asked the hungry ghost:
"Sister! What karmic actions did you perform in your previous life to undergo such suffering?"
The hungry ghost replied, "Where there is the sun, there is no need for lamps or candles; since there is a Tathāgata in the world, you should ask him yourself.
Thereupon Ānanda immediately went to where the Buddha was and said:
“World-Honored One!
Earlier, as I entered the city to beg for alms, I saw a hungry ghost undergoing immeasurable and incalculable suffering.
I have come to relate these circumstances in detail to the Buddha, the Tathāgata.”
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What karma did those hungry ghosts create in their past lives to receive such retribution?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall explain this to you in detail.
In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Kāśyapa. He traveled about with a multitude of bhikṣus, teaching and transforming sentient beings."
Next, he arrived at the Deer Park. At that time, there was a woman carrying a child in her womb who, upon seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, conceived profound faith and reverence.
When the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter who was exceptionally beautiful and outstanding, inspiring the admiration of all who beheld her.

As he gradually grew older, he went to where the Buddha was staying to listen to the Buddha’s teaching of the Dharma. With a heart full of faith and reverence, he returned home and said to his parents:
"I pray that you will show me compassion and grant me permission to enter the ranks of the Path."
Her parents tried to restrain her firmly but could not stop her; she subsequently left the household life and became a bhikṣuṇī.
At that time, her parents, for the sake of this daughter, constructed a saṃghārāma and invited various bhikṣuṇīs to reside together within the monastery.
At that time, the daughter of a householder had committed a minor transgression against the precepts. The bhikṣuṇīs expelled her from the monastery.
Feeling ashamed and remorseful, she was unable to return home and took up temporary residence in another's house. There, she gave rise to great anger and spoke these words:
"I have my own house in which I dwell; why now do they instead expel me so that they may occupy it themselves?"
He then proceeded to speak of the various faults and evils of those bhikṣuṇīs to that elder householder:
"They resemble hungry ghosts; unable to support themselves, they rely entirely upon the common people. May I never again receive a body that must encounter such as these."
Having made this vow, she later passed away and fell among the hungry ghosts; she has now been born blind.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If you wish to know who that daughter of the elder was at that time—she who left the household life to enter the Path, was driven out of the monastery, and reviled with evil speech—it is she who is now this blind hungry ghost."

When the Buddha had spoken this account of the hungry ghosts, the bhikṣus each guarded their actions of body, speech, and mind, and grew weary of and detached from birth and death. Among them, some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some sakṛdāgāmin, some anāgāmin, and some arhat; some conceived the aspiration for pratyekabuddhahood, and some conceived the aspiration for unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
48. The Story of the Elder Jotika’s Fall into the Realm of Hungry Ghosts due to Stinginess and Greed (48). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in that city, there was an elder named Jyotidatta, whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable; his slaves, servants, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep were beyond counting.

At that time, the elder happened to go out for an excursion and arrived at the Jetavana Grove, where he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns, adorning his body. With a heart filled with faith and reverence, he went forward and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet; then, withdrawing to sit to one side, he listened to the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma. His heart was filled with joy, and upon returning home, he took leave of his family and kinsmen, seeking to enter the Path.
At that time, all his kinsmen gave their full consent.
He returned home and informed the Buddha, requesting to leave the household life.
The Buddha then said to him:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!
At these words, his beard and hair fell away naturally, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Then his kinsmen and the common people, because he was formerly the son of a wealthy and noble family who had left home to enter the Way, vied with one another to offer him robes, alms bowls, and all manner of necessities.
Once they have obtained them, they give rise to a mind of stinginess and greed, unable to bestow them upon their fellow practitioners of the Brahma-faring life.
Thereafter, when their lives end, they fall among the hungry ghosts and continue to guard their robes and bowls.

At that time, when the assembly of monks saw that he had passed away, they opened his room’s door, intending to collect his remains, robes, and bowl for cremation according to the *karmavācanā*. However, within this chamber, they beheld a hungry ghost whose body was like a charred pillar and whose appearance was terrifying; it guarded these robes and bowl, such that no one dared to approach.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they went to inform the World-Honored One, recounting in detail what they had seen.
Thereupon, the Tathāgata led the bhikṣus into the room and spoke to the hungry ghost, saying: "Ho!
You who have no shame or remorse!"
"In a previous life, when you left the household life to enter the Path, you were greedily attached to gain and offerings and were unwilling to practice charity;
thus, you have now fallen among the hungry ghosts and received this hideous form."
"How is it that you now feel no shame or remorse, yet have returned once more to continue guarding your robes and bowl?
He rebuked him for the many faults of stinginess and greed, which can cause sentient beings to fall into the evil realms.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma to him in various ways; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he felt a profound sense of shame and remorse. He immediately gave away his robes and bowl to the assembly of monks.

At midnight that very night, he passed away and took on another form, falling among the hungry ghosts who travel through the air. He was exceptionally handsome and exquisite, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments to grace his body. His body emitted a brilliant light that illuminated the Jetavana Monastery; as he traveled through the void, he was no different from a celestial being.

He came to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha then preached the Dharma to him in various ways; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he departed with joy.
At dawn, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"World-Honored One!
Last night, a radiance shone upon the Jetavana; was it Brahmā, Śakra, or the Four Heavenly Kings?"
"Are these the generals of the twenty-eight classes of ghosts and spirits?
Or have the great Bodhisattvas from other directions come to listen to the Dharma?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"It is not Śakra, Brahmā, or the various kings and spirits of the twenty-eight divisions; rather, it is a great wealthy elder from the city of Śrāvastī who left the household life to enter the Path. Having passed away recently, he has fallen among the flying hungry ghosts (preta) and has come to make offerings to me with incense and flowers—it is his radiance."

When the Buddha had spoken this discourse on causes and conditions, the bhikṣus abandoned stinginess and greed, grew weary of birth and death, and some attained the stage of srotāpanna, some of sakṛdāgāmin, some of anāgāmin, and some of arhat; some conceived the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and some conceived the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
49. The Story of the Hungry Ghosts Who Ate Their Own Five Hundred Sons (49). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, the Venerable Naradatta put on his robes, took up his bowl, and entered the city to beg for food. Having returned to his own quarters and finished his meal, he saw from afar that the Jetavana was as red as the color of blood, and he wondered at the cause of this marvel.

He went to look immediately and saw a hungry ghost whose fat and flesh had completely wasted away, leaving only his joints and bones standing out. Day and night, five hundred sons were born to him; they were emaciated and frail, lacking all strength and vigor.

At the moment of birth, they fall into a state of frantic distress and die; their limbs and joints dissolve as they are utterly tormented by hunger and thirst, devouring immediately upon birth yet never reaching satiety.
Then Naladatta went forward and asked,
"What karma did you create to receive such a retribution of suffering?
The hungry ghost replied:
"You may now ask the Buddha, the World-Honored One, yourself; he shall explain it for you.
Thereupon, Naladatta went at once to where the Buddha was, prostrated himself before the Buddha's feet, and withdrew to stand to one side.
It is the constant custom of all Buddhas to first inquire with kind intent:
"What extraordinary thing have you seen today? Nara replied:
"Recently, while wandering about, I saw a hungry ghost who gives birth to five hundred sons every day and night; being extremely hungry and thirsty, he devours them as soon as they are born."
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What karma did he create in his past life to receive such retribution?
The Buddha told Naradatta:
“If you wish to know, listen with a sincere and attentive mind!
I shall explain it to you in detail.

In this Bhadrakalpa, there was an elder in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who possessed immeasurable wealth in gold, silver, and precious gems, as well as male and female slaves, servants, elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep beyond counting.”
The sole wife had no children; she prayed to the gods and spirits, seeking to have an offspring, but was utterly unable to obtain one.
At that time, the elder took another woman from a family of good standing, and before long, she became pregnant.
When the principal wife saw that she was pregnant, she became envious and secretly gave her poisoned medicine to cause an abortion.

Her sisters-in-law and kinswomen immediately went to her location and engaged in a violent quarrel with the principal wife; they eventually came to blows and beat her, demanding to know the truth of the matter.

The senior wife, wishing to speak the truth yet fearing she might die from the ordeal, and wishing not to speak it yet finding her agony beyond words, was driven by such desperate urgency that she uttered this curse:

"If what I say is true—that you have caused me to miscarry—then when I leave this body, may I be reborn among the hungry ghosts (preta), giving birth to five hundred children every day and night; as soon as they are born, may I devour them one after another, never reaching satiety."
Having made this vow, she released him immediately.
The Buddha told Naladatta:

"If you wish to know who that chief wife was at that time—she who, having conceived a heart of jealousy and caused the miscarriage of another's child, made a false oath and vow and fell among the hungry ghosts—it is she who now receives this retribution."

At that time, when the bhikṣus heard the Buddha speak thus of how the mind of jealousy possesses many faults and afflictions, capable of causing sentient beings to fall into the evil realms, they all together renounced it. Loathing birth and death, their minds were opened and their intentions liberated. Some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some *sakṛdāgāmin*, some *anāgāmin*, and some *arhat*; some resolved to attain the state of a *pratyekabuddha*, and some resolved to attain unsurpassed *bodhi*.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
50. The Story of Caṇḍāla Resembling a Preta (Lūtapuruṣa) The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī, in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall on the Monkey River bank.
At that time, there was an elder in that city named Śroṇa, who selected a suitable match and took her as his wife, providing her with various musical performances for her entertainment.
His wife became pregnant, and her odor was so unbearable that she could not be approached. Her husband then asked her:
"Previously you were not like this; for what reason do you now have such foul stench?"
The wife replied to her husband, "This must be my child in the womb; it is due to the power of karma that it has become thus.

When the ten months were fully completed, a male child was born, standing with his skeletal frame exposed, emaciated and withered, unfit to be shown to others, and moreover, he was born with excrement and urine smeared over his body.
As he gradually grew older, he did not wish to remain at home; he craved excrement and filth, refusing to abandon them.
When his parents and kinsmen saw him in such a state, they loathed the sight of him and drove him away to a distant place, ensuring that he could not come near.
Even when wandering about, he sought after excrement and urine to use as his sweet meal.
When the masses of people saw him acting in this way, they gave him a name accordingly, calling him the *caṇḍāla* ghost.
At that time, there were various non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthikas) in that country who happened to encounter him while traveling. They praised him, saying, "Excellent!
Upon hearing these words, he was filled with great joy and could not contain his delight;
he stepped forward and said to the non-Buddhists, "Out of compassion and pity, please allow me to join your ranks."
At that time, the various non-Buddhists immediately left the household life; they were instructed to go naked, smear their bodies with ashes, and practice pure conduct.
Although Caṇḍāla was now on the path [of renunciation], he still craved places of filth and impurity, such as latrines.
At that time, the various non-Buddhists, seeing him in such a state, all rebuked him together, or even saw to it that he was whipped, saying:
"You are now a human being; for what reason do you thus delight in dwelling in impurity?"
At that time, Caṇḍāla was repeatedly rebuked by the various non-Buddhists, or even flogged; he abandoned them and departed, going to a ditch by the riverbank where he took delight in himself.

At that time, there were five hundred hungry ghosts dwelling along the riverbank. When they saw Caṇḍāla approaching—his body emitting an extreme stench—they remained where they were, and none dared to draw near him.
Yet he constantly turns toward the hungry ghosts and praises himself, saying:
"When I was among humans, I was sometimes reviled or even whipped, and I suffered extreme torment."
"Now, being here, we shall not see anyone scold us or whip us; let us enjoy ourselves alone.
At that time, the hungry ghosts, seeing that the place of Caṇḍāla was foul-smelling and impure, all abandoned it and departed.
Then Caṇḍāla said to the spirits:
"It was by relying upon you that this foul body of mine has been able to survive for several days; now that you are abandoning me once more, how shall I live on in my final moments?"
Having spoken these words, he was deeply distressed and fell to the ground in grief and sorrow.
At that time, the World-Honored One, throughout the six periods of the day and night, observed sentient beings to see who should be delivered, and would immediately go to deliver them.

Seeing Caṇḍāla, who had lost his companions and was overcome with grief, distress, and suffering, falling to the ground in a swoon, [the Buddha] immediately went to the pit and preached the Dharma for him, causing him to rejoice.

At that time, Caṇḍāla, seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, with his faculties serene and composed, his radiance shining brilliantly like a hundred thousand suns adorning his body, felt joy in his heart and prostrated himself on the ground, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"In this world, could there be such lowly persons as we, who might obtain ordination?
The Buddha told Cāṇūra:
"In this Dharma of mine, there are no distinctions of noble or base; none are prohibited from seeking ordination."
Then, having heard the Buddha’s words, Cāṇūra came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“Out of compassion and pity, please grant me permission to enter the ranks of the Path.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One immediately raised his golden right arm and said to him:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu!

At these words, his hair and beard fell away naturally, the Dharma robes clothed his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa; his dignified deportment was as orderly and composed as that of a bhikṣu with twelve years of seniority, without any difference whatsoever.
Having received the Buddha’s grace and attained the state of a renunciant, he immediately spoke these verses before the Buddha:
"Now, having received the Buddha’s grace, I have obtained merit as desired and according to my wishes;
Casting off this foul and impure body, I have become a śramaṇa."
At that time, the World-Honored One said to Caṇḍāla, "You have now attained renunciation within my Dharma.

He diligently practiced with focused mindfulness, and before long, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and being fully endowed with the eight liberations; thus all devas and people of the world alike revered and honored him.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen this matter, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What karma did this Caṇḍāla bhikṣu create in his past lives to receive such a retribution for his offenses?"
"Furthermore, by what causes and conditions did he encounter the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and attain the fruit of Arhatship?
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the bhikṣus:
"Wholesome and unwholesome karma created in past lives Does not perish even after a hundred kalpas."
"Due to the causes and conditions of sinful karma, one now receives such retribution.
When the bhikṣus had heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!"
Regarding events in past lives, what were they like?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain them in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

During this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was forty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Krakucchanda. Leading a multitude of bhikṣus, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings until he arrived at the kingdom of Ratnavimāna.

At that time, the king of that land, hearing that the Buddha had arrived, felt great joy in his heart. Accompanied by his ministers, he went out of the city to welcome him. Upon arrival, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and knelt for a long time, entreating the Buddha:
"I only pray, World-Honored One!"
“Out of compassion and pity, please accept my offerings of the four requisites for three months.
The Buddha immediately consented.

At that time, the king, knowing that the Buddha had granted permission, promptly constructed dwellings for the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus. He appointed one bhikṣu as the monastery master to manage monastic affairs, who remained on duty every day except when traveling elsewhere.

There was an arhat bhikṣu who entered that monastery; his deportment was composed and orderly, making him most worthy of being beheld. When the monastery’s presiding donor saw him thus, he invited him into the bathhouse to bathe him and further anointed his body with fragrant oil.
At that time, the monastery’s resident superior entered from outside and saw this arhat anointing his body with fragrant oil; harboring feelings of jealousy, he immediately uttered harsh abuse:
"You who have left the household life, why do you act in such a manner?"
"It is as if human excrement has been smeared upon your body.
Having spoken these words, the arhat who had his body anointed with fragrant oil felt compassion and leaped into the air, manifesting the eighteen miraculous transformations.

At that time, the abbot of the monastery, having witnessed this transformation, was deeply filled with shame and remorse; he prostrated before the arhat to repent and apologize for his transgressions, and they each returned to their respective dwellings.
"By reason of this karmic condition, for five hundred lifetimes, his body was constantly foul-smelling and could not be approached.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that temple-abbot bhikṣu was who reviled him with harsh words, he is none other than the bhikṣu Caṇḍāla here now."
"Because he had gone forth as a monk at that time, he confessed his transgressions to that Arhat; thus, he has now encountered me, gone forth, and attained the Way.

When the Buddha had finished speaking this story of Cāṇūra, each person guarded their own actions of body, speech, and mind, abandoned the mind of envy, and grew weary of birth and death. Among them, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some Sakṛdāgāmin, some Anāgāmin, and some Arhat; some conceived the aspiration for Pratyekabuddhahood, and some conceived the aspiration for Unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Compendium of One Hundred Karmic Conditions*, Fascicle Five.
*The Compendium of One Hundred Karmic Conditions*, Fascicle Six.
Translated by the Yuezhi Upāsaka Zhi Qian of Wu.
Chapter Six: The Descent of the Gods to Make Offerings. Section Fifty-one:
The Story of the Face of Virtue, Who, Due to Stinginess and Greed, Received the Body of a Poisonous Snake. The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Bhadramukha, who possessed immeasurable wealth and treasures beyond calculation. He was full of deceit, crookedness, stinginess, greed, and envy; he never had the intention to give, even to the point that he would drive away birds so they would not approach his house.
There are certain śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas who, when beggars come to them in poverty and destitution, revile them with harsh words;
they diligently seek wealth and property, making its accumulation their primary occupation, and do not practice the giving of alms.

Thereafter, when his life ended, he was reborn with the body of a venomous snake; he continued to guard his former wealth, and anyone who approached him would be met with such fierce and violent rage that the snake would glare at them with angry eyes, causing them to die. Eventually, word of this reached King Bimbisāra.
Having heard this, the king was filled with wonder and thought to himself:
"This venomous snake’s wrath is now so intense that it will kill anyone who sees it; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, is able to subdue it."
Having formed this thought, he immediately took his ministers and went to where the Buddha was; prostrating at the Buddha’s feet, he withdrew to sit to one side and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

"Now, within this city, there was an elder of immeasurable wealth who was unwilling to practice charity; he has now passed away and been reborn with the body of a venomous snake. He still guards his original wealth, and with his fury blazing intensely, he harms anyone who approaches him."
"I only pray, World-Honored One,
that you will subdue this snake so as not to allow it to harm people.
The Buddha silently gave his consent.
On the following day, having dressed and taken his bowl, he went to where the snake was.
When the snake saw the Buddha approaching, its fury blazed up and it sought to bite the Tathāgata.

By the power of his compassion, the Buddha emitted five-colored light from the tips of his five fingers, which illuminated the serpent’s body; it immediately attained coolness, its burning venom was eliminated, and its heart was filled with joy.
He raised his head and looked around:
"What fortunate person is this?
Able to emit such light that it illuminates my body, making me feel a refreshing coolness beyond words?"
At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing that the snake had been tamed, addressed it, saying:
"Worthy-faced Householder!
Because of your stinginess and greed in a previous life, you have received this wretched form."
Why now, out of old habit, do you again cling to these things and indulge in harming others like a venomous stinger? Your evil deeds are increasing all the more;
in a future life, you will surely undergo great suffering.

Upon hearing the Buddha’s words, the snake deeply reproached itself; its obscuring clouds were dispelled, and it recalled its past lives. Realizing that the evil karma it had committed during its time as a householder was now bearing this fruit, it conceived deep faith and reverence toward the Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the mind of this venomous snake had been tamed, addressed it, saying:
"In your previous life, you did not comply with my words and thus received this snake form; now you should become compliant and accept my instructions."
The snake replied to the Buddha, “I shall comply with what the Buddha has granted me; I dare not disobey your command.
The Buddha said to the snake:
"If you become docile, enter my almsbowl.
When the Buddha had finished speaking, [the snake] immediately entered the bowl, and he set out for the forest.

At that time, King Bimbisāra, along with his ministers and subjects, heard that the World-Honored Buddha had tamed the venomous snake and was bringing it back in his bowl; consequently, the people of the entire kingdom all went together to see it.
Within the Buddha’s almsbowl, the snake beheld the multitude and felt profound shame; loathing its serpent body, it immediately passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
He then thought to himself:
"What merit have I created that I have been born here in the heavens?
He immediately observed his past life and saw that while in the world, he had received the body of a venomous snake.
"Because I beheld the Buddha, I gave rise to a heart of faith and reverence; weary of my serpent body, I have been able to be reborn here and experience celestial bliss.
Now I must repay the kindness of the Buddha, the World-Honored One."

Wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorning his body with various necklaces, he brought fragrant flowers and was radiant with light as he approached the Buddha’s dwelling. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and having completed his offerings, withdrew to sit to one side. As he listened to the Buddha’s teaching, his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he praised the Buddha in verse:
“Lofty and majestic is the Great Holy Honored One, Whose merits are entirely fulfilled;
He is able to open the eyes of all who are blind and in darkness, And has swiftly attained the fruit of Buddhahood.”
"Having removed the stains of affliction and transcended the ocean of birth and death,
we now, by the grace of the Buddha's virtue, have closed the gates to the three evil realms.
At that time, having praised the Buddha, the devaputra circumambulated him three times and returned to his celestial palace.
Then, in the early morning, King Bimbisāra went to where the Buddha was and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
Last night, a radiance shone upon the World-Honored One; was it Śakra, Brahmā, a Cakravartin Wheel-Turning Sage King, or one of the generals of the twenty-eight classes of ghosts and spirits?"

The Buddha told the king, "It was neither Śakra, Brahmā, nor any of the other devas who came to hear the Dharma; rather, it was that former miserly and greedy elder who has been reborn in the heavens and has come to make offerings to me—it is his radiance."

At that time, when King Bimbisāra heard the Buddha speak on the causes of stinginess and greed, among those present in the assembly, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat; some conceived the aspiration for Pratyekabuddhahood, and some conceived the aspiration for unexcelled Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
52. The Story of Candraprabha’s Son Reborn in Heaven (52). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in that city, there was a brahmin whose occupation was farming. He took a wife from a family of equal status, and after ten full months had passed, she gave birth to a son named Candraprabha (Moonlight).

As he gradually grew older, he went out with the son of Sudatta to sightsee. Upon arriving at the monastery, he saw the bhikṣus diligently engaged in recitation and study. At that time, the Brahmin’s son heard a four-line stanza and conceived a profound sense of faith and reverence, whereupon he immediately returned home.
Seven days later, his life came to an end, and he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.

At that time, the child’s parents wailed and wept in grief; their hearts were filled with such anguish that they could not control themselves. They took the corpse in their arms, went to the cemetery, and cried out as they lamented:
"This was my only son; now he has abandoned us and departed. Who will look after us?"
"The pain is beyond description; I would rather die than return home.
At that time, his relatives offered various kinds of counsel and exhortations, yet he remained unwilling to return.

The resonance of this sincere devotion caused my palace to tremble and become unsettled. Upon investigating the cause, I realized that I had been reborn in the heavens from among human beings; furthermore, I saw my parents in a cemetery, embracing my corpse, their grief so profound that they were choked with sobs, unable to restrain themselves, which moved my palace to such an extent that it shook.

Out of compassion for his parents, he immediately descended from heaven, transformed his body into the form of a *ṛṣi*, and went before his parents, performing the ascetic practice of "scorching the body with five fires."
Then the brahmin asked the seer, saying:
"For what reason do you now scorch your body with the five heats? What is it that you seek?"
The seer replied, "I now wish to become a king;

I would have a chariot made of gold, inlaid with various jewels, with the sons of the Sun and Moon deities at my left and right, and the Four Heavenly Kings walking as they pull my chariot. To travel throughout the four continents—would that not be most delightful?"
Then the brahmin replied to the seer, saying:
"Even if you were to roast your body day and night for a hundred years now, you could never obtain such a precious chariot as this, nor those celestial attendants who serve you."
Thereupon, the seer asked the brahmin again,
"What vow do you seek by now embracing this corpse?
The brahmin replied:
"This is my only son; he has abandoned me and died. Therefore, I embrace him, hoping that he might yet return to life.
The seer replied, "If you now embrace this corpse, weeping day and night for a full hundred years, you will ultimately never regain your son."
At that time, having heard the words of the rishi, the brahmin felt shame and remorse; he ceased his weeping and remained silent.
Then the son, who was a deva, transformed the rishi’s form back into his own original body and said to his parents:
"The one and only son of yours is this very person, myself."
Once, at a certain time, I went to a monastery and heard a four-line verse; my heart was filled with joy, and faith arose within me. I then passed away and have now been reborn in heaven.
"I have now come in the form of a rishi to explain the cause of your parents' sorrow and suffering, and to instruct you.
Thereupon, when the parents heard the words of the devaputra, they immediately attained faith and understanding, their joy beyond measure.

At that time, the devaputra, wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorning his body with various necklaces and ornaments, brought fragrant flowers and exhorted his parents to go together to the Buddha’s dwelling. Having made offerings to the Buddha, they withdrew to sit at one side.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he simultaneously attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having witnessed this event, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what merit did this son of heaven plant roots in his past lives?"
"Being able now to comfort them with kind words, you have explained matters to your parents so that they have ceased their weeping and attained the fruits of the Path.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"It was not only today that you explained matters to your parents to prevent them from being distressed; in past lives as well, you have likewise explained matters to them, preventing them from being distressed."
When the bhikṣus had heard these words, they again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What were the events like in past ages?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a foolish man who constantly delighted in thievery, committing adultery, fraud, and deception. When the authorities caught him, they bound him and brought him before the king. The king questioned him regarding his crimes, and as he confessed the facts exactly as they were, the king immediately ordered that he be executed."

At that time, I was his son; by nature I was compassionate, kind, disciplined, virtuous, and gentle, such that my reputation was known throughout the entire kingdom. Because he was my father, I appealed to the king for the sake of saving his life, doing so as many as three times. The king could not refuse me; he released him so that he would not be killed and allowed him to depart as he pleased.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that thief was at that time, he is now the father of this prince; the son at that time is now this prince."
"Because he once received the Three Refuges under Kāśyapa Buddha, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
While the Buddha was speaking of this celestial son’s causal conditions, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, and others even gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 53.
The Story of How One Attained Birth in Heaven by Gathering Flowers as an Offering to the Buddha (53). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, the wealthy and eminent elders within the city all gathered together and went to the spring, where they performed music and song to amuse themselves, holding a Śāla-flower festival.
At that time, from within that assembly, one person was sent to the grove of trees to gather *sāla* flowers to make various flower garlands.

When the flower-gatherer returned to the assembly, he encountered the World-Honored One along the way. Seeing the Buddha’s thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns, his heart was filled with joy. He went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and scattered the flowers he had gathered over the World-Honored One, then departed.

He climbed back up the tree, intending to gather more flowers, when a branch broke; he fell and died, being reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where he was exceptionally handsome and sublime, with a palace made of sāla flowers.
Śakra asked,
"In what place did you cultivate meritorious deeds to come and be born here?
The devaputra replied:
"In Jambudvīpa, while gathering sāla flowers, I encountered the World-Honored One; by scattering these flowers upon the Buddha, through the merit of this deed, I have been able to be born here."
At that time, Śakra, seeing this devaputra, whose body was preeminent and whose comeliness was foremost, spoke a verse in praise:
"Your body is like the color of pure gold, Radiant and exceedingly bright;
Your features are most perfectly handsome, The most excellent among all the gods."
At that time, the devaputra immediately spoke a verse in response to Śakra, saying:
"Having received the Buddha’s grace and virtue, I scattered sāla flowers;
By virtue of these wholesome causes and conditions, I have now obtained this karmic fruit."
At that time, having spoken these verses, the devaputra, together with Śakra, went to where the Buddha was, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma to him in various ways; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened. He shattered twenty billion karmic obstacles of false views and attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. With a heart full of joy and celebration, he spoke a verse before the Buddha in praise of him:
"Lofty is the Great Holy Honored One, Supreme and beyond compare.
Neither parents nor teachers Possess merit equal to yours."
"He has dried up the four great oceans, transcended the mountain of white bones, blocked the three evil paths, and is able to open the gates of the three virtues.
When the devaputra had spoken this verse, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, circumambulated the Buddha three times, and returned to the heavens.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the bhikṣus approached the Buddha at dawn and said to him:
"World-Honored One!
Last night, a brilliant light illuminated the entire Jetavana. Was it Śakra, Brahmā, or one of the Four Heavenly Kings?"
"Is it the generals of the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"It is not Śakra, Brahmā, the spirits, the Four Heavenly Kings, or others; rather, it is the light of those who in former days gathered sālā flowers to make offerings to me, who have now been reborn in heaven and have come to offer various fragrant flowers to me."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
54. The Story of Guṇamati Making Offerings to a Stūpa and Rebirth in Heaven (54) The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, King Bimbisāra went to visit the World-Honored One three times every day, accompanied by his officials and attendants, to pay homage to the Blessed One.
Later, as he grew older and his body became increasingly heavy, he was unable to go there daily for prostration.
At that time, the officials addressed the King, saying:

"We have requested hair and nail-clippings from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and have erected a stupa and temple within the inner palace. We pay homage there and offer incense, flowers, lamps, and light as offerings."
The King then agreed.

He went to where the Buddha was staying and made his request. The World-Honored One immediately gave him his hair and nails. Within his palace, the King erected a stupa and temple, hanging silk banners and canopies, and offering incense, flowers, and lamps three times each day as an act of worship.
At that time, Prince Ajātaśatru, in league with Devadatta, conspired together to assassinate his father, the King, and established himself as ruler. He immediately issued an edict within the palace:
"The worship and offerings of that stūpa are forbidden; anyone who violates this shall suffer punishment without pardon."
Later, on the fifteenth day of the seventh month during the *pravāraṇā* ceremony of the Saṃgha, there was a palace lady named Guṇamati who thought to herself:

"This stūpa was built by the Great King; yet now it is covered in dust and filth, with no one to sweep or sprinkle it. Even if I must personally undergo execution for this, I shall sweep and sprinkle that stūpa, and offer it incense, flowers, and lamps."
Having formed this thought, he immediately lit a lamp and made an offering to that stūpa.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru, who was far away atop his palace, saw the light of that lamp and became greatly incensed; he immediately dispatched men to go and see who it was.
Having seen this, Guṇamati lit lamps as an offering; the messenger returned and reported the circumstances to the king.
The king ordered him to be summoned and questioned him regarding the cause.
At that time, Guṇamati replied to the king:
"This stupa is a place of worship established by our former king; on this auspicious day, we shall sweep it clean and offer lamps in worship."
At that time, having heard these words, Ajātaśatru said to Guṇamati,
“Have you not heard the instructions I previously gave? Guṇamati replied:
"Having heard the King's command,
yet the governance and transformation of the kingdom now do not surpass those of the former kings.
When Ajātaśatru heard these words, his anger redoubled, and he immediately slew Guṇamati with his sword.
Riding upon this wholesome mind, he immediately passed away and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, where the radiance of his body illuminated an area of one yojana.
At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, and the other devas all came to behold him and asked:
"What merit did you create?"
"I have been able to be born here, where my radiance is extraordinary and twice as superior as that of all the devas.
At that time, the deva-son replied to Śakra in verse:
"The Tathāgata has appeared in the world, Like the radiance of the sun and moon."
Illuminating all those dark places, you cause them all to be universally bright.
Those who see you give rise to joy, and the defilements of their minds are naturally removed.
How excellent is the Unsurpassed Honored One, the noble field of merit for all sentient beings!
"By cultivating merit with a faithful heart, I did not spare my own body or life;
though harmed and brought to the end of my life, I have attained rebirth in the heavens.

At that time, after the deva-son had spoken this verse to Śakra, he donned his celestial crown and put on various necklaces to adorn his body.
