Leading a host of devas, each carrying incense and flowers, he descended to make offerings to the Buddha. His radiance shone everywhere, illuminating the Bamboo Grove with a brilliance twice that of usual times. He approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. He then spoke these words:

"I reflect that in the past, the white bones I have accumulated exceed Mount Sumeru, and the tears I have shed in weeping are more than the vast oceans; my flesh and blood have been withered away, and my life has been lost in vain, yet now I have attained liberation from them."
Having spoken these words, he circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his celestial palace.
Then, at the break of dawn, the bhikṣus addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
"Last night, the radiance was many times greater than usual; was it Śakra, Brahmā, or one of the Four Heavenly Kings?"
"Is he one of the great generals of the twenty-eight classes of ghosts and spirits?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"He is neither a great general of the Brahmā-devas nor a ghost or spirit; rather, he was a lady-in-waiting in the inner palace of King Bimbisāra named Guṇamati, who, because she had made offerings to the stūpa, was killed by King Ajātaśatru."
"Having ended his life, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and came to make offerings to me; this was merely his radiance.

When the Buddha spoke these words regarding the causal conditions for this merit, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat; some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
55. The Circumstances of Sudatta’s Exhortation While Riding an Elephant (55). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in that city named Sudatta, who gave one hundred thousand pieces of gold to the Buddha and thought to himself:
"As for someone like me, whose wealth is immeasurable, it would not be difficult to offer one hundred thousand pieces of gold for the Jetavana Vihāra to the Buddha and the Sangha;

however, if I were now to exhort the poor and lowly to sacrifice even a needle or a thread for the sake of almsgiving, that would truly be called difficult, and yet it would yield immeasurable and boundless merit."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to inform King Prasenajit, who promptly gave his consent.
The king then dispatched his ministers and officials to beat the drums and proclaim within the city, addressing the people:
"The elder Sudatta now wishes to exhort the masses to practice the giving of alms."
At the end of seven days, he mounted a great white elephant and traveled through the crossroads, streets, lanes, and alleys everywhere to exhort and convert the people.

At that time, the people were filled with joy and vied with one another to practice giving; some offered clothing, necklaces, gold, silver, and precious objects, while others gave various kinds of bracelets, rings, needles, thread, collars, and belts—whatever each household possessed, they brought forth to offer as alms.

At that time, there was a poor woman who, after working as a hired laborer for three months, obtained a single piece of cotton cloth which she intended to use for a garment. Seeing the elder Sudatta exhorting various people for alms, she immediately asked those nearby:

"That elder Sudatta possesses abundant wealth and many treasures, lacking nothing at all; he is even able to perceive hidden hoards beneath the earth. What is it now that he lacks, such that he must go about begging from others?"
The people said, "That elder truly lacks for nothing; out of compassion, he exhorts all the people, desiring that we together cultivate merit by inviting the Buddha and the Sangha."
At that time, having heard these words, the poor woman felt great joy in her heart and spoke thus:
"Because I failed to practice generosity in my past lives, I am now impoverished;
if I do not give now, my condition will become even more severe in future lives."
He further reflected to himself:

"A Buddha appears in the world but rarely. Although I now wish to invite the Buddha and the Sangha, I possess nothing at all. On my person, there is only this single garment; if I give it as an offering, I shall sit here naked;
yet if I do not use it, there will be no hope for me in the future."
"I am now impoverished and suffering; I shall surely meet my death soon. It would be better for me to give up this cotton cloth and use it as an act of almsgiving.
Having thought this, he immediately took the cloth and threw it through the window to Sudatta.
Having received it, Sudatta sent a messenger to investigate, who saw a poor woman sitting there naked.
At that time, the messenger asked her,
"For what reason are you now giving this garment as an offering?"
The poor woman replied, "I fear that in future lives I shall become even more destitute; for this reason, I offer this as a gift.
Then the messenger went and reported the circumstances of the matter in full to Sudatta.
Having heard this, Sudatta exclaimed in wonder, "How marvelous!
He immediately removed the garments he was wearing and gave them as alms to the poor woman.
Having received them, the poor woman felt great joy in her heart.
"I have now made this offering and received its fruit in the present life; how much more so shall I in future lives?
After several days had passed, the poor woman’s life came to an end, and she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. She then thought to herself:
"By what merit did I create that I have been born in the heavens?"
He then examined himself and realized that he had been born here because he had given a piece of fine cloth as a gift while he was among humans and was extremely poor.
"I must now repay the kindness of the Buddha and of Sudatta."

Wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorning his body with various necklaces and ornaments, he brought fragrant flowers and descended to make offerings to the Buddha and Sudatta; he then prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding attained, and he realized the fruit of Srotāpanna. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the heavens.
Then, at the break of dawn, the bhikṣus went before the Buddha and said to him:
"Last night, a radiance shone upon the Tathāgata; was it Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Heavenly Kings?"
"The Great Generals of the Twenty-eight Classes of Ghosts and Spirits?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It was neither Śakra nor Brahmā, nor any of the divine kings; rather, it is the light of Sudatta’s poor woman, who, having been exhorted by him, gave a piece of cloth as an offering and was reborn in the heavens, coming now to make offerings to me."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that poor woman was at that time, she is this very devaputra here.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
56. The Story of the Parrot King Inviting the Buddha (56). The Story of the Parrot King Inviting the Buddha. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
When the summer retreat had concluded, he took the bhikṣus and intended to travel to other lands.
At that time, King Bimbisāra, accompanied by his ministers, went out of the city and saw the Tathāgata from afar, asking, "Where is the World-Honored One?"
“I only pray that you, out of compassion, together with the community of bhikṣus, will come and accept my offering.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar that the king’s mind had conceived a profound longing, gradually traveled with the community of bhikṣus until he arrived in the kingdom of Magadha. There, among a flock of birds, there was a king of śuka parrots who, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar, soared into the air and went out to meet him on the road, saying:
“I only pray that the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus, out of compassionate pity and mercy, will visit my grove and accept my invitation for one night.”
The Buddha immediately granted his consent.
Then the King of Parrots, knowing that the Buddha had permitted it, returned to his original forest and commanded all the parrots:
"Each of you come to welcome him."
At that time, the World-Honored One, accompanied by the bhikṣus, went to the Śuka Grove; there they each spread out their sitting mats beneath the trees and sat in meditation and contemplation.

At that time, the parrot king, seeing the Buddha and the bhikṣus sitting in silent meditation, was filled with great joy. Throughout the entire night, he flew about, circling the Buddha and the bhikṣus, looking in all four directions to see whether there were any lions, tigers, wolves, birds, or beasts, or any thieves, who might disturb or trouble the World-Honored One and the community of bhikṣus.
When morning arrived, the World-Honored One proceeded forward; the parrot, filled with joy, led the way toward Rājagṛha and addressed King Bimbisāra, saying:
"The World-Honored One is now leading his bhikṣus and has come near."
"I only pray, Great King,
that you will prepare various delicacies and go out to welcome him on the road.

When King Bimbisāra heard these words, he ordered the preparation of delicacies and, taking up banners, streamers, incense, flowers, and musical instruments, led his ministers to go out and welcome him on the road.
At that time, the king of parrots passed away during the night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. He suddenly grew to the size of an eight-year-old child and thought to himself:
"What merit did I create to be born as this son of heaven?"
He then examined himself and realized that it was because the parrot had requested the Buddha to stay for one night that he had been able to come and be born here.
"I must now go and repay the kindness of the World-Honored One."
Wearing a celestial crown upon his head and adorning his body with various necklaces and ornaments, he brought fragrant flowers as offerings to the Buddha and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to the heavens.
Then, at the break of dawn, the bhikṣus went before the Buddha and said to him:
"Regarding the radiance last night, was it that of Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Kings?"
"Is it the generals of the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts?
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:

"It was neither Śakra nor Brahmā, nor any of the various divine kings; rather, it was the king of the śukas (parrots) on the road who invited me and the Saṃgha to stay for one night among the forest trees. Having passed away, he was reborn in heaven and came to make offerings to me—it was his radiance."
Then the bhikṣus again addressed the Buddha, saying:
“What karma did this son of heaven create in his past lives to be born among the parrots?
And what merit did he cultivate to hear the Dharma and attain the fruit?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain it in detail for you."

In this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa. Within his Dharma, there was an elder who upheld the five precepts; however, at one time he violated one of them and was consequently reborn among the parrots. Because the other four precepts remained intact, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that upāsaka was at that time, he is the present Śuka-devaputra.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
57. The Story of the King Sending an Envoy to Invite the Buddha and His Subsequent Rebirth in Heaven (57). The Buddha was staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove in Rājagṛha.
When the summer retreat had concluded, he intended to travel to other lands with the bhikṣus.
At that time, the elder Sudatta addressed King Prasenajit, saying:

"We have not seen the Buddha for a long time now; I pray that Your Majesty will compose a letter and dispatch a messenger to invite the World-Honored One to come to this place, so that we may together make offerings to him."
When King Prasenajit heard these words, he immediately dispatched a messenger to invite the World-Honored One, conveying his greetings through a letter:
"I pay my respects from afar to the World-Honored One!"
"It has been a long time since we last had the honor of seeing you; we pray only that you will deign to show us compassion and come to accept our invitation.
At that time, the Tathāgata immediately granted his consent.
The messenger returned and informed the king, saying:
“The World-Honored One has granted permission.
The king commanded his messengers to adorn a carriage and, together with those messengers, went to welcome the World-Honored One, saying:
“We pray that you will deign to show us compassion; please mount this carriage and accept the king’s invitation.”
Then the Buddha replied:

"I possess the supernormal power of the sixfold abhijñā, the flower-garland of the seven factors of enlightenment, the constituent parts of the Eightfold Noble Path, and the peaceful carriage of the five vehicles; these are my supernormal powers, so you need not provide me with a carriage."
Then that messenger earnestly made his request three times:
"I only pray that you will take pity on us; do not employ your supernormal powers, but please accept the King's invitation by riding in this chariot."

At that time, the World-Honored One, out of compassion for the messenger, immediately ascended the carriage; by means of his supernormal powers, he caused the vehicle to travel through the air until they reached Rājagṛha, where he accepted the king’s invitation.
At that time, the messenger passed away during that very night and was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. He suddenly grew up to the size of an eight-year-old boy and thought to himself:
"By what merit did I cultivate myself to be born in this heavenly realm?"

He immediately examined himself and saw that while in the world, he had been employed by a king to urge the Buddha, the World-Honored One, to travel there by carriage and accept the king's invitation; by virtue of this wholesome mind, he had attained rebirth in heaven.
"I shall now return to repay the Buddha's kindness.

Adorning his head with a celestial crown and wearing various necklaces to embellish his body, he carried fragrant flowers whose radiance shone everywhere, illuminating the Jetavana Grove. He came to make offerings to the Buddha, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding attained, and he realized the fruit of Srotāpanna. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his celestial palace.
Then, at the early hour of the morning, the bhikṣus went before the Buddha and said to him:
"Was that light last night from Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Kings?"
"Are these the generals of the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts?
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"It is neither Śakra nor Brahmā, nor any of the kings of the gods, who have come to hear the Dharma. Rather, it is one sent by the king to invite me; because of this wholesome mind, he shall be reborn in the heavens. He has come to make offerings to me—it is his radiance."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 58.
The Story of the Buffalo Who Was Saved and Reborn as a Deva (58). The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Kośala, leading his bhikṣus, intending to go to the foot of the Laṅgula tree.
They arrived at a marsh where there were five hundred water buffaloes that were extremely fierce and malevolent.
There were also five hundred cowherds who, seeing the Buddha approaching from afar with his bhikṣus traveling along this path, cried out in a loud voice:
"We only pray that the World-Honored One will not travel by this path!"
"Within this herd of cattle, there is a large, vicious bull that gored and injured people; it is difficult to pass through.
At that time, the Buddha said to the cowherds: "You all, now!"
"Do not be greatly distressed or afraid!
Even if that water buffalo should come to gore me, I myself shall know the proper time.
While he was speaking these words, the wicked bull suddenly arrived, tail raised and horns lowered, pawing the ground and bellowing as it leaped straight forward.
At that time, the Tathāgata manifested five lions from the tips of his five fingers; they stood to the left and right of the Buddha, while great pits of fire surrounded him on all four sides.
At that time, the water buffalo was seized by great terror and fled in all four directions, finding no place to go.

Only before the Buddha’s feet was there a small patch of ground that was peaceful and cool; it rushed toward it, its mind becoming composed and free from further fear. It knelt down on its haunches and bowed its head, licking the World-Honored One’s feet, then raised its head again to gaze upon the Tathāgata, overcome with joy beyond measure.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that the mind of that wicked ox had been tamed, immediately addressed the ox in verse:
"With a fierce heart you gave rise to evil intent, Desiring to come and harm me;
Seeking victory through sincere devotion, You have instead returned to lick my feet."

At that time, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the water buffalo felt profound shame and remorse. Suddenly awakening to understanding, the clouds of obscuration were cleared away; he recognized the evil karma he had committed in his previous life while in the human realm. Feeling redoubled shame and remorse, he ceased eating water and grass, and immediately passed away.
Having been born in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, he suddenly grew to the size of an eight-year-old child and thought to himself:
"By what merit did I cultivate that I was born here in this heavenly realm?"
He then examined himself and realized that while in the world he had received the body of a water buffalo; having been transformed and delivered by the Buddha, he was now able to be reborn in heaven.
"I must now return to repay the Buddha's kindness," he thought.

Having formed this thought, he donned his celestial crown and various necklaces to adorn his body; carrying incense and flowers, he approached the place where the Buddha was. His radiance was brilliant and majestic, illuminating the World-Honored One. He prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then expounded the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding attained, and he realized the fruit of Srotāpanna. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his celestial palace.
Then, at the break of dawn, a cowherd addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Regarding that radiance last night—was it Śakra, Brahmā, or the Four Great Heavenly Kings?"
"Are these the generals of the twenty-eight classes of spirits and ghosts?
The Buddha told the cowherd:

"It is not Śakra, Brahmā, or the various divine kings who have come to hear the Dharma. Rather, it is those evil oxen of whom you spoke; because they saw me, their lives ended and they were reborn in heaven, where they have come to make offerings to me. This is their radiance."
At that time, having heard the Buddha’s words, the five hundred cowherds said to one another:
“If even that wicked water buffalo could see the Buddha and be reborn in the heavens,
how much more so should we, who are now human beings— why should we not cultivate various wholesome dharmas?”
Having spoken these words, they joined their palms in reverence to one another, prepared various delicacies, and invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha.

When the meal was finished, the Buddha preached the Dharma to them in various ways; their minds were opened and their intentions understood, and each attained the fruit of the Path, seeking to leave the household life.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!

His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa. Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all devas and worldlings.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen this matter, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"What karma did these water buffaloes and the five hundred cowherds create in their past lives to be born among the water buffaloes?"
"Furthermore, what merit did they cultivate to encounter the Buddha, the World-Honored One, leave the household life, and attain the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"If you now wish to know the causes and conditions of the various evil karmas created by the water buffalo and the cowherd in their past lives, I shall now recite a verse for you."
"Wholesome and unwholesome karma created in past lives does not perish even after a hundred eons;
by the causal conditions of wholesome karma, one now receives such a retribution.
When the bhikṣus had heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What was that matter like in the past? I only pray that the World-Honored One will [explain it to me]."
"Expound and explain it.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

Within this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha named Kāśyapa. During his Dharma, there was a bhikṣu learned in the Tripitaka who, leading five hundred disciples, traveled through other lands and engaged in discussion amidst a great assembly.
When there are those who pose difficult questions and he is unable to provide a thorough explanation, he gives rise to anger and instead reviles them further, saying:
"You people now have no understanding whatsoever; you insist on questioning me so forcefully, like water buffaloes charging headlong at a person."
At that time, all the disciples agreed, saying, "It was none other than him.
Having spoken these words, they each dispersed.

Because of the causal conditions of this evil karma of harsh speech, for five hundred lifetimes they were born among water buffaloes and cowherds, following one another until now, and thus have not yet attained liberation.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that bhikṣu versed in the Tripiṭaka was at that time, he is this very water buffalo among the herd here;
those who were his disciples at that time are these five hundred cowherds."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this account of the water buffalo, each person guarded their own actions of body, speech, and mind, and grew weary of birth and death. Among them, some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some of *anāgāmin*, and some of *arhat*; some conceived the aspiration for *pratyekabuddhahood*, and some conceived the aspiration for unexcelled *bodhicitta*.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
59. The Story of Two Brahmins Who Together Observed the Fast (59). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

During the first watch of the night, five hundred devaputras—wearing celestial crowns upon their heads, adorned with various necklaces and ornaments to grace their bodies, and carrying fragrant flowers whose brilliant radiance illuminated the Jetavana grove—approached the place where the Buddha was staying.

Having first prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and completed his offerings, he withdrew to sit to one side to listen to the Buddha’s teaching. His mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*. He circumambulated the Buddha three times and returned to his celestial palace.
At dawn, Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

Last night, a radiance illuminated the Jetavana Monastery, surpassing its usual brilliance. Was it Śakra, Brahmā, the Four Great Heavenly Kings, or the great generals of the twenty-eight divisions of spirits and ghosts who have come to listen to the Dharma?"
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"It is not that Śakra, Brahmā, or the various kings of the gods have come to listen to the Dharma; rather, it was during the time of the past Buddha Kāśyapa that there were two brahmins who followed a king to the place where the Buddha was, prostrating themselves and paying their respects."
At that time, there was a lay follower among them who exhorted the two brahmins, saying:
"You have now come along with the king to see the Buddha, the World-Honored One; you should therefore receive the precepts of fasting."
The brāhmaṇa said:
"What benefit is there in receiving this dharma of the fast?
The upāsaka replied:
"By observing this method of fasting, whatever you seek according to your wishes shall surely be fulfilled as you desire.
When the brahmin heard these words, he immediately observed the fast together with him; one sought rebirth in heaven, while the other sought to become a king of men.
Having completed the observance of the fast, they all returned together to the place where the brahmins were assembled.
The brahmins said, "You are hungry and thirsty; you may eat and drink together."
The one observing the fast said:
"I have observed the Buddha's fast; once the time has passed, I do not eat.
The brahmins said:
"We already possess our own Brahmanical laws; why must we accept the fast of those śramaṇas?

Since he had previously observed the fast together with him, he was born within the waters of the royal garden’s pond.

"Although I enter and exit [the palace], I am always stopped and turned back by the gatekeeper. I shall take this fruit and give it to him."
Having had this thought, he immediately took it and gave it to the gatekeeper.
Upon receiving it, the gatekeeper further thought:
"Although I enter and exit, I am still obstructed by this eunuch; I shall give it to him."
Having had this thought, he immediately took it and gave it to the eunuch.
Upon receiving it, the eunuch further thought:
"The Queen has always praised my virtues to the Great King on my behalf; I shall take this fruit and give it to her."
Having thought thus, he immediately brought it and gave it to the lady.
Having received it, the lady presented it to the Great King.
Once the King had received the fruit, he ate it immediately; perceiving it to be exceedingly fragrant and delicious, he then asked the lady:
"From where have you obtained these fruits?
The lady immediately replied truthfully,
"I obtained these fruits from a eunuch."
He further asked the eunuch,
"From where did you obtain these fruits?
Thus, through successive questioning, he traced them back to the gardener, whom the king immediately summoned.
"In my garden, there is such a beautiful fruit; why did you not bring it to me, but instead give it to another?
Thereupon, the gardener explained the matter from beginning to end.
The king did not heed his words, but said to him:
"From this day forward, you must constantly send these fruits; if you do not, I shall have you executed."
The gardener returned and entered his garden, wailing and weeping so profusely that he could not control himself.
"These fruits have no seeds; how could they possibly be obtained? he cried.
At that time, the Dragon King, hearing this sound of wailing, transformed himself into human form and came to ask him:

The gardener replied, "Yesterday,
I found a fine fruit in the pond of this garden and brought it to the gatekeeper;
having received it, the gatekeeper gave it in turn to a eunuch."
Having received it, the eunuch gave it to his wife;
having received it, the wife presented it to the king.
Now, observe this instruction:
"From this day forward, you must deliver these fruits; if you do not, you shall face execution.
Now, there is no seed of such fruit within this garden, and for this reason, we weep and wail.

At that time, having heard these words, the transformed person returned to the water, took some exquisite and delicious fruits, placed them upon a golden platter, and presented them to the gardener, further saying:

my precepts were incomplete, so I was born among the dragons.
Now I wish to return to the practice of the fasting ritual (upavāsa) in order to seek release from this body."

At that time, Āmrapālī accepted the fruit dish and, having presented it to the king, proceeded to repeat the words with which the nāga had entrusted her.
Upon hearing this, the king was deeply displeased.
The reason for this is that at such a time, even the name of the Buddha-dharma would not exist; how much less could the text of the Eightfold Precepts (Aṣṭāṅga-upavāsa) possibly be found?
"If I do not obtain it, I fear I shall meet with harm.
Reflecting on this matter, there is no way to accomplish my purpose.

The minister replied, "In this world there are no such teachings; how could they be obtained?"
The king spoke again, saying:
"If you do not succeed in finding someone to escort him away, I shall surely put you to death.
Having heard this, the minister withdrew and returned home; his countenance was unusual, and he was deeply distressed with grief.
At that time, the minister had a father who was advanced in years; whenever he returned from outside and saw his son’s countenance altered and unusual, he would immediately ask:
"What has happened to you?"
"Your complexion is such as this.
Thereupon, the minister immediately related the full circumstances and reasoning to his father.
The father replied to his son:

Thereupon, the minister followed his father's instruction and promptly went to cut it down. Having taken it and broken it open, they found two scrolls of scripture: one was on the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (*dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda*), and the other was a text on the Eight Precepts of the Fast (*aṣṭāṅgasamanvāgata-upavāsa*).
Having received it, the minister was filled with great joy; he placed it upon a golden tray and presented it to the king.
Upon receiving it, the king was overcome with delight and sent it to the Dragon King.
Having received them, the Dragon King was filled with great joy; he took precious jewels as gifts for the King and each returned to his own abode.

Together with five hundred dragon sons, he diligently practiced the Eight Precepts of the Fast. Later, when his life ended, he was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven and came to make offerings to me—it was that very light.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know those five hundred dragon sons who at that time reverently practiced the dharma of the fast, they are these five hundred devaputras here and now.

When the Buddha spoke this causal account, there were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; there were those who gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and there were those who gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.

The Story of the Five Hundred Geese Hearing the Buddha’s Dharma Teaching (60) The Buddha was staying in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, within a forested marsh, expounding the sublime Dharma for the sake of devas and worldlings.

At that time, there were five hundred flocks of wild geese in the air; hearing the Buddha preach the Dharma, they felt deep affection and joy in their hearts, and circling and soaring about, they descended to listen to the teaching.

At that time, there was a hunter who spread out a net; a flock of five hundred geese fell into it and were all killed by the hunters. Having ended their lives there, they were reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Suddenly he grew to the size of an eight-year-old boy, upright and exceptionally handsome; the radiance of the bodies of the devas and their palaces shone forth like a mountain of jewels.
He then thought to himself:
"By what merit did I cultivate that I have been reborn here in heaven?"

He then examined himself and realized that he had heard the Buddha preach the Dharma while in the body of a goose; having developed deep faith and joy, and by virtue of this wholesome mind, his life had ended and he was reborn here.
They then spoke these words:
"We shall now repay the Buddha's kindness.

Immediately, they simultaneously donned celestial crowns upon their heads, adorned their bodies with various necklaces, anointed them with many fragrant scents, and, carrying incense and flowers, came to where the Buddha was to make offerings to the World-Honored One.
Having completed the offerings, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit on one side, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!
Having now received the sublime Dharma expounded by the World-Honored Buddha, faith and joy have arisen in our hearts, and we shall be reborn in an excellent realm.”
"We only pray, World-Honored One!
Out of compassion for us, please explain once more and reveal the essentials of the Path.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately expounded various essential teachings for them. Their minds were opened and their understanding attained; the five hundred devaputras simultaneously realized the fruit of *srotāpanna*. With hearts full of joy, they circumambulated the Buddha three times, prostrated at his feet, and returned to the heavens.

"I pray that you will instruct me.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

Previously, while I was expounding the sublime Dharma to the devas and humans in a forest grove, there were five hundred flocks of geese who, out of love and reverence for the sound of the Dharma, felt great joy in their hearts. They flew together toward my location, intending to reach me, but were killed by a hunter.
"Because of this wholesome mind, he was able to be born in the heavens; therefore, he has come now to repay my kindness.
When Ānanda heard the Buddha speak these words, he marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence!

“The appearance of a Tathāgata in the world is truly sublime and wondrous; there are none who do not rely upon his grace. Even flying birds, upon hearing the Buddha’s voice, may yet attain the fruits of the Path;
how much more so for human beings who receive and uphold it with faith! Their merit exceeds that of the former by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all comparison.”
"Therefore, you all! You should be of one mind, believe in and revere the Buddha-dharma, and practice according to the Dharma.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, among the bhikṣus there were those who attained the stage of Srotāpanna, Sakṛdāgāmin, Anāgāmin, and Arhat; some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.

Story Sixty-one: The Circumstances of the Body Becoming Golden. The Buddha was staying at the Nigrodha tree grove in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, there was a householder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman of noble lineage to be his wife and provided her with various musical performances for her entertainment.

His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son whose body was golden in color, exceptionally handsome and marvelous, such as was rarely seen in the world; his body emitted a radiance that illuminated the city within, turning it all to gold.

At that time, the child’s parents, seeing him in such a state, felt great joy in their hearts and marveled at this unprecedented occurrence; they summoned various physiognomists to examine the child's marks.
Having observed this, the physiognomist asked his parents,
"What auspicious signs appeared at the time this child was born?
His parents replied:
"When this child was born, his body was golden in color and he was endowed with radiance.
For this reason, they bestowed upon him a name, calling him Kanakavarna (Golden-Body).
As he gradually grew up, his nature was virtuous and gentle, and he was compassionate, benevolent, filial, and obedient.
Hearing that there was a Buddha in the world beneath a nyagrodha tree, he took his kinsmen and friends and went to where the Buddha was.

Upon seeing the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance illuminating everywhere like a hundred thousand suns, his heart was filled with joy. He stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha immediately preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind opened and his understanding was realized, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He returned and said to his parents:
"Today I went to the foot of the Nyagrodha tree and beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One; his divine countenance was radiant and brilliant, like a hundred thousand suns.
I also saw the bhikṣus, their faculties serene and composed, their dignified deportment worthy of admiration—this is what my heart desires."
"I only pray that you will look upon me with compassion and grant me permission to leave the household life.
When the boy's parents heard these words, because of their deep affection for their son, they could not refuse him; they immediately took him to the Buddha’s presence to seek ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship; possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and endowed with the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What merit did this Golden-Colored Bhikṣu plant in his past lives such that he was born into a noble family, his body became golden in color, he encountered the World-Honored One, left the household life, and attained the Way?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Listen well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, ninety-one kalpas ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. Having completed his work of teaching and transforming beings, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, there was a king named Bandhumatī who collected the śarīras and erected a stūpa made of the four precious substances, one yojana in height, and made offerings to it.

At that time, there was a man who, while traveling, came upon a stupa that had some minor damage and peeling; he repaired it with mud, purchased gold leaf, and applied it to the surface before departing after making a vow.
By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas, he did not fall into the evil realms; among gods and humans, his body was always golden in color, and he experienced celestial bliss.
"Even until now, having encountered me, his body has become golden in color, and through leaving the household life he has attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that man was at that time who applied gold leaf, it is this present Bhikṣu Golden Color."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

74. The Story of the Bhikṣuṇī Sumana’s Eloquence (74). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin in that city named Brahmā, who was widely learned and possessed of eloquence; he clearly understood the sūtras and śāstras, and there was nothing among the four Vedas that he did not master. He chose a family of high standing and took a wife from it.
When ten months were complete, she gave birth to a daughter who was exceptionally beautiful and refined; her wisdom and eloquence were such that none could equal them.

Hearing the various Brahmins debate with her father, she was able to receive and retain it all without losing a single word; in this manner, through successive repetitions, what she had heard became vast.
The elders and senior monks all came to consult him, and there was nothing he did not understand.

Hearing that there was a Buddha in the world who had just attained perfect enlightenment and was teaching and transforming sentient beings, they sought to receive the flavor of the Dharma. Upon seeing the World-Honored One, with his thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns, they prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for her; her mind was opened and her understanding awakened, and she attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. She then requested to leave the household life.

"Welcome, Bhikṣuṇī!"
Her hair fell away of its own accord, the Dharma robes clothed her body, and she became a bhikṣuṇī.

“World-Honored One!

At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen well now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
Within this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha named Kāśyapa. Having completed his work of transforming sentient beings, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
