"In a future life, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, may I clearly understand the sūtras and śāstras."
Having made this vow, she passed away and was reborn among gods and humans, endowed with such intelligence and wisdom that none could equal her.
The Buddha told Ānanda:

"If you wish to know who it was that preached the Dharma and taught the bhikṣuṇīs at that time, she is the one who has now encountered me, left the household life, attained the Way, and is foremost in extensive learning."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
75. The Story of the Female Dancer Who Became a Bhikṣuṇī (Seventy-five). The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.
At that time, the wealthy and influential elders within the city each led others together to establish a great festival, performing various musical entertainments for their own amusement.

At that time, there were a husband and wife who were dance masters coming from the south, bringing with them a beautiful woman named Blue Lotus (Utpalavarṇā). She was exceptionally handsome and exquisite, rare in the world; she was intelligent and wise, such that it would be difficult for anyone to match her in debate.
She was fully proficient in all sixty-four arts possessed by women; she was skilled in the methods of dance, executing turns, postures, and inclinations with rhythmic precision, and she proclaimed:
"Is there anyone in this city who can dance as well as I?"
"Are you one who clearly understands the sūtras and śāstras, and is able to engage in questions and answers?
The man replied, "There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, staying at the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove; he is skilled in questions and answers and can cause you to have no more doubts."

Having heard this, the dancing girl immediately led the others along with her; singing and dancing, they arrived at the Bamboo Grove and beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, yet they remained arrogant and heedless, laughing and playing without showing reverence to the Tathāgata.

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing her in such a state, immediately employed his supernatural power to transform this dancing girl so that she appeared like a hundred-year-old old woman, with white hair, wrinkled face, sparse and missing teeth, and walking with a stooped back.
At that time, the dancing girl observed her own body and form, which had become extremely aged, and spoke these words:
"By what causes and conditions has such a state of senility and decay suddenly appeared in this body of mine?"
"This must surely be due to the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power that has caused me to be thus.
Immediately before the Buddha, he felt deep shame and remorse, and stepping forward, he addressed the Buddha, saying:
"At this moment, in the presence of the World-Honored One, I have been arrogant and conceited, letting my passions run wild and my mind unrestrained."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me forgiveness! At that time,
the World-Honored One, knowing that the mind of this dancer had been tamed, used his supernormal powers to transform the dancer's body back to its original state, no different than before.

At that time, the great assembly, seeing this dancer—how she was suddenly old and suddenly young, with no constancy whatsoever—each gave rise to weary detachment and realized impermanence; their minds were opened and their intentions liberated.

There were those who attained the stage of srotāpanna, sakṛdāgāmin, anāgāmin, and arhat; there were those who gave rise to the mind of a pratyekabuddha, and there were those who gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed bodhi.
At that time, the dancing girl, together with her parents, immediately sought ordination before the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣuṇīs!"
Her hair fell away of its own accord and the Dharma robes clad her body; she became a bhikṣuṇī.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, she attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations. She was revered and honored by devas and worldlings alike.
At that time, the great assembly, having witnessed this event, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"You have been able to transform these people of dissolute and seductive appearance who lack faith, causing them to attain awakening, leave the household life, and realize the Way."
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"It is not only now that I have been able to transform them!
In a past life as well, I transformed them."
At that time, the great assembly, having heard these words, again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What were the events like in past ages?"
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
“Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you.

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a crown prince named Sundarī who was the son of the King of Vārāṇasī. He entered the mountains to study the Way and attained the five supernormal powers.”

I saw a kinnarī woman, upright and exceptionally beautiful, appearing like a goddess; she displayed various graceful gestures while singing and dancing, stirring my heart with the hope of causing me to become defiled by passion and fall away from the path of the rishis.
At that time, my mind became firm and free from any thought of desire, and I said to her:

"All conditioned things are without permanence or stability. As I now observe you, your physical form is filled with foulness and impurity; covered only by a thin skin, it cannot be maintained for long."
"Very soon you shall have white hair and wrinkled faces, walking with a stoop.
Why do you now act with such arrogance and indulgence?
Your singing voice from earlier has already changed; for what reason do you display such coquettish gestures here?"
Thereupon, having heard these words, the kinnarī immediately turned toward the rishi, repented of her transgressions, and made this vow:
"May I, in a future life, attain the cessation of birth and death, and may I obtain the fruit of the Path from you."
The Buddha told the great assembly:
"If you wish to know who that prince practicing the way of the seers was at that time, it was I myself;
the kinnarī woman of that time is now the bhikṣuṇī Utpalavarṇā."
"Because of the power of the vow he made at that time, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
76. The Story of the Birth of the Kāśī Bhikṣuṇī Wearing a Kaṣāya (76). The Buddha was staying at the Deer Park in Vārāṇasī.

At that time, King Brahmadatta’s wife became pregnant; when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a daughter who was clad in a *kāṣāya* robe, of such exquisite beauty and grace that she was a rarity in the world.
He summoned various physiognomists to examine the girl's features.
Having observed her, the physiognomists asked her father, the king:
"When this girl was born, what auspicious signs were there?"
The father king replied, “When this girl was born, she was already wearing a *kāṣāya* robe; for that reason, she was given the name Kāśisundarī.
As she gradually grew up, her robes likewise grew with her. By nature she was virtuous and gentle, compassionate, benevolent, and filial.”

Accompanied by his attendants, he went out of the city to enjoy himself, traveling by stages until he arrived at the Deer Park (Mṛgadāva). There he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like that of a hundred thousand suns. With a heart full of joy, he approached and prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to sit to one side. The Buddha immediately preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Returning, he reported to his father the king:

"I have now gone out of the city to observe, and arrived at the Deer Park where I beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One. His body is adorned with the marks and signs of a hundred merits; his deportment is dignified and orderly, and his countenance is most worthy of admiration."
"I pray that Your Majesty, out of compassion and pity, will grant me permission to join the ranks of those on the Path.
At that time, the King, her father, out of pity for his daughter, could not refuse her; he led her to the Buddha’s dwelling to request ordination.
The Buddha then addressed her, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣuṇī!
Her hair fell away of its own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon her body, and she became a Bhikṣuṇī.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was fully endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all devas and people of the world.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the bhikṣus came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What merit did this bhikṣuṇī Kāśisundarī plant in her past lives such that she was born into a noble family, with this monastic robe appearing upon her body at birth, and further attained the fruits of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared in the world a Buddha named Kāśyapa Muni, who, accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, traveled about teaching and transforming sentient beings.
At that time, there was a princess who, while traveling, encountered the Buddha; her heart was filled with joy, and she went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, requesting him and the Saṃgha:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One..."
"Please accept from me for three months the fourfold offerings.
The Buddha immediately consented.
At the end of the three months, after having received the offerings, he further bestowed upon each of them a set of exquisite robes.
"By virtue of this merit, among gods and humans, she will always be honored, illustrious, and noble, and a *kāṣāya* will always be with her at birth.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that princess was at that time, she is now the bhikṣuṇī Sundarī."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
77. The Story of the Bhikṣuṇī with the Pearl Garland upon Her Forehead (77). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city named Vimala, whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation. He chose a woman from a distinguished family to be his wife, and provided various musical performances to entertain her.

His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a daughter who was exceptionally beautiful and rare in the world; upon her forehead there was naturally a pearl necklace.
When the parents saw this, they were filled with great joy and summoned various physiognomists to examine the girl's features.
Having observed her, the physiognomists asked her parents:
"What auspicious signs appeared at the time of this girl's birth?"
The parents replied,
"When this girl was born, a natural pearl necklace appeared upon her forehead.
Because of this, they gave her the name Muktikā (Pearl Necklace).

As she gradually grew older, her nature was virtuous and kind; she felt compassion for the orphaned and the destitute, and whenever anyone came to beg, she would take off this pearl necklace and give it to them immediately, whereupon it would grow back again, no different from before.

At that time, the elder Sudatta heard from Bīsala that he had such a beautiful daughter; he sent a messenger with a letter and message to request the pearl necklace, wishing to betroth her as a wife for his son.
At that time, having heard that Sudatta was seeking a wife for his son, Muktikā came forward and said to her parents:
"Out of compassion and pity, if you wish to give me to that boy, you must make a solemn vow that we shall both go forth from the household life together; only then may you give me to him."
"If it were not so, I would not be attached to worldly glory and splendor.
At that time, because the girl’s parents loved her dearly, they could not refuse her; they immediately went there and spoke to Sudatta, fully expressing the girl's intention.
When Sudatta heard these words, he agreed with him; they were immediately married.
Before long, both felt a sense of world-weariness and, taking one another’s hands, went to where the Buddha was to seek ordination.
The Buddha then addressed her, saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣuṇī!
Her hair fell away of its own accord, the dharma robes were donned upon her body, and she became a bhikṣuṇī.

Through diligent cultivation, each attained the fruits of the Path; endowed with the three insights, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, they were revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What merit did this husband and wife who possess this pearl necklace cultivate in their past lives, such that at birth it appeared spontaneously—this pearl necklace being worn upon their heads—and having not long since left the household life, they have attained the fruit of arhatship?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha in the world named Kāśyapa. Leading a company of bhikṣus, he turned the wheel of the True Dharma within the Deer Park, delivering and liberating sentient beings.
At that time, there was an elder named Aśvala who, hearing that the Buddha was there converting sentient beings, spoke these words:
"I shall exhort the people of the city to perform a *pañcavārṣika* assembly for the sake of the Buddha and the Sangha."

Having spoken these words, he reported them to the king; then, riding upon a great white elephant, he traveled through the marketplaces and, at every street corner, exhorted the people to perform the Pañcavārṣika festival.
At that time, there was a woman who, seeing his exhortation and conversion, took a pearl from atop her head and immediately untied it to give him.
When her husband returned from outside and saw that there was no pearl garland on his wife's head, he immediately asked:
"To whom did you give this pearl garland?"
The wife replied to her husband:
"The elder Asāḷha has come here and is exhorting and transforming the people;
I have taken off this pearl and am holding it out to give as an offering."
The man was immediately filled with joy; he took another precious jewel and used it for almsgiving, making this vow:
"May I not fall into the evil realms in future lives; among gods and humans, may a jeweled garland always be born together with me."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because of the gift of that jewel at that time, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
78. The Story of the Reconciliation of Two Kings upon the Birth of Bhikṣuṇī Kṣemā (78). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit and King Brahmadatta were constantly at odds and contending with one another; each leading a host of troops—elephant forces, cavalry, chariot forces, and infantry—they stationed themselves on opposite banks of a river, each establishing boundary markers.
When the months were complete, each lady gave birth to a child, either a son or a daughter, who were exceptionally handsome and marvelous.
The King was greatly delighted; he beat the drums and proclaimed an edict, assembling his military forces and bestowing wealth and goods upon them all, as they celebrated together in joy.
Seeking reconciliation, they said, "Let us form a marriage alliance so that from this day forward, our two nations shall never again offend one another, even unto our descendants.
Having made this covenant, each returned to his own country.

At that time, Prince Brahmadatta was seven years of age; he brought various kinds of precious gems and miscellaneous articles as gifts to King Prasenajit, seeking to enter into marriage with his daughter.
When the girl heard this, she addressed her father, the king, saying:
"A human body is difficult to obtain; I have now obtained it.
The faculties are difficult to possess in their entirety; I have now possessed them."
Faith is difficult to produce, yet now faith has been born;
a Buddha’s appearance in the world is difficult to encounter, yet now I have encountered one.
I only pray, Great King!
"Do not leave this daughter of yours amidst various perils, causing her to be forever separated from all spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra).
I only pray that you will show her compassion and grant me permission to renounce the household life.
The king replied to the girl:
"When you were in the womb, I granted him my promise;
it was because of you that the two nations became harmonious and friendly, no longer encroaching upon one another.

If I were now to fail to honor his request, I would violate my word and my integrity. He would surely return and treat me as an enemy; the devas would despise me and cease to provide their protection; the ministers and the people would lose all trust in me; and I would also contravene the ancient laws and regulations established by former kings."
Have you not heard that King Ajātaśatru, King Bimbisāra, and dozens of other kings like them all fell into hell because of their false speech?
Why now do you wish to cause me to suffer the torments of hell like those other kings by telling a lie?
It is not fitting for you to offer such a request to me.
When King Prasenajit had finished speaking these words, he immediately dispatched a messenger to King Brahmadatta, telling him to come quickly within seven days to take her in marriage.
The messenger, having received these instructions, went quickly to that place and said to King Brahmadatta:
"Within seven days, I shall be married.

At that time, when the princess heard that the king had dispatched a messenger to summon her, she was filled with grief and distress. She put on soiled garments, cast off all her ornaments, and disfigured her appearance; she then ascended to a high tower, knelt for a long time with palms joined, and spoke these words while facing toward the Jetavana from afar:
“Tathāgata, World-Honored One!
You possess great compassion and pity for all sentient beings, being able to know the three periods of time within a single thought-moment.
I am now beset by suffering and distress; I pray that you will look upon me with mercy and grant me deliverance.”

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar the princess’s sincere earnestness and her piteous plea for deliverance, manifested before her in an instant and preached various Dharmas; her mind was opened and her understanding clarified, and she attained the fruit of Anāgāmin.
On the seventh day, Prince Brahmadatta, accompanied by several tens of millions of attendants and carrying various precious jewels and diverse garments, came intending to take a wife.

Upon arriving at her palace, he wished to take her as his wife, but he suddenly realized she was no longer a woman; she was in mid-air, performing the eighteen miraculous transformations—leaping up in the east and sinking down in the west, leaping up in the south and sinking down in the north, walking, standing, sitting, and reclining with sovereign mastery over her manifestations—before finally descending from the sky.
At that time, King Prasenajit, seeing the woman in such a state, was deeply struck with terror and said to her:
"I am now ignorant and deluded; I did not know you possessed such supernatural powers, and thus I defiled you with impurity and worldly taints."
"Having repented for your transgressions, I permit you to leave the household life.
Her husband, the prince, also gave rise to faith and reverence, saying these words:
"I too was foolish and lacked discernment to harbor such thoughts."
"I pray that you will also grant me permission to repent for my transgressions and allow you to leave the household life.
At that time, having heard these words, the princess immediately went to the Jeta Grove, where she saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and requested ordination.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission; she became a bhikṣuṇī and, through diligent cultivation, attained the fruit of arhatship.
When the bhikṣus witnessed this event, they said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One!”
"Now, what merit did this Bhikṣuṇī Kṣamā plant in her past lives that she was born into a royal family, remained free from lustful thoughts, and attained the Way upon leaving the household life?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively; I shall explain this to you in detail."
In this Bhadrakalpa, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there appeared a Buddha named Kāśyapa.
Within his Dharma, there was a woman who did not feel mutual affection for her husband; they were constantly at odds and quarreling with one another.
Every day, they would each exhort one another to go to the bhikṣus and receive the eightfold precepts of the fast, and thereby together make this vow:
"May we, in whatever place we are born, be honorable, illustrious, and wealthy; and amidst strife and contention, may we always live in harmony and reconciliation."
Having made this vow, they each reached the end of their lives according to the length of their respective lifespans and were reborn together in a royal family.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If you wish to know who that husband and lord was at that time, he is now King Brahmadatta.”
The father-in-law at that time was the present King Prasenajit;
the husband at that time was the present prince;
and the wife at that time was the present princess.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
79. The Story of King Prasenajit’s Ugly Daughter (79) The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, King Prasenajit’s Queen Māllī gave birth to a daughter whose countenance was exceedingly ugly, whose body was coarse and rough like snake skin, and whose hair was coarse and stiff like horse tails.
When the king saw this woman, he felt not the slightest joy; he then commanded the inner palace:
"Guard her with diligent care, and do not allow her to go outside where others may see her."
The king thought to himself:
"Although this girl is ugly and her appearance is unlike that of a human, she was born of Queen Mallikā; therefore, I shall raise her."
As the years passed and she grew older, it became time for her to be married.
At that time, the king was filled with anxiety and wondered what he should do;
having no other recourse, he addressed a minister:
"You may search for one who was originally of a noble clan and lineage, but who is now impoverished and possesses no wealth; bring such a person here.
The minister immediately received these instructions and went everywhere to seek him out. He found the son of a poor noble family, summoned him, and brought him before the king.
When the king saw this man, he went with him to a secluded place and spoke to him in private:
"I have heard that you, though from a noble family, are now impoverished; I shall provide for you."
"I have a daughter whose appearance is extremely ugly; I hope Your Majesty will not refuse her, but will accept her as your wife.
At that time, the poor man knelt for a long time and said to the king, "I shall obey your command."
"Even if Your Majesty were to grant me a dog, I would accept it and not disobey the King's command;
how much more so now for this daughter born of Queen Mallikā?"
"If you now grant me this in favor, I shall accept it by your command.
The King then gave his daughter in marriage to that poor man; he built a residence for them and secured the doors and gates so firmly that they were sevenfold.
The king instructed his daughter’s husband:
“From now on, you must grasp the door-bolt yourself; whenever you wish to go out, close it yourself.
My daughter is hideous, so do not allow outsiders to see her face.”
"She always keeps her door firmly closed, with the bolt fastened from within.
The king provided wealth and goods according to whatever his son-in-law required, ensuring he lacked for nothing.
The king immediately prostrated himself and appointed him as a great minister.
Thereafter, he possessed abundant wealth and jewels, lacking for nothing.
He joined with various noble clans to form a guild association, which rotated its leadership month by month.
At the time of the assembly, husbands and wives came together; men and women mingled, enjoying themselves in mutual pleasure.
All those who attended the gathering each brought their own wives to the assembly, yet that minister alone did not bring his wife.
The crowd was filled with doubt and wonder:
"If that man's wife were upright and virtuous, her countenance would surely be radiant;
yet if she were exceedingly ugly, it would not be fitting for her to appear in public."
"Therefore, that man has not brought his wife with him.
We should now devise a plan to go and observe her.

Thereupon, they all agreed in spirit and secretly consulted one another; they offered him wine to encourage him until he was intoxicated and lay prostrate on the ground. They then took the door-bolt and dispatched five men to his house to open the door and observe his wife.
At that time, her heart was filled with distress as she reproached herself for her transgressions:
"What sin have I sown that I am so loathed by my husband? Why am I constantly confined in this dark chamber, unable to see the sun, the moon, or any other person?"
He further thought to himself:
"Now that the Buddha is in the world, he constantly observes all sentient beings with compassion; whenever there is one in distress or peril, he immediately goes to deliver them."
At that time, the woman immediately paid homage from afar with a sincere heart to the World-Honored One, saying:
"I pray only that you will take pity on me!
Come before me for a moment to grant me your instruction."

The girl’s sincerity was such that her reverent mind was pure and profound. The Buddha, knowing her intention, went immediately to her home; before the girl, he manifested the mark of the deep-blue hair, emerging from the earth.

The girl raised her head and beheld the mark of the Buddha’s hair; her joy redoubled and her heart of reverence became exceedingly deep. Her own hair then naturally became fine and soft, possessing the characteristic color of deep blue-black.

As the Buddha gradually revealed his face, the woman saw him; her heart was filled with joy, and her countenance became upright and handsome, while her evil features and coarse skin naturally vanished.
The Buddha gradually manifested his body, its golden hue radiating brilliantly, causing the woman to behold it.
Upon seeing the Buddha’s form, her joy increased all the more; his body was so upright and majestic that he resembled a celestial maiden.

The Buddha then expounded for him various essential teachings; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. His heart was filled with such exultation that it was beyond compare in this world.
Then the Buddha departed.
At that time, the five men opened the door and entered within; seeing his upright and majestic form, which was exceptionally wondrous and peerless, the five men each said to one another:
"I wondered why this man had not brought his wife, yet upon seeing her, she is so exceedingly beautiful.
Having finished observing her, he firmly closed the doors and fastened the door-bolt back onto the man's headband at its original place.
When the assembly had dispersed and each had returned home, he entered his house and saw that his wife was exceptionally beautiful and far surpassed others in her grace.
Delighted, he asked her: "Who are you?"
The wife replied to her husband, "I am your wife.
The husband then asked:
“You were extremely ugly before; for what reason have you now become so handsome?
His wife answered her husband with all that had transpired:
“It is by virtue of the Buddha’s divine power that I have now obtained such a body.”
The wife spoke again to her husband:
"Now, it is my wish to meet with the King; you should convey this intention to him on my behalf.
The husband accepted her words and immediately went to inform the King.
"The young woman wishes to come and see you now.
The king replied to his daughter's husband:
"Do not speak of such a thing; you must quickly and securely lock her up and take care that she does not go out."
The groom replied to the king:
"Why have things come to this?
This maiden has now, through the majestic spiritual power of the Buddha, attained such exquisite beauty that she is no different from a celestial nymph."
Having heard this, the king said,
"If it is truly so, go quickly and bring her here.
He immediately prepared a carriage and went to welcome the woman into the palace.
When the king beheld the maiden’s form—so upright, extraordinary, and peerless in the world—he was filled with immeasurable joy, unable to contain himself.

The king immediately issued orders to prepare a carriage, and they went together to the Buddha’s dwelling. There, he prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, withdrew to sit to one side, and knelt for a long time, addressing the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!...”
I do not understand what merit this woman planted in her past lives such that she was born into a family of noble status, wealth, and pleasure?
And what karma did she create to receive such an ugly form, with skin and hair as coarse and tough as those of a beast?
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will grant me an exposition!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great King’s consort:
"Listen well now, and I shall explain it for you.
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a great kingdom named Vārāṇasī. There lived a householder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation."

At that time, the elder, together with his entire household, constantly made offerings to a pratyekabuddha whose body was coarse and unrefined, and whose appearance was so hideous and emaciated as to be unbearable to behold.
At that time, there was a young daughter in the house of the elder who, seeing the Pratyekabuddha approaching, gave rise to an evil mind of contempt and spoke words of abuse and disparagement:
"His face and features are ugly, and his skin is coarse and foul; how loathsome he is!"

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha frequently went to his house to receive his offerings. Having remained in the world for a long time, he desired to enter nirvana; he then manifested great supernormal powers for him, leaping into the air, emitting water and fire from his body, rising in the east and sinking in the west, and rising in the south and sinking in the north. In mid-air, he performed walking, standing, sitting, and reclining, manifesting transformations at will so that everyone in the elder’s household could see them.
Descending from the sky once more, she arrived at the house of the elder; the elder was so filled with joy that he could not contain himself.
The girl immediately repented her transgression and reproached herself, saying:
"I only pray that you will show me compassion!"

I pray that you will grant me your forgiveness; my former evil intentions were grave offenses and transgressions. I hope you will not harbor them in your heart, but will now accept my repentance so that no guilt remains.
The Buddha told the Great King:
"If you wish to know who that daughter of the elder was at that time, because she reviled the Pratyekabuddha, she has constantly received an ugly form in all her subsequent places of birth."

Later, having witnessed his supernatural transformations, he repented toward him; therefore, he has now attained such upright and handsome features, transcendent and extraordinary, with none equal to him.

Because he made offerings to the Pratyekabuddha, in every place where he was born, he was always born into wealthy families, honored, illustrious, and noble, lacking for nothing, and furthermore encountered me, whereby he was liberated from his sorrows and suffering.

At that time, King Prasenajit, along with his ministers and subjects, having heard the Buddha’s discourse on the causes and conditions of karmic retribution, had their minds opened and their intentions clarified. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat; some resolved to attain the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some resolved to attain unexcelled Bodhicitta.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 80.
The Story of the Robber (Lūḍaka-purāṇa-kathā). The Buddha was staying at Vaiśālī in the Multi-storied Lecture Hall.
At that time, there was a foolish man in that city whose mind was constantly delighted by theft as his livelihood; this was known to all the people of that land.

Furthermore, at one time, hearing that there was a fine copper jar within a monastic dwelling (saṃghārāma), he intended to steal it. He then went with several travelers into the monastery, wishing to steal the jar, but in the end he did not succeed.
There, he heard various bhikṣus recite a four-line verse (gāthā) discussing how the blinking of the eyes of the devas is extremely slow, whereas that of worldly people is swift.
At that time, having heard these words, the thief took them to heart and immediately departed.
At that very moment, there were some merchants arriving from another land who brought a highly valuable maṇi jewel to present as an offering to the king.
Once the king had obtained the pearl, he immediately dispatched men to fasten it to the pinnacle of the stūpa.

At that time, the thief, hearing that the king had fastened the pearl to the top of the stūpa’s finial, kept this secret in his heart; he then stole it and concealed it, not coming forward to reveal its whereabouts.
When the king heard that the pearls had been lost from the stupa's pinnacle, he was seized with great anger and immediately issued a proclamation throughout the kingdom:
"Should anyone see them, come secretly to inform me; I shall grant a generous reward."
Thus several days passed, yet no one dared to respond to the call.
At that time, King Yuan was beset by resentment and had no plan left to follow.
Then there was a wise minister who addressed the king, saying:

“Now, within the capital of Your Majesty’s realm, there is boundless abundance and joy; thieves are very few, yet this one man alone makes theft his profession to sustain himself, as is known by all throughout the land.”
"This precious jewel must have been seen and stolen by that man.
If we were now to bind him and subject him to flogging and whipping, he would certainly refuse to confess."
"Your Majesty should devise a plan; how can you determine whether that man's stratagem is real or false?
The King asked his wise minister:
"What plan should be devised?"

The wise minister replied, “Secretly dispatch other persons to invite the thieves; encourage each of them with wine and food until they are thoroughly intoxicated, then carry them onto the palace terrace so that they remain unaware.”
The halls and pavilions were adorned, and the female musicians were made exceedingly exquisite; they performed various kinds of music to entertain him.
At this, the thief would surely be startled awake.
He commanded all the celestial maidens, each of whom spoke thus:

"Because you stole the crest-jewel from the stupa in Jambudvīpa, you have now been born here in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven; we, the celestial maidens, shall perform songs and music together to attend upon you."
"Is it truly so?
At that time, the thief was dazed and intoxicated; he wished to speak the truth, yet feared it might not be right, and he wished not to speak, yet was pressured by the women to say something.
At that time, the thief suddenly recalled:

"In the past, I heard the discourses spoken by śramaṇas: 'The blinking of the eyes of devas is extremely slow, while that of worldly people is rapid. Now, these female performers blink so rapidly; they must certainly not be devas."
He immediately lowered his head and refused to speak.
Not long after, he regained his senses; the official did not charge him with a crime, and he escaped death.
Then that wise minister spoke again to the king:
"We should devise another stratagem to steal the man.
The king asked again:
"What stratagem should be employed?

The wise minister replied, "The King may feign intimacy and summon that thief, granting him the rank of high minister. Then, having secretly calculated the total number of items in all the treasuries, entrust them all to him."
At a later time, the king may speak to him with gentle words:
"Now there is no one as dear to me as you; guard the treasury well and let nothing be lost or stolen.
Upon hearing this, the thief will surely feel great joy.
The King may ask slowly:
"Do you know of the mani-jewel that I previously wore and which was tied to the pillar of the stupa?
The thief will surely confess the truth.
"How do we know this?
Now that you have become king, you are held in high esteem; all wealth and treasures are entrusted to you, and they will surely come forward and confess to you.
At that time, King Prasenajit, following the advice of his minister, devised a plan and strategy.
Thereupon the thief, following the words of the wise minister, confessed the truth to the king:
"This precious gem was indeed stolen by me, a slave; I was afraid and did not dare to come forward."
The king asked again:
"Previously, you were lying drunk upon my palace floor while the women questioned you.
Now that you are in the heavens, why do you not confess?"
The thieving minister replied,

"In the past, I once entered a monastic dwelling and heard various bhikṣus reciting a four-line verse, which said that the blinking of the eyes of the devas is extremely slow, whereas the speed of worldly people is swift."
Upon reflecting and recollecting this, he knew that it was not born from being in the heavens, and for this reason he did not claim it as his own.
Thereupon, King Prasenajit recovered the precious gem; filled with great joy, he did not inquire after the transgressions committed by his minister who had stolen it.
Then that thief-minister, having been released, came forward and said to the king:
"I pray you, forgive my transgression and permit this servant to leave the household life.
The king said to the thief-minister:
"You are now honored and illustrious, wealthy, noble, and happy; this is indeed most fitting for you.
For what reason now do you insist on leaving the household life?
The minister-thief replied to the king:
"Since I have heard from a śramaṇa a single four-line verse, I have escaped this deadly calamity;
how much more so for one who is learned, recites and practices it, and practices according to the teaching—such a person will certainly obtain great benefit."
"Therefore, I now wish to leave the household life.

Through diligent and arduous cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was fully endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all devas and worldlings.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
