Chapter Nine: The Disciples. Disciples Chapter, Number Nine.
Story Eighty-One: The Merchant Captain Samudra. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there were five hundred merchants in that city who wished to enter the great ocean to gather precious treasures.
Then, the leader of the caravan selected a woman of noble lineage and betrothed her as his wife.
They were about to set out together upon the sea; when ten months had been completed, she gave birth to a son, for whom they established the name Sāgaraja (Sea-born).
Possessing great merit and virtue, he enabled all the merchants to obtain vast treasures and return in safety, whereupon they all cried out together: "Sāgaraja is safe!"
As he grew older, his parents repeatedly exhorted him to enter the great ocean once more to obtain precious jewels, and so he set out on his return journey.
There, he encountered a great black wind that blew his ship, casting it adrift into the realm of the rākṣasa demons amidst swirling waves and dark gales.
At that time, the merchants each knelt and prostrated themselves before the various devas and benevolent spirits, yet not one responded or rescued them from their distress.
Among them was an upāsaka who said to the merchants:

"There is a Buddha, a World-Honored One, who constantly, with great compassion, observes sentient beings throughout the six periods of day and night. He protects those suffering in calamity and distress, immediately going to deliver them."
"You all should together invoke the name of that Buddha; perhaps he will come here to save our lives.
Then, at that very moment, the merchants all simultaneously cried out, "Namo Buddhāya! (Homage to the Buddha!)

At that time, the World-Honored One, seeing from afar that the merchants were encountering extreme peril, immediately emitted a radiance that illuminated the black wind, which was instantly extinguished.
All were liberated, and each spoke these words:

"We have now, by the majestic light of the Buddha, escaped these various calamities. If we reach our destination safely, we shall build stupas and monasteries for the Buddha and the Sangha; we shall invite the Buddha and the Sangha to dwell therein, provide them with various delicacies, and supply all their needs so that they lack for nothing."
Having spoken these words, they all agreed.
Thereupon they set forth, and everyone reached their home country in safety and peace.

In accordance with their previous agreement, they constructed stūpas and monasteries, invited the Buddha and the Saṃgha, prepared various delicacies, and completed the offerings. Then, withdrawing to sit on one side, they listened to the Buddha’s teaching; their minds were opened and their understanding clarified, and each attained the fruits of the Path. They immediately sought ordination before the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣus!
Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.

Through diligent and ardent cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship; endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by devas and humans alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen these events, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!

What karma did these five hundred merchants and bhikṣus create in their past lives such that they encountered these various calamities and hardships? How is it that, by relying on the majestic radiance of the Buddha, they were able to escape all perils, and furthermore, having met the World-Honored One, they left the household life and attained the Way?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"It is not only today that I have rescued him from his distress; in past lives as well, I rescued him and delivered him from all calamities."
Then the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha again, saying:
“We do not understand, World-Honored One!
What were the events like in a past life?”
"I only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain this!
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain this to you in detail.
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a seer possessing the five supernatural powers who dwelt on the bank of a river."

At that time, there were five hundred merchants who wished to enter the great ocean; as their route led along the riverbank, they saw the rishi and each approached him to inquire after his well-being, urging the rishi to accompany them into the sea.
The seer replied, "You may go on your way yourselves; should you encounter fear or danger, simply invoke my name and I shall protect you.

When the merchants heard these words, they proceeded into the sea and obtained a great abundance of precious treasures. As they were returning home, they encountered on the road the perils of rākṣasas and black winds.
At that time, the merchants, with one mind, invoked the name of the seer, and he immediately went to rescue and protect them, delivering them from all their calamities and hardships.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that seer was at that time, it was I myself."
Those five hundred merchants at that time are now these five hundred bhikṣus.
At that time, even though I had not yet severed my afflictions, I was still able to rescue them from their various perils;
how much more so now, having escaped the three realms, should I be unable to transform and deliver them?
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 82.
The Story of the Birth with a Sumanā Flower Garment Adhering to the Body (82). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman from a noble family and took her as his wife, providing her with all kinds of music for her entertainment.
When ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and marvelous; a garment of sumana flowers was born with his body.
She summoned various physiognomists to examine and interpret the child's marks.
The physiognomist, having observed this, asked:
"What auspicious signs appeared at the time this child was born?
His parents replied:
"He was born wrapped in garments of *sumana* flowers;
because this was established as his name, he was called Sumanas.
His nature was virtuous and gentle, and he was compassionate and filial."
As he gradually grew older, his robes likewise grew large.
Out of affection, his parents took the young boy and gave him to Aniruddha, requesting that he become a śrāmaṇera and instructing him to practice seated meditation.

Before long, he attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all devas and people of the world.
At that time, Aniruddha commanded a śrāmaṇera, saying:
"You should now go to the banks of the Bahudā River and fetch pure water.
He immediately went to that river, filled a flask with water, and threw it into the air; it then flew back after him.
At that time, the bhikṣus, seeing this śrāmaṇera, marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What merit did this Śrāmaṇera Sumana plant in his past lives that he was born into a family of great wealth, and that the *sumana* flower robe was born along with his body?"
“Not long after going forth, he attained the fruit of arhatship?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Listen well!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, a Buddha appeared in the world named Vipaśyin. Having completed his work of teaching and transforming others, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, there was a king named Brahmadatta who collected the relics and constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances to make offerings to them.

At that time, there was a youth who, upon seeing that stupa, felt joy in his heart and immediately left the household life. When he reached old age, he had gained nothing at all; deeply reproaching himself, he bought *sumana* flowers, strung them together with thread, and covered the entire top of the stupa before departing while making a vow.

By virtue of this merit, for ninety-one kalpas, he did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts. Among gods and humans, he was always born with *sumana* flower garments upon his body, enjoying celestial bliss until now, when he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
83. The Story of the Bhikṣu Ratnapāṇi (83). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city who possessed immeasurable wealth and treasures. He selected a woman from a family of noble repute and took her as his wife, providing her with entertainment through the performance of music and dance.

His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and marvelous, such as was rarely seen in the world. From his two hands, gold coins emerged; once taken, they would reappear, and though this process continued repeatedly, the coins could not be exhausted.
He summoned various physiognomists to examine the child's marks.
Having observed him, the physiognomists asked:
"What auspicious signs were there at the time this child was born?"
The parents replied, "From his two hands, gold coins emerge; as soon as they are taken, they reappear.
Because of this, they gave him the name Ratnapāṇi, meaning "Jewel-Handed."

As he gradually grew older, his innate nature was virtuous and gentle; he possessed a compassionate heart and was filial and obedient. He delighted in giving alms, and whenever anyone came to beg, he would stretch out both hands; if he had fine gold coins, he would immediately give them away.

Accompanied by his kinsmen and friends, he went out of the city to observe the sights; traveling by stages, he arrived at the Jeta Grove and beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns. With a heart full of joy, he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and, with palms joined, invited the Buddha and the community of bhikṣus, saying:
“Out of compassion and pity, please accept my offerings.”
At that time, Ānanda was standing by the Buddha’s side and asked the boy,
"If you wish to provide an offering,
you will need wealth and treasures. Upon hearing Ānanda’s words, the boy immediately extended both hands, and gold coins fell like rain, accumulating in an instant.
The Buddha commanded Ānanda:
"Now take these gold coins and precious goods, prepare the delicacies, and invite the Buddha and the Sangha.
Having received these instructions, Ānanda prepared the food and drink.
When the offerings were completed, the Buddha preached the Dharma for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He returned to inform his parents and requested permission to enter the Path.
Out of their parents' affection and concern, they could not go against their wishes; so they were led to the Buddha’s dwelling to seek ordination.
The Buddha then addressed them, saying:
"Welcome, bhikṣus!"
His beard and hair fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship; endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, having witnessed this event, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what merit did this Bhikṣu Ratnapāṇi plant roots in his past lives that he was born into the family of a wealthy and eminent elder? Furthermore, how is it that his two hands possess these gold coins which, as soon as they are taken, regenerate;
and how is it that, meeting the World-Honored Buddha, he has attained the fruits of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall explain this to you in detail."
In this present Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa. Having completed his work of teaching and transforming others, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the king of that land, named Kāśi, collected the relics and constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances.
At that time, there was an elder who, seeing him setting up the crossbar, felt sympathetic joy in his heart; he took a single gold coin, placed it beneath the bar, and departed after making a vow.

By virtue of these merits, he did not fall into the evil realms; among gods and humans, gold coins would always appear as soon as he extended his hand. Even until now, having encountered me, he possesses gold coins which he takes and returns; having left the household life, he has attained the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 84.
The Story of the Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu (84). The Story of the Tripiṭaka Bhikṣu: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, the consort of King Prasenajit was pregnant; when her ten months were complete, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and rare in the world. He was clad in a *kāṣāya* robe and, immediately upon birth, was able to speak, asking his father the king:
"Is the Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, present now?"
"Venerable Kāśyapa, Śāriputra, Mahāmaudgalyāyana—have you thus inquired after all the great disciples, and are they all present? The Father King replied, "They are all here now."
“May Your Majesty, for my sake, provide an offering and invite the Buddha and the Sangha.
He immediately issued the command to prepare it and invited the Buddha into the palace; there he saw the crown prince and asked him:
"Do you yourself remember that during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, you were this bhikṣu of the Tripiṭaka?
He replied, "Indeed I was."
“Was it peaceful while dwelling in this womb?
“Having received the Buddha’s grace, I have preserved my life and been able to pass the days and nights.
At that time, the King’s consort, seeing the Prince and the World-Honored Buddha conversing with one another, was overcome with joy and addressed the Buddha, saying:
“By what merit did this crown prince plant roots in his past lives that he was able to speak as soon as he was born, and is now able to engage in dialogue with the Buddha?
We pray only that the World-Honored One [will explain].”
"Expound and explain it.
Thereupon, the World-Honored One spoke these verses for the king:
"The various wholesome karmas created in past lives do not decay even after a hundred kalpas."
"By the causal conditions of wholesome karma, one now obtains such a retribution.
At that time, King Prasenajit and his queen, having heard these verses spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"We do not understand, World-Honored One!"
What were the events of that past life?
We only pray that the World-Honored One will expound and explain them in detail.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Great King, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Kāśyapa. Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, he traveled about teaching and transforming beings until he arrived at the kingdom of King Kāśi.

At that time, the king’s crown prince, named Sujāta, upon seeing the Buddha, the World-Honored One, conceived deep faith and reverence; he returned to inform the Great King and requested permission to enter the Path.
The king did not grant permission, saying:
"I have but this one son, who shall succeed me on the throne and nurture the people; I will never allow you to leave the household life to enter the Way."

When the prince heard these words, he was overcome with grief and fell to the ground; he broke off his grain and ceased to eat for one day, two days, and even up to six days, abstaining entirely from food and drink.
At that time, the various ministers addressed the king, saying:
"The Crown Prince has not eaten for six days already; we fear his life may not be preserved.
We pray that Your Majesty will now grant him permission to leave the home-life, so that we may yet behold him."
When the Great King heard the minister’s words, he could not refuse them and commanded his crown prince:

"Make a solemn vow with me: if you can now read and recite the scriptures of the Tripitaka until you have mastered them, I shall permit you to leave the household life; only then may you come to see me."

At that time, having heard the king’s command, the prince was filled with joy; he immediately left the household life and applied himself diligently to the study and recitation of the Tripiṭaka, mastering them all thoroughly before returning to see the king.
The king asked the bhikṣu,
"I previously commanded you that you must first master the recitation of the Tripiṭaka scriptures before coming to see me.
Are you proficient in them now?"
The bhikṣu replied,
“I have now mastered them all.
The king was greatly delighted and immediately said to the bhikṣu:
"I now offer all the wealth and treasures in my treasury for you to take and use as you please; I shall never be stingy.

When the prince-monk heard the king's instruction, he took a great quantity of wealth and prepared various kinds of food and delicacies of a hundred flavors. He invited Kāśyapa Buddha and twenty thousand bhikṣus, and after making these offerings, he bestowed three robes and six articles upon each individual bhikṣu.

By virtue of this merit, he did not fall into the evil realms; among gods and humans, he was always born with a *kāṣāya* wrapped around his body. Thus, having now encountered me, he possesses the *kāṣāya*, has left the household life, and attained the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
85. The Story of Yaśomatī (85). The Story of Yaśomatī: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was an elder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he selected a woman of noble lineage and took her as his wife, providing her with music and performances for her entertainment.
His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and marvelous, a rarity in the world.
On the day of his birth, a great rain fell from the heavens; the parents were filled with joy and summoned various physiognomists to examine and interpret the child's marks.
When the physiognomist beheld him, he said:
"This child possesses such merit that rain shall fall at his birth.
When the entire kingdom heard this, they accordingly gave him a name, calling him Yaśomatī.
He did not drink milk or take nourishment; instead, from between his teeth there naturally issued forth water possessing the eight meritorious qualities, with which he sustained himself.

As he gradually grew older, he went out to travel and sightsee with his relatives and friends. Upon arriving at the Jetavana Grove, he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, whose radiance shone everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns. With a heart full of joy, he stepped forward, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they instantly became śramaṇas.

Through diligent and arduous cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by gods and humans alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen this matter, they said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One!

What merit did this bhikṣu Yaśas plant in his past lives, such that he was born with the power to cause sweet rain to fall; and though he does not drink milk or nurse, there is naturally the water of eight virtues between his teeth, by which he sustains himself?"
Furthermore, how did he encounter the World-Honored One, leave the household life, and attain the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Listen well!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
During this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa.

Within his Dharma, there was an elder who, being advanced in years and decrepit, left the household life to enter the Path; however, he was indolent and lazy, unable to practice with diligence, and furthermore, he fell gravely ill.
A skilled physician examined him and declared that he must consume *ghṛta* (clarified butter) for his illness to be cured.
He immediately followed the physician’s instructions and took the *ghṛta*.
During the night, as the medicine took effect, he became feverish and thirsty; he ran about in search of water, but all the water vessels were empty.
He went again to the springs and ponds, but they were all parched; he went to the rivers, but the rivers were also parched; thus, in every place he sought water, he found none.

Deeply repenting and reproaching himself, he stripped off his clothes by the riverbank, tied them to a tree, and left them there before returning. When morning came, he reported the matter to his teacher. Upon hearing these words, the teacher replied to him:
"You have encountered such suffering that you resemble a hungry ghost; you should now take the water from my flask and go distribute it among the monks."
He immediately followed his teacher’s instruction and took the pitcher to serve water.

When the water was completely exhausted, he was filled with grief and fear, thinking that his life had come to an end and that he might fall into the realm of hungry ghosts. He went at once to where the Buddha was, related the matter in detail, and addressed the World-Honored One:
"I have encountered this calamity and am greatly terrified; I fear I shall fall among the hungry ghosts."
"I only pray that the World-Honored One,
out of great compassion and pity, will deign to show it to me.
The Buddha told the bhikṣu:
"You should now distribute pure water among the assembly of monks; by doing so, you may escape this body of a hungry ghost.
When that bhikṣu heard the Buddha's instruction, his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately began to regularly distribute pure water within the saṃgha.
After twenty thousand years, his life came to an end.

In every place where he was reborn, there was always pure water endowed with the eight meritorious qualities between his teeth; he used this for his own sufficiency and did not drink milk or take nourishment from a breast, until now, when he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that aged bhikṣu was at that time, it is this very Yaśomitra here.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.

86. The Story of the Apparitional Bhikṣu (86). At that time, the World-Honored One was staying for the three-month summer retreat upon the Jewel Palace beneath the Pāriyātra tree in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven. Having finished preaching the Dharma for his mother, Māyā, he desired to descend back to Jambudvīpa.

At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, knowing that the Buddha intended to descend, commanded the devas, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kiṃnaras, mahoragas, kumbhāṇḍas, and others to construct three jeweled staircases for the Buddha.

As the Buddha descended from heaven, there were immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of devas, nāgas, yakṣas, humans, and non-humans on both sides of the jeweled ladder. Seeing the Tathāgata descending from heaven, they all rejoiced, longing with thirsting devotion to hear the Dharma.

At that time, the World-Honored One, observing that the roots of goodness among the great assembly had matured, immediately preached the Dharma for them; their minds were opened and their understanding was resolved. Some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat; some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, suddenly there appeared within the assembly a bhikṣu of miraculous birth, who addressed the great multitude:
"You all should now each accept my invitation; as for delicacies, food and drink, and the hundreds of necessities you require, I am able to provide them all."
When these words had been spoken, each member of the great assembly thought to themselves that they had obtained celestial jeweled vessels filled with food and drink of a hundred flavors,
and all were fully satisfied and satiated.
At that time, Ānanda, having witnessed this event, came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what merit did this bhikṣu born by transformation plant roots in his past lives, such that he is now able to satisfy and fill this great assembly?"
"I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What is the matter?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
“Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.
Ninety-one kalpas ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Vipaśyin.”

Among those practitioners, there were bhikṣus who, during the three months of the summer retreat, stayed in mountain forests to practice meditation and cultivate the Path. Because the places for alms-gathering were distant, it hindered and interrupted their cultivation of the Path, causing them great exhaustion.
At that time, there was a bhikṣu among the assembly who addressed the community of monks, saying:
"For your sake, I shall exhort and convert donors so as to provide for the community of monks, ensuring that nothing is lacking."
"You need only settle your minds and practice the Way; there is no need for concern.
When the bhikṣus heard these words, they each applied their minds and practiced the Way for three months, and all attained the fruits of the Path.
By virtue of these merits, in whatever place they are born, they will always have various foods and drinks of a hundred flavors, which they obtain as soon as they think of them;
even until now, having encountered me, they arrive as soon as they think of them, providing for the great assembly so that there is no lack whatsoever.
At that time, Ānanda again addressed the Buddha, saying,
"By what causes and conditions has he now attained birth by transformation?
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"In this present Bhadrakalpa, during the time of Kāśyapa Buddha, there was a merchant leader who, together with a caravan of merchants, traveled through foreign lands to trade and seek profit."
While his wife was pregnant, she encountered great difficulty in labor midway along the road and could not die.
At that time, the merchant leader felt a sense of revulsion and abandoned her to depart; he left the household life to enter the Way, making this great vow:
"By the merit and roots of goodness from this renunciation, may I, in all places where I am born in future lives, never again receive a womb-born body, but always attain miraculous birth."
"It is for this reason that he has now received this retribution.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that caravan leader was at that time, it is this bhikṣu born by transformation."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 87.
The Story of Adornments of Various Jewels (87). The Story of Adornments of Various Jewels: The Buddha was staying under a nyagrodha tree in the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

At that time, in that city, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond reckoning; yet he had no son, so he made offerings to the gods and spirits, seeking to obtain one.
Through the resonance of their sincere devotion, after ten full months, they gave birth to a son who was exceptionally handsome and marvelous, a rarity in the world.

Spontaneously, a spring of water welled up from the earth within the house, filled with various precious jewels; furthermore, there were flowering trees with celestial robes and fine garments hanging from their branches.
At that time, seeing this, the elder was overcome with joy beyond measure. He summoned various physiognomists to examine the child's marks.
Having observed him, the physiognomists asked his parents, "When this child was born, what auspicious signs were there?"
The parents replied:

"When this child was born, a spring of water spontaneously gushed forth from the earth within our home; it was filled with various precious jewels, and upon the trees there were fine celestial garments."
Because of the inscription [on his birth], he was named Sarvaratnavyuha.
As he gradually grew up, his nature was virtuous and gentle, and he was compassionate and filial.

Accompanied by his relatives and friends, he went out of the city to sightsee; as they traveled along, they arrived beneath a nyagrodha tree and beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns. With a heart full of joy, he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to sit to one side. Listening to the Buddha’s teaching, his mind opened and his understanding was resolved, and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
He returned home and informed his parents, seeking permission to enter the Way.
Out of their deep affection for him, his parents could not bear to oppose him; they accompanied him to the Buddha’s dwelling, where he requested ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent and ardent cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship; endowed with the three insights and six supernormal powers, and possessing the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What merit did this bhikṣu adorned with various jewels create in his past lives, such that he was born with such extraordinary qualities? And how is it that, not long after leaving the household life, he has further attained the fruits of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain this for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Kāśyapa. Having completed his work of transforming sentient beings, he passed away into parinirvāṇa.
At that time, the king of that country, named Brahmadatta, collected the relics and constructed a stupa made of the four precious substances, one yojana in height, and made offerings to it.

At that time, there was an elder who brought flowering trees, suspended various precious jewels and diverse garments, as well as vases of water, and placed them before the stupa, making a vow to offer them in worship.

By virtue of these merits, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; whether among devas or humans, there were always springs and flowering trees that arose together with him. Thus it continues until now, when he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who it was that offered the flowering trees as an offering to the stūpa at that time, it is this very bhikṣu Adorned with All Jewels."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
88. The Story of King Kapphiṇa (88). The Story of King Kapphiṇa: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, in the south, there was a kingdom named Suvarṇabhūmi; its king was named Kaśmīra, who enjoyed himself together with his consort.
When ten months were fully completed, a son was born, with sturdy joints and great physical strength;
on the very day of his birth, eighteen thousand sons of ministers were also born together with the prince, all possessing great physical strength as well.

In time, that prince gradually grew to maturity; when his father, the king, passed away, he succeeded to the throne. He then selected eighteen thousand sons of various ministers and granted them the rank of high officials to assist him in governing the affairs of state.
At that time, King Kaniṣka was out hunting with his ministers, engaging in the sport of archery.
He asked his ministers, "In this world today, is there anyone capable of possessing such great physical strength as I?"
At that time, there was a merchant among the king’s retinue who, having heard the king’s words, immediately replied to him:
“In that capital city, there is another great king named Prasenajit, who possesses immense power, surpassing Your Majesty by many hundreds of thousands of times.”
When King Kapphiṇa of Kaśmīra heard the words of the merchants, his wrath flared up intensely. He immediately dispatched a messenger to King Prasenajit with this message:
"Seven days from now, bring your attendants and wait for me as I arrive in your kingdom to pay my respects and inquire after your welfare;
if you do not do so, I shall go there myself and execute your five clans, ensuring their total extermination."
When King Prasenajit heard the messenger’s words, he was filled with great terror and knew not what to do. He immediately went to the Buddha’s dwelling and addressed the World-Honored One, saying:
“King Jibin has commanded me to lead my attendants to his kingdom within seven days to pay court and offer greetings;
if I do not do so, he shall come to execute me.”
“I do not understand, World-Honored One!
What is the matter?
At that time, the Buddha addressed King Prasenajit:
"Do not be anxious or afraid!
Simply say to that messenger:
'I am but a minor king; there is a Great King nearby at the Jetavana.'"
"You may now go and deliver your king's command. At that time, the messenger immediately set out for Jetavana.

Upon arrival, he saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, appearing as a Wheel-Turning Sage King, having commanded Mahāmaudgalyāyana to serve as the Minister of War. Leading a vast host of troops, they surrounded Jetavana on all sides. There were seven tiers of moats and rows of trees made of the seven precious gems, standing in perfect alignment. Within the moats were various lotus flowers of countless colors and beyond measure, their brilliant radiance shining throughout the city. The King sat upon his palace throne, majestic and awe-inspiring.
When the messenger beheld the king, he was struck with great alarm and thought to himself,
"My lord has brought this calamity upon himself through his recklessness.
Nevertheless, having no other choice, he stepped forward to present the royal letter.
At that time, having received the letter, the transformed king stepped on it with the sole of his foot and said to the messenger:
"I am the Great King, presiding over the four realms."
When you arrive there, convey my instructions to him:
"On the day your letter arrives, hasten to come and visit me.
When you hear my voice while lying down, you should immediately rise and sit up."
If you hear my voice while sitting, you shall immediately rise;
if you hear my voice while standing, you shall immediately set out on the road.
Having fixed a period of seven days, you shall lead your attendants to pay their respects and see me.
"If you violate this decree, the guilt shall not be excused.
The messenger returned in haste and reported these matters in detail to that king.
Upon hearing this, the king reproached himself deeply and immediately assembled thirty-six thousand ministers; he prepared his carriage solemnly, intending to come and pay homage to the Great King.
However, having a doubt, before I could yet advance to present it, I first dispatched a messenger to say to the Great King:
"Regarding the thirty-six thousand minor kings under our command, should they all go together, or shall half of them come?"
Then this emanated king replied to the messenger, saying,
"Bring half of it here quickly.
The messenger returned in haste and informed King Kaniṣka of Jibin:
"The Great King has issued a command, permitting us to remain here for half [the term].
Thereupon, leading eighteen thousand minor kings, they hurried and arrived swiftly; having paid their respects to the King, they thought to themselves:
"Although the Great King’s appearance is now superior, his strength is not equal to ours."
At that time, the transformed king, knowing the other’s intention from afar, commanded his minister in charge of the treasury:
"Bring forth the great bows and crossbows of my ancestors.
He presented them to the king, but the king was unable to lift them.
The transformed king took it back and drew the bow with his finger.
He then gave it back to him, telling him to pull it; yet he could not move the string at all.
The transformed king took it back again and plucked it with his finger; the sound shook the trichiliocosm, causing it all to tremble.

Next, he again shot an arrow, which transformed into five clusters; on each of the arrowheads was a lotus flower, and upon each flower there was a manifested Buddha emitting great radiance that illuminated the trichiliocosm, so that no sentient beings within the five realms failed to receive its benefit.
Among the devas and human beings, some attained the fruits of the Path;
those in the hells found the boiling water cooled and the fires extinguished;
and those among the hungry ghosts all obtained full satiety.
Those among the animal realm are freed from their heavy burdens;
those with greed, hatred, and the afflictions of ignorance, upon encountering this light, are all tamed and come to have faith and reverence for the Buddha-dharma.
At that time, King Jing of Kaśmīra, having witnessed this transformation, prostrated himself with his five limbs touching the ground before the manifested king, and his mind was immediately subdued.

Then the manifested king, knowing he had been subdued, returned to his original form; surrounded by the fourfold assembly, he preached the Dharma in various ways for those eighteen thousand minor kings, so that their minds were opened and their intentions understood, and each attained the stage of the Path, realizing the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Thereupon, before the Buddha, he requested ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His hair and beard fell away of their own accord, and Dharma robes appeared upon his body; he thus became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, before long he attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernatural powers, and being fully endowed with the eight liberations. He was revered and looked up to by all devas and people of the world.
At that time, Ānanda came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:

"By what merit did these bhikṣus, such as King Niṅ of Kaśmīra and the others, plant in their past lives, that they were all born into noble clans, possessed great power and influence, encountered the World-Honored Buddha, and each attained the fruits of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
In the distant past, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Vipaśyin. Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, he arrived at the kingdom of Ratnavatī.

At that time, the king’s name was Bandhumat; hearing that the Buddha had arrived, his heart was filled with joy. He led eighteen thousand ministers out of the city to welcome him, prostrated before the Buddha’s feet, and knelt for a long time, entreating the Buddha and the assembly of bhikṣus:
"Out of your compassionate pity and mercy!"
"Please accept my offerings of the four requisites for three months.
When that Buddha and his Saṃgha had accepted the King's offerings, the Buddha immediately preached various teachings to the King.
The King was greatly delighted, and each of them made a vow, saying:
"By the roots of goodness and merit from making this offering, may we all be born on the same day as this Great King in every place where we are reborn.
Having made this vow, they each returned to their respective dwellings.

By virtue of this merit, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the evil realms; born together with me in the heavens and among humans, he experienced celestial bliss until now, when he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that King Bandhumat was at that time, he is this present bhikṣu Niṅ of Kaśmīra;
those who were his ministers at that time are these present eighteen thousand bhikṣus."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
89. The Story of King Bimbisāra of the Śākya Clan Becoming a Bhikṣu (89). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, after the Tathāgata had completed twelve years since first attaining perfect enlightenment following six years of ascetic practice, he was about to travel with one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus toward the kingdom of Kapilavastu.
He thought to himself:
"I am now going there, but not as I usually do. The Śākyas of that land are full of arrogance; I must each manifest supernatural transformations before I may go to that land."
He then commanded his one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus:
"I now wish to return to my native land.
Each of you must manifest supernatural transformations so that those Śākyas may be moved to sincere faith and submission."
At that time, the World-Honored One emitted a great radiance and, together with the bhikṣus, traveled through the air to the kingdom of Kapilavastu.

When King Śuddhodana heard that the Buddha had arrived, he commanded the Śākyas and others to level the roads, remove all impurities, erect banners and streamers, hang precious bells, sprinkle fragrant water upon the ground, scatter various exquisite flowers, and perform musical performances to welcome the World-Honored One.
He first prostrated at the Buddha’s feet and requested that he enter the palace to receive the King’s offerings.
At that time, King Śuddhodana saw the Buddha’s retinue; although they possessed supernormal powers, their physical appearances were ugly and ill-suited to human sensibilities.
"I shall now select more than five hundred men from among the Śākyas and others, of handsome appearance, to serve as attendants to the World-Honored One.
Having spoken these words, he immediately commanded that five hundred men be chosen; they were led to the Buddha’s dwelling, and Upāli was instructed to shave their hair and beards.
Tears flowed from his eyes and fell upon the King of the Śākyas.
The King immediately asked him:
"For what reason are you weeping now?"
He wept thus. Upāli said,
"Since Your Majesty is now the most honored among all the Śākyas, you could not have anticipated that one day you would alter your appearance, eat coarse food, and wear robes of discarded rags."
Seeing the King in this state, his eyes flowed with tears.
At that time, having heard these words, the Licchavi Vajjiputta felt despondent in his heart, yet he still harbored arrogance.

Having completed the shaving of his beard and hair and prepared his robes and bowl, he desired to receive full ordination. He entered the midst of the Saṃgha and paid obeisance to them in due order; however, when he came before Upāli, he stood still and did not prostrate.
The Buddha asked King Śākya,
"For what reason do you now alone refrain from paying homage to Upāli?
Vatsa Śākya replied:
"He considers me lowly and himself noble; that is why he does not pay me respect.
The Buddha said, "Within this Dharma of mine, there is neither noble nor lowly; all things are like illusions and transformations, their safety and peril impossible to guarantee."
Vatsa Śākya said, "He is my slave;
I cannot bear to pay him homage.
The Buddha spoke again, saying:
“What difference is there between all slaves—whether poor or wealthy, noble or lowly—and the suffering of being separated from those one loves?

When King Bandhula the Śākya heard these words of the Buddha, he bowed his head and raised himself up to pay homage. At that moment, the earth shook violently, and the devas in the sky marveled at this unprecedented event, exclaiming:
“For the sake of seeking the Way, King Bandhula the Śākya has been able to bend his body and prostrate before those of low station; the banner of his self-conceit is about to collapse.”

Then, having received full ordination, the Śākya Vatsa withdrew to sit on one side to listen to the Buddha’s teaching. His mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he attained the fruit of Arhatship and, taking up his alms bowl, went forth to beg for food.
He went to the cemetery and stayed overnight beneath a tree; his mind was serene and he was no longer afraid, saying to himself:
"In the past, when I was in the royal palace, I recruited strong men to hold weapons and stand at my side, and thus I harbored fear and anxiety."
"I have now left the household life to enter the Way; dwelling here amidst these burial mounds, I am no longer afraid, and my joy is beyond words.
At that time, having heard these words from the Licchavi Vatsa, Ānanda stepped forward and said to the Buddha:
"By what merit did this Bhikṣu Vatsa plant roots in his past lives that he was born into a noble clan, and after leaving the household life not long ago, attained the fruit of Arhatship?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Ānanda, saying:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a pratyekabuddha who, carrying his alms-bowl, went about begging for food.
At that time, there was a man, poor and famished, traveling along the road with only a few cakes which he intended to eat himself.
Seeing a Pratyekabuddha walking for alms with dignified and composed deportment, his heart was filled with joy; he immediately took a cake and offered it to the Pratyekabuddha.

Having accepted the cake, the Pratyekabuddha leaped into the air and manifested the eighteen transformations: leaping up in the east and sinking down in the west, leaping up in the south and sinking down in the north, emitting water and fire from his body, and performing various such transformations, totaling eighteen.
At that time, the person who gave the cakes, having witnessed this transformation, felt profound faith and reverence; he made a vow and departed.

By virtue of this merit, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the realms of hell or animals; among gods and humans, he was honored, illustrious, and noble, constantly experiencing happiness. Thus, even until now, he has encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told Ānanda:
"If you wish to know who that man was who gave the cakes at that time, he is none other than this Bhikṣu King Bimbisāra of the Śākya clan.

When the Buddha spoke this causal narrative, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some attained Sakṛdāgāmin, some attained Anāgāmin, and some attained Arhatship; some conceived the aspiration for Pratyekabuddhahood, and some conceived the aspiration for Unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
90. The Story of the Buddha’s Ordination of Prince Rāṣṭrapāla The Buddha was staying under a tūra tree in the kingdom of Kuvera. He thought to himself:
"Now I shall go to ordain that prince, Rāṣṭrapāla, and cause him to leave the household life."

Having formed this thought, he led the bhikṣus to the city gate; as his feet stepped upon the threshold, the earth shook in six ways, celestial flowers rained down, and a great radiance was emitted that illuminated the interior of the city. The blind regained their sight, the deaf regained their hearing, the mute were able to speak, and the lame were able to walk.
At that time, having beheld this light, the prince marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence. He immediately proceeded to the place where the Buddha was;

seeing the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining universally like a hundred thousand suns, his deportment dignified and orderly, and most delightful to behold, he felt great joy in his heart. He stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet, then withdrew to stand to one side. The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind opened and his understanding was resolved, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
Returning to report to his father, the King, he marveled at the Buddha’s merits, saying:

"Had he remained a householder, he would have become a Wheel-Turning Sage King, presiding over the four continents with the seven treasures following him, traveling with sovereign ease; yet even such a one could renounce it all to leave the home life and enter the Way."
"How much more so should I now follow him and seek to leave the household life to become a Buddha?
Having formed this thought, he went before the King and said:
"I only pray, Great King!"
"Out of compassion and pity, please grant me permission to leave the household life and follow the World-Honored One.
When King Suddhodana heard the prince's words, he forbade him and would not grant his request.
The king was filled with distress and grief; he abstained from grain and did not eat for one day, two days, and even up to six days.
At that time, the various ministers, seeing that the Crown Prince had not eaten for six days, knelt and addressed the King, saying:
"The Crown Prince has now abstained from grain and food for six days; we fear his life may not be preserved."
"I pray that Your Majesty will now grant permission for him to leave the household life, so that we may meet again.
When King Suddhodana heard the words of his ministers, he granted permission for him to enter the Way.
He immediately went to where the Buddha was and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His beard and hair fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship; possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and endowed with the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they came forward and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"By what merit did this Prince-rakṣa bhikṣu plant roots in his past lives that he was born into a royal family and, not long after leaving the household life, attained the fruit of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
“Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.”
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there was a king named Videha who raised an army and drew up battle lines to engage in combat with a neighboring king.

At that time, the neighboring king, having been defeated by him, led his troops in flight and retreat; arriving in the midst of a vast wilderness, they encountered the scorching heat of the day, with neither water nor grass to be found, and were on the verge of death from hunger and thirst.
He immediately went to where the Pratyekabuddha was and showed him water and grass; thus the king’s thirst and exhaustion were relieved, and he was guided along the path back to his own country.
Overjoyed beyond measure, they spoke these words:
"We have now been liberated from the affliction of hunger and thirst; all this is due to the merit of that Pratyekabuddha. We shall now prepare an offering and invite the Pratyekabuddha."
Having spoken these words, he ordered various delicacies and foods to be prepared, and invited the pratyekabuddha to enter the palace for offerings.
Once the pratyekabuddha had accepted the offerings, he immediately entered parinirvāṇa.

At that time, King Suddhodana, along with his ministers, queens, and court ladies, wailed and wept, overwhelmed by grief and distress; they collected the relics and constructed stupas made of the four precious substances to make offerings to them.

By virtue of these merits, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; instead, among gods and humans, he was honored, illustrious, and noble, enjoying celestial bliss, until now, when he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that King Suddhi was at that time, it was because of his making offerings to a pratyekabuddha that he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
