Chapter Ten: On All Conditions (Sarvapratyaya-varga).

[91] Subhūti’s Ill-Tempered Condition. At that time, when the World-Honored One had first attained Buddhahood, wishing to convert the various nāga kings, he went to the foot of Mount Sumeru and manifested in the form of a bhikṣu, sitting upright in contemplation.
At that time, there was a King of the Garuḍas who entered the great ocean, seized a small dragon, and returned to the summit of Mount Sumeru, intending to devour it.

While the life of that small dragon had not yet been severed, he saw from afar a bhikṣu sitting upright in meditation; with a sincere heart, the dragon cried out for mercy, whereupon his life immediately ended, and he was reborn in a brāhmaṇa family in the kingdom of Śrāvastī, named Pūrṇa.
His features were upright and exceptionally wondrous, rare in this world; therefore, he was given the name Subhūti.
As he gradually grew older, his wisdom and intelligence were such that none could equal them;
yet he possessed an exceedingly foul temperament, and whenever he saw anyone or any animal with his eyes, he would immediately revile them in anger, never ceasing for a moment.

His parents and kinsmen all grew weary of him and none took pleasure in seeing him; he subsequently abandoned his home to enter the mountain forests, yet even upon seeing birds, beasts, trees, and grasses swaying in the wind, he gave rise to anger, never once feeling joy in his heart.
At that time, there was a mountain deity who said to Subhūti:
"For what reason have you now left your home to come here into these mountain forests? If you do not cultivate goodness, it will be of no benefit; you are merely exhausting yourself in vain."
"Now there is a World-Honored One residing within the Jeta Grove; he possesses great merit and virtue, and is able to teach sentient beings to cultivate goodness and sever evil.
If you go to him now, he will surely be able to eliminate the poisonous venom of your anger and hatred."
At that time, Subhūti, having heard the words of the mountain deity, was immediately filled with joy and asked him:
"Where is the World-Honored One now?"
The mountain deity replied, “Simply close your eyes, and I shall carry you to the presence of the World-Honored One. Then Subhūti followed the mountain deity’s words;

closing his eyes for a brief moment, he was unaware that he had naturally arrived within the Jeta Grove. There he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns. With a heart full of joy, he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then explained for them the faults and evils of anger and hatred, and how the affliction of ignorance burns away roots of goodness and increases all manner of evils; that one subsequently undergoes retribution by falling into hell, where they must endure immeasurable suffering and pain beyond description.
Even if they were to escape [this state], they might become dragons, snakes, rākṣasas, or ghosts and spirits, their minds constantly harboring venom as they further harm one another.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, Subhūti’s heart was struck with alarm and his hair stood on end. He immediately repented and reproached himself, and before the Buddha, he confessed his transgressions. Suddenly and clearly, he attained the fruit of srotāpanna; filled with joy, he sought to enter the stages of the Path.
The Buddha then granted his permission,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they immediately became śramaṇas.

Through diligent and ardent practice, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and the six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all gods and people of the world.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the bhikṣus said to the Buddha:
“World-Honored One!

What karma did this bhikṣu Subhūti create in his past lives, such that although he has attained human birth, he constantly harbors anger without ever ceasing it, yet has now encountered the World-Honored Buddha, left the household life, and attained the Way?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Listen well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
In this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa.
Within his Dharma, there was a bhikṣu who constantly practiced exhortation and conversion; for ten thousand years, he led various bhikṣus to make offerings everywhere.
Later, when the Saṃgha had some minor business, they did not follow at all, whereupon [the monk] uttered these abusive words:
"You are all perverse and stubborn, resembling venomous dragons."
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed.
Due to these karmic conditions, for five hundred lifetimes he took the body of a venomous dragon, his mind constantly harboring poison to harass and disturb sentient beings through his touch.
"Although he has now attained the Dharma, his past habitual tendencies have not been eliminated; therefore, he has again given rise to anger.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that bhikṣu was at that time who exhorted him and reviled him with harsh words, it was Subhūti."
"Because he made offerings to the Sangha at that time, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
92. The Story of the Elder Bhikkhu Who Had Been in the Mother’s Womb for Sixty Years (92). The Buddha was staying at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove of the Kalandakas.

At that time, in that city, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman from a noble family and took her as his wife, providing her with various kinds of music for her entertainment.

When ten months were complete, she was about to give birth, yet the child would not emerge; she soon became pregnant again, and when ten months were once more fulfilled, she gave birth to another son, while the one she had previously conceived remained in her right flank.
In this manner, she conceived nine children in succession; each was born after ten months had passed, yet only the first-born child remained in the womb and could not emerge.
Her mother fell gravely ill; she prepared various decoctions and medicines to treat herself, yet her illness did not abate. She then entrusted her family with these instructions:
"The child within my womb is still alive and has not died. If I should pass away, you must open my belly and take out the child to raise him."
At that time, her mother did not recover from her illness and soon passed away.
Her relatives then carried her corpse to the cemetery and invited the great physician Jīvaka to open her belly and examine it.
He obtained a young boy whose physical form was as before, yet his hair and beard were white and he walked with a stoop; looking around in all four directions, he spoke to his relatives, saying:
"You should all know!..."

Because in a previous life I used harsh speech to revile and insult the Sangha, I have been dwelling within this matured storehouse of excrement for sixty years, undergoing such suffering and affliction that it is difficult to endure.
When the relatives heard the child’s words, they wailed and wept, overcome with grief and unable to respond.
At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing from afar that this child’s roots of goodness had matured, led the great assembly to the place where the corpse lay and addressed the little boy:
"Are you an elder bhikṣu?"
He replied, "It is indeed so.
A second and third time, he was asked in the same manner, and thus he said, "It is so."
At that time, the great assembly, seeing this young child conversing with the Buddha, each harbored doubts and approached the Buddha, saying:

"What karma did this old man create in his past lives such that, while still within the womb, his hair was already white and he walked with a stoop, yet he could engage in dialogue with the Tathāgata?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain it for you."
In this Bhadrakalpa, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa.

There were certain bhikṣus observing the summer retreat; as the Saṃgha was in harmony, they appointed a bhikṣu of advanced age to serve as the *karmadāna* for the community, and together they established a formal regulation.
During this summer retreat, those who have attained the Path are permitted to participate in the *pravāraṇā*;
however, those who have not yet attained it are not permitted to do so.
Now, this *karmadāna* alone has not attained the Path, and as the Saṃgha does not permit him to perform the *poṣadha* or the *pravāraṇā*, he harbors resentment in his heart and speaks these words:

"I alone have managed the affairs of the Saṃgha on your behalf, enabling you all to practice the Path in peace; yet now you turn back and refuse to allow the *pravāraṇā*, the *poṣadha*, and the *karmavācanā*."
He immediately became enraged and reviled the assembly of monks.
He then seized them by force and confined them within a room, declaring:
"May you all dwell forever in darkness and never see the light, just as I now dwell in this dark chamber."

Having spoken these words, he took his own life and died, falling into hell where he underwent great suffering and affliction. Only now has he finally attained liberation; therefore, while still in the womb, he undergoes this suffering and affliction.

At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, those in the assembly each guarded their own actions of body, speech, and mind; they grew weary of and sought liberation from birth and death. Some attained the stage of *srotāpanna*, some of *sakṛdāgāmin*, some of *anāgāmin*, and some of *arhat*. Some gave rise to the mind of a *pratyekabuddha*, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Then his relatives took the old man back home to raise him.
As he gradually grew up, they allowed him to leave the household life; through diligent cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!
What merit did this elderly bhikṣu cultivate in his past lives, such that not long after leaving the household life, he has attained the fruit of arhatship?"
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"Because in the past he made offerings to the Saṃgha and served as a karmadāna to manage the affairs of the Saṃgha, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 93.
The Story of the Bhikṣu with Severed Hands (93). The Story of the Bhikṣu with Severed Hands: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, in that city, there was an elder whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman from a distinguished lineage to be his wife and provided her with various musical performances for her entertainment.
His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were complete, she gave birth to a male child who was born without hands. As soon as he was born, he was able to speak, uttering these words:
"These hands are extremely difficult to obtain; cherish them deeply!"
The parents, finding this strange, summoned various physiognomists to examine the child's features.
Having observed him, the physiognomists asked his parents,
"What auspicious signs were there at the time of this child’s birth?"
The parents replied,
"After this child was born, he uttered these words:
'Now, such hands as these are exceedingly rare.'"
Because of this, he was given the name Wushou (Stump-Hand).
As he gradually grew up, his disposition was harmonious and compliant, and he was clever and wise.

Accompanied by his relatives and friends, he traveled about sightseeing until he reached the Jetavana Grove. There he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance blazing like hundreds of thousands of suns. His heart filled with joy, he went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to stand to one side.
The Buddha then preached various teachings for him; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He returned home to take leave of his parents and requested permission to enter the Path.
His parents, out of love and affection, could not go against his wish; they took him to the Buddha’s presence to seek ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His beard and hair fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship; endowed with the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by devas and humans alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:

"What merit did this bhikṣu with the severed hand plant in his past lives, such that he was able to speak immediately upon birth, yet remained without hands; and furthermore, how did he encounter the World-Honored One and attain the fruit of the Path?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."
In this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa.
There were two bhikṣus: one was an arhat and the other was an ordinary person, both serving as Dharma-preachers.
At that time, the populace vied with one another to invite him, and they would regularly take the Dharma Master with them when accepting the invitations of donors (*dānapati*).
Once, on a certain day, the Dharma Master was absent, and they took someone else instead.
He spoke with anger and abuse:
"I have always washed your bowl and provided you with water; now you instead take the leftovers and travel together with them.
From this day forward, I shall serve as your servant, yet you leave me without hands."
Having spoken these words, they each took their leave and ceased traveling together.
Due to these karmic conditions, for five hundred lifetimes they underwent this retribution; therefore, he cried out:
"This hand is now most difficult to obtain."
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that bhikṣu-dharma-preacher was who made the oath at that time, he is none other than this bhikṣu with the severed hand.
Because he provided for the sages at that time, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way."

When the Buddha had finished speaking this account of the one with severed hands, the bhikṣus each guarded their own actions of body, speech, and mind, and grew weary of birth and death. Among them, some attained the stage of Srotāpanna, some of Sakṛdāgāmin, some of Anāgāmin, and some of Arhat; some gave rise to the mind of a Pratyekabuddha, and some gave rise to the mind of unsurpassed Bodhi.
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
94. The Story of the Bhikṣu Liñjika (94). The Story of the Bhikṣu Liñjika: The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a brahmin in that city whose wife, having carried her pregnancy for a full ten months, gave birth to a son. His appearance was hideous and his body foul-smelling; when he drank his mother’s milk, it would turn sour, and even if she hired others to nurse him, their milk would likewise spoil.
He could only be sustained by licking butter and honey applied to her finger, and so they gave him the name Li-jun-zhi (Likhita).
As he gradually grew older, his merit was once again meager; though he sought food and drink, he never obtained enough to satisfy himself.

Seeing various śramaṇas with dignified and orderly deportment, carrying their alms-bowls, entering the city to beg for food and returning with their bowls full, he was filled with joy upon seeing them and thought to himself:
"I shall now go to the Buddha, the World-Honored One, and request to become a śramaṇa; perhaps I may then obtain my fill."
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to the Jetavana Grove to seek ordination under the Buddha.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His hair and beard fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship.

However, while going on almsround, he failed to obtain any food; he then reproached himself and entered the stūpa, where he saw a small amount of dust and filth, which he immediately swept and sprinkled.
When the time came for almsround, food was provided in abundance.
With a heart full of joy, he addressed the community of monks, saying:
"From this day forward, please allow me to sweep and sprinkle water at the monasteries and stupas of the Sangha."
"Why is this so? It is because by sweeping and cleaning, you have enabled me to obtain food and be satisfied.
The monk then gave his consent and regularly ordered him to sweep and clean.
On another day, bound by ignorance, he slept through the night without waking and had not yet swept or sprinkled the area.

At that time, Śāriputra, leading five hundred disciples, came from another land to pay his respects to the World-Honored One; seeing some dust and dirt within the Buddha’s stūpa, he immediately swept it away.
At that time, Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa woke from his sleep and, seeing Śāriputra having finished sweeping and sprinkling the ground, felt regret in his heart and said to Śāriputra:
"You have swept my grounds, causing me to suffer from hunger and exhaustion for an entire day."
When Śāriputra heard these words, he said to him:
"I shall now go into the city with you to accept the invitation; you will be able to eat your fill, so do not worry."
When Liǔmúnzhī heard these words, his mind became tranquil.

When the time for the invitation arrived, he entered the city with Śāriputra to accept it; however, they encountered the donor couple quarreling, and consequently were unable to obtain any food, returning home hungry.
Then, on the second day, Śāriputra spoke to him again:
"This morning, I shall personally take you to accept the elder’s invitation and cause you to be fully satisfied."

When the time arrived and they were about to depart, those of superior, middling, and inferior status all received food, yet this one person alone did not receive any; he cried out in a loud voice, "I have received no food!"
At that time, the host heard nothing at all and returned home hungry and exhausted.
When Ānanda heard of this matter, he felt deep compassion and, on the third day, said to Liṅgin:
"This morning, I followed the Buddha in accepting an invitation; I shall obtain food for you and ensure that you are fully satisfied."

"Yet Ānanda, who has received and upheld the eighty-four thousand dharma-treasury gates of the Tathāgata without ever missing or omitting a single one, now, for the sake of this bhikṣu Liñcchi, took his food and drink but suddenly failed to remember it, returning with an empty bowl."

On the fourth day, Ānanda again went out to fetch food for him; on his way back to his dwelling, he encountered a vicious dog that bit and tore at him, causing him to drop the food on the ground and return with an empty bowl, once more failing to obtain any food.

On the fifth day, Mahāmaudgalyāyana again went out to collect food and was returning to his dwelling when, on the way, he was spotted by a king of the garuḍas, who seized him, took his bowl, and carried it off to the great ocean; thus, he again failed to obtain food.

On the sixth day, Śāriputra again went to fetch food; upon arriving at the door of that room, the door closed of its own accord. Using his supernormal powers, he entered the room and leaped up before him, whereupon his alms bowl was lost and fell to the ground, reaching as far as the Diamond Realm (vajrakoṭi).
Again, by means of his supernatural power, he extended his hand to take the bowl, but his mouth closed once more, and he was ultimately unable to eat;
when the time for the meal had passed, his mouth opened of its own accord.
On the seventh day, having failed to obtain any food at all, he felt profound shame and, before the fourfold assembly, ate sand and drank water, immediately entering nirvana.
At that time, when the bhikṣus saw this matter, they marveled at its cause:

"What karma did the bhikṣu Liñjia create in his past lives such that he was born into hunger and never had abundance? Furthermore, by what conditions did he leave the household life and attain the Way?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Śakraketu. Accompanied by a multitude of bhikṣus, he traveled about, teaching and transforming sentient beings.
At that time, there was an elder named Gomi who, upon seeing the Buddha and the Sangha, conceived deep faith and reverence; he invited them to receive offerings, doing so every day in this manner.

Some time later, his father passed away. Although the mother continued her practice of giving, the son was extremely stingy and forbade her from giving. He even calculated the food to be given to his mother, yet she still divided it and gave portions to the Buddha and the Sangha.

Upon hearing of her mother's anger, the son immediately seized her, confined her in an empty room, locked the door, and departed. When the seventh day arrived, the mother was extremely hungry and exhausted; she begged her son for food, to which the son replied to his mother:
"How would it be if you were to survive by eating sand and drinking water?"
"Why do you now seek food from me?
Having spoken these words, she abandoned him and departed.
He ultimately failed to obtain food, and his mother then passed away.
Later, that son passed away and entered the Avīci Hell; having finished undergoing his suffering there, he was reborn among humans, remaining thus hungry and destitute.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who it was that cut off his mother's food at that time, he is none other than the bhikṣu Liñjī today.
Because he made offerings to the Buddha in the past, he has now encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way."
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 95.

The Discourse on Proclaiming the Extreme Suffering of Birth and Death (95). The Discourse on Proclaiming the Extreme Suffering of Birth and Death. The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a virtuous and noble woman to be his wife and provided her with entertainment through music and performance.

His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son who remembered his past lives; immediately after being born, he cried out, "Birth and death are the ultimate suffering."
Because he established this name, it was called "the suffering of birth and death.

As he gradually grew older, whenever he saw anyone, he would still cry out, "Birth and death are extremely painful! Nevertheless, toward his parents, teachers, monks, elders, and those of virtue, he was compassionate and filial; his speech was always accompanied by a smile, and he never uttered coarse or evil words.

Accompanied by his kinsmen and friends, he went out of the city to observe the sights; traveling by stages, he arrived at the Jetavana Grove and beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining brilliantly like hundreds of thousands of suns. With a heart full of joy, he approached to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.
He returned home to take leave of his parents and requested permission to enter the Path.
His parents, out of love and affection, could not oppose him; they brought him to the Buddha’s presence to seek ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying:
“Welcome, Bhikṣu!”
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.

Through diligent and earnest cultivation, he attained the fruit of arhatship; possessing the three knowledges and the six supernatural powers, and endowed with the eight liberations, he was revered and honored by gods and men alike.
At that time, when the bhikṣus had seen this matter, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

What merit did this bhikṣu of birth and death cultivate in his past lives, such that he was able to speak immediately upon birth, remembered his own past lives, and furthermore encountered the Tathāgata, left the household life, and attained the Way?"
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: “Listen well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you.”
In this Bhadrakalpa, when the human lifespan was twenty thousand years, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa.
Within his Dharma, there was a śrāmaṇera who served his upādhyāya.
At that time, a great festival was being held in that city. Then the śrāmaṇera said to his preceptor:
"On this day of the festival, we should go for alms early; we shall surely obtain much."
The teacher immediately replied, "It is still too early; you should practice seated meditation for now.
A second and a third time he addressed the teacher in this manner, yet the teacher still did not comply.
The śrāmaṇera, filled with anger, reviled him with harsh words, saying:
"Why did you not die while still inside?
Having spoken these words, he immediately departed, entered the city to beg for food, and upon returning to his dwelling, confessed his transgression to his teacher.

Due to these karmic conditions, for five hundred lifetimes he fell into the hells and underwent various sufferings; having only now been liberated from them, he therefore cries out that birth and death are the ultimate suffering.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that śrāmaṇera was at that time who reviled his teacher, he is this bhikṣu Saṃjīva here.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
96. The Story of the Elder’s Body Breaking Out in Sores (96). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.

At that time, there was a householder in that city whose wealth and treasures were immeasurable and beyond calculation; he chose a woman from a noble family to be his wife and entertained her with all kinds of music.
When ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son; his body was covered in sores that caused him extreme suffering and pain, such that he groaned and cried out without ever ceasing.

As he gradually grew older, the sores all became suppurated and rotted; pus and blood flowed profusely, and he was constantly afflicted by pain. Consequently, they gave him a name, calling him Śunāṣa (The Groaner).
His parents, out of compassion, prepared various remedies and medicines; though they applied these treatments with great care, the ulcer would not heal.
As he gradually grew older, he heard people say:
"In the Jetavana Monastery there is an excellent physician who skillfully treats all manner of ailments and is able to bring them to complete recovery."

He immediately went there to the Jetavana Grove, where he beheld the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining brilliantly like a hundred thousand suns. With a heart full of joy, he approached, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then explained for him that the five aggregates of clinging are suffering; they are like sores and abscesses, and like a poisonous arrow piercing the heart to harm a person—they are the root of all maladies.

At that time, having heard these words spoken by the Buddha, the World-Honored One, the son Śvāsaka deeply reproached himself and, before the Buddha, the World-Honored One, repented of his transgressions. His sores were immediately healed, and with a heart full of joy, he sought to leave the household life.
The Buddha then addressed him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Through diligent cultivation of the path, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
When the bhikṣus witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!..."

What karma did this wailing bhikṣu create in his past lives, such that at the time of his birth, his body was covered in malignant sores from which pus and blood flowed profusely, making him most loathsome to behold?
"Furthermore, by what conditions did he leave the household life and attain the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.

In the past, countless eons ago, in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, there were two elders, both of whom were immensely wealthy with immeasurable assets; they fell into a state of mutual resentment and contention.
One of the elders brought a great quantity of rare treasures as an offering to the king.
Having accepted them, the king slandered that elder, saying:
"That man harbors evil intent; he constantly conceives treacherous schemes, intending to harm me."
"I only pray, Great King,
that you will permit me to deal with that elder as I see fit.
The king immediately granted his consent.

He soon arrived at the man's house, seized the elder, bound him, and flogged him with immeasurable cruelty; his entire body was mangled and broken, with pus and blood flowing profusely, such that the pain was beyond description.
At that time, once the elder had been granted his release, he reflected deeply within himself:
"To have a body is entirely suffering; it is the gathering place of all evils and the source of many calamities—it is truly something to be weary of and loathe."
"I have no great enmity toward that person, yet he has needlessly caused me injury and ruin to such an extent.

Thereupon, he reflected deeply and went into the mountain forests; observing that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent, he profoundly realized emptiness and became a Pratyekabuddha, regarding all enemies and kin with a mind of perfect equanimity.
He thought:
"That householder has treated me with malice; in a future life, he will fall into hell and undergo great suffering.
I should now go and manifest supernatural transformations for him, so that he may attain awakening."
Having formed this thought, he went before the elder and leaped into the air, performing the eighteen miraculous transformations.

When the elder saw these transformations, he felt a profound sense of longing and admiration; his faith and reverence redoubled, and he immediately invited him to sit, providing various kinds of food and offerings as hospitality. He then confessed his prior transgressions before the Pratyekabuddha.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that person was at that time who slandered the elder to the king and subjected him to interrogation, flogging, and scourging, it is this Bhikṣu Śunāhu here."
At that time, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, the bhikṣus rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
97. The Story of the Ugly Bhikṣu (97). The Buddha was staying at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
At that time, there was an elder in that city who selected a woman from a noble family to take as his wife; he provided her with performances and music to entertain her.

His wife became pregnant, and when the ten months were fully completed, she gave birth to a son whose appearance was exceedingly ugly; he looked like a malevolent spirit, and anyone who saw him would abandon him and depart.
As he gradually grew older, his parents grew weary of him and drove him away to be abandoned.
Even animals, upon seeing such ugliness, would feel fear and dread; how much more so would human beings?
Furthermore, at one time, he went among the forest trees to gather flowers and fruits to sustain himself.
Whenever birds or beasts saw him, they were all struck with fear; they fled from this forest, and none dared to remain.

At that time, the World-Honored One, ever with compassion, observed sentient beings throughout the six periods of day and night. Whenever there was someone who could be delivered, he would immediately go to deliver them.
Knowing that the roots of goodness of that ugly man had ripened and that the time for his transformation and deliverance had arrived, the Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"We shall now all go together into those mountain forests to transform that ugly man."
At that time, the World-Honored One, taking the bhikṣus with him, went into a mountain forest.
When the Ugly One saw the Buddha, the World-Honored One, he immediately sought to flee.
By the Buddha’s supernormal power, they were rendered unable to depart.
At that time, the bhikṣus each sat beneath a tree in the full lotus posture, binding their mindfulness before them.
At that time, the World-Honored One immediately manifested as a person of ugly appearance, holding an alms bowl filled with midday food, and gradually approached the ugly man.
Upon seeing him, the ugly man observed that his form resembled his own and felt great joy in his heart, thinking:
"Now this person is truly my companion."
He immediately came forward to converse with him and ate from the same vessel.
At that time, the food was fragrant, delicious, and sweet; having finished eating it, the emanated person suddenly became upright and handsome.
The ugly one asked,
"For what reason have you suddenly become so handsome?
The transformed person replied:
"I shall eat this rice and, with a virtuous mind, observe that bhikṣu sitting in meditation under the tree so as to make myself handsome.
Having heard this, the ugly man immediately followed his example; observing that bhikṣu sitting in meditation with a virtuous mind, he immediately became handsome.
With a heart full of joy, he conceived deep faith and understanding toward the transformed person.
At that moment, the transformed person returned to his original form.

When the Ugly One beheld the Buddha—adorned with the thirty-two marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns—he went forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.

The Buddha then preached the Dharma to him in various ways; his mind was opened and his understanding clarified, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. Thereupon, before the Buddha, he sought ordination.
The Buddha then addressed him,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
His beard and hair fell away of their own accord, the Dharma robes were donned upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Through diligent cultivation of the path, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, having witnessed this event, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"

What karma did this ugly bhikṣu create in his past lives, that although he has received a human form, he is so exceedingly ugly, yet has further encountered the World-Honored One, left the household life, and attained the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus: "Listen well!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī; his name was Puṣya, and he sat beneath a tree with his legs crossed in the full lotus posture.
Both I and Maitreya were bodhisattvas; we went to the presence of that Buddha, made various offerings, and stood upon one foot for seven days, reciting these verses in praise of the Buddha:
"In the heavens and the world, none is like the Buddha; Even throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is no such being.
He perceives all that exists within the worlds; None can equal the Buddha."
"At that time, after the Bodhisattva had spoken these verses, there was a spirit in that mountain who assumed a hideous form and came to terrify me."
By my supernatural power, I have caused the path where he travels to become a precipitous and treacherous cliff that he cannot cross.
At that time, the mountain deity thought to himself:
"Because I harbored an evil mind to terrify him, this path of mine has now become so perilous that he cannot pass."
"Now I shall go there to repent for my past transgressions.
Having formed this thought, he immediately went to that place; having finished his repentance, he made a vow and departed.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
"If you wish to know who that mountain deity was who terrified me at that time, it is this ugly person here who has attained arhatship."
Because he was terrified of me, for five hundred lifetimes his physical form was hideous, and those who saw him would flee in alarm;
yet it was entirely due to his confession and taking leave at that time that he encountered me, left the household life, and attained the Way.
At that time, the bhikṣus, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
98. The Story of Gaṅgāda (98). The Buddha was staying at Vārāṇasī in the Deer Park.
At that time, there was a chief minister in that country whose family was very wealthy, yet he had no children.
On the banks of the Ganges River, there was a shrine to the deity Maṇibhadra, which all the people of the land collectively revered and served.
Then this minister went to the place of worship and made this incantation:
"I have no offspring; I have heard that the heavenly deity possesses great merit, protects all living beings, and can grant their wishes, and so I now take refuge in him."
"If my wish is granted and you would bestow upon me a son, I shall adorn his celestial body with gold and silver, and I shall smear fragrant incense upon your divine temple;
if there is no efficacy, I shall destroy this shrine and smear your body with excrement."
Having heard this, the deva reflected to himself:

"This man is wealthy and his power is great; he is no ordinary person who could become his son. My own strength is meager and I cannot grant him this wish. If my vow is not fulfilled, I shall surely suffer disgrace and ruin at the shrine."
He then went again to report this to Maṇibhadra.
Maṇibhadra was not able to accomplish it through his power, so he went once more to King Vaiśravaṇa and personally informed him of the matter.
King Vaiśravaṇa said:
"It is not by my power that I can cause you to have a son.
I shall go at once to the Lord of Devas and petition him for this boon."
King Vaiśravaṇa immediately ascended to heaven and addressed Śakra, saying:

"I have a minister named Maṇibhadra who spoke to me recently, saying that there is a chief minister in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who has requested a son from him, having made a solemn vow: 'If my wish is fulfilled, I shall increase my offerings twofold;
if my wish is denied, I shall destroy your temple and subject you to humiliation.'"
That man is fierce and violent; he will surely be able to do so.
We pray, O Heavenly King, that he may have a son!
Śakra replied:
"This matter is extremely difficult!
One must seek out those with whom there is a karmic connection."
At that time, there was a deva whose five celestial virtues had departed from his body as his life was about to end.
Śakra addressed him, saying:
"As you are now approaching death, would you wish to be reborn into the family of that minister?"
The devaputra replied:

"I wish to leave the household life and practice the correct path; however, if one is born into noble and honorable status, it is difficult to renounce desire. I hope to fulfill my aspiration by remaining in the middle state."
Śakra replied again:
"Simply go there;
if you wish to study the Way, I shall assist you."
When the deva-son’s life came to an end, his spirit descended to take conception in the womb of a high minister.
Upon being born and brought outside, his appearance was upright and handsome; the minister immediately summoned a physiognomist to bestow a name upon the child.
The physiognomist asked,
"From where did you originally obtain this child?
The counselor replied:
"Formerly, I requested him from the deity Gaṅgā;
therefore, he was given the name Gaṅgāda.
As he gradually grew older, he petitioned his parents to seek ordination."
The parents replied:
"We are now wealthy and noble, and our livelihoods are vast and extensive. You are our only son and shall succeed to the family estate.
While we are still alive, we will never permit you to leave home and enter the Way."

The son did not follow his wishes and was deeply despondent; he then intended to sacrifice his life to seek a more ordinary station, thinking, "If I seek deliverance from within this state, it will surely be easier."
Thereupon he departed in secret and threw himself from a mountain cliff; yet when he fell to the ground, he suffered no injury.
He went again to the riverbank and cast himself into the water, but the current immediately swept him out, and he likewise felt no pain.
He again took poison and swallowed it, but the toxic vapors did not take effect, and there was no way for it to cause his death.
He then thought to himself:
"I shall violate the laws of the state and be put to death by the king."

He encountered the king’s consort and her maidservants as they had come out of the palace to bathe in a pond within the garden; having removed their garments, they had left them among the trees and bushes.
At that time, Upagupta secretly entered the grove, took the clothing and ornaments, and departed carrying them away.
The gatekeeper saw him and immediately led him away to inform King Ajātaśatru.
Upon hearing this news, the king’s wrath flared up; he took up his bow and arrows and shot with his own hand, but the arrow turned back and struck the king himself.
When he had done this three times and still could not stop him,
the king grew afraid and cast aside his bow, asking the man:
"Are you a deva, a nāga, a yakṣa, or a spirit?"
Gaṅgada said,
"If you grant me one wish, I shall venture to speak.
The king said:
"I shall give it to you," he replied.
Gaṅgāda said, "I am neither a deva, nor a nāga, nor a ghost; I am the son of the prime minister of Śrāvastī."

I wish to leave the household life, but my parents do not permit it; therefore, wishing to take my own life to be reborn in another realm, I threw myself from a cliff, leaped into a river, and drank poison, yet I did not die. Thus, I have committed a crime against the king’s law in the hope of ending my precarious life.
"Your Majesty now seeks to harm me, yet you cannot succeed.
Such is the nature of things; how extreme is this cruelty!
I pray that you will show compassion and grant me permission to practice the Way."
The king immediately replied,
"I grant you permission to leave the household life.
He then led him back to the place where the Buddha was, and reported the matter to the World-Honored One exactly as it had occurred.
At that time, the Tathāgata granted him permission to become a śramaṇa; with the dharma robes upon his body, he was ordained as a bhikṣu.

The Buddha preached the Dharma for him, and his mind was opened and his understanding awakened; he attained the fruit of arhatship, possessing the three knowledges, the six supernormal powers, and the eight liberations.
At that time, King Ajātaśatru addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!

What roots of goodness did this Gaṅgika plant in a previous life, such that he was not killed when thrown from a mountain, did not drown when falling into water, suffered no pain from eating poison, and remained unhurt by arrows; furthermore, having encountered the World-Honored One, he has attained liberation from birth and death?"
The Buddha told the king:

"In the past, countless eons ago, there was a great kingdom called Vārāṇasī. Its king was named Brahmadatta. Once, while he was sporting with his palace ladies in a grove, he sent forth a group of court maids to sing with melodious voices."
Outside, there was a man who joined in with a loud voice.
When the king heard this sound, he became filled with anger and jealousy; he dispatched men to capture him and commanded that he be put to death.
At that time, a high minister arrived from outside and saw this one man being held in captivity; "For what reason has he come to such a state?
he asked. The people nearby then related the details of the circumstances.
The minister said,
"Wait! Let me see the King first."
The minister entered and addressed the king, saying:
"That man’s offense does not reach the level of being deeply grave; why then do you seek to harm him?
Although he blended his voice with yours, he did not reveal his form, nor did he engage in any act of lewdness. We pray that you will show compassion and grant him his life."
The king could not go against this and pardoned him instead of executing him.
Having escaped, the man entered the service of the high minister, serving with diligence and care without fail.
After attending to him in this manner for many years, he thought to himself:
“Lust harms people more than swords or blades; my present misfortune is entirely due to desire.
He then said to the great minister, “Grant me permission to leave the household life and follow the path of spiritual cultivation.”
The minister replied, "I dare not go against your wish; once you have attained the Way through study, I shall return to see you.

He then departed for the mountain forests, where he focused his mind on correct contemplation. His spirit was awakened, and he became a pratyekabuddha. Returning to the city, he went to the house of the minister.
Upon seeing this, the minister was filled with great joy and invited him to receive offerings; he provided him with delicious food and drink, and his four requisites were never lacking.

At that time, the Pratyekabuddha manifested supernatural transformations in mid-air, emitting water and fire from his body and radiating a great light. Seeing this, the minister’s delight was immeasurable, and he immediately made a vow:

"By virtue of my kindness in saving your life, may I be wealthy, noble, and long-lived in every lifetime; may my excellence be many thousands of times superior and extraordinary; and may my wisdom and virtue be equal to yours."
The Buddha told the king:
"The great minister who at that time saved one person and enabled them to escape is none other than this present-day Gaṅgādatta.
By virtue of these causes and conditions, in every place where he was born, his life was not cut short prematurely; now, having encountered me, he has attained arhatship."
When the Buddha had finished speaking these words, all those present in the assembly believed, honored, and rejoiced; they received [the teaching] upon their heads and practiced it accordingly.
99. The Story of the Brahmin Dīrghanakha (99) The Story of the Brahmin Dīrghanakha: The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandakanivāpa Bamboo Grove.
At that time, in that city, there was a brahmin named Śarabhaṅga.
He had two children: a son named Dīrghanakha and a daughter named Śārī.
The son, Dīrghanakha, was intelligent and widely learned, skilled in debate; whenever he engaged in discussion with his sister Śāri, he always prevailed over her.
However, once she became pregnant, when they debated again, the brother was no longer as successful.
Then his younger brother, Dīrghanakha, spoke these words:

"My sister previously came to debate with me and was always defeated by me; yet since she became pregnant, her debating has become exceptionally superior—this must surely be due to the power of the merit of the child in her womb."
"If my son is born, he will surely defeat me in debate.
I must now travel abroad to study extensively the four Vedas and the eighteen branches of learning; only then shall I return to the kingdom to debate with my nephew."
Having formed this thought, he went to South India to study various treatises, vowing: "If I have not mastered them to become a preeminent teacher, I shall never clip my nails."

Thereupon, his elder sister’s months of pregnancy having been fulfilled, she gave birth to a son. He was named after his mother, and his personal name was Śāriputra. He was exceptionally handsome and extraordinary, possessed of keen intelligence and wisdom, and so profoundly versed in all treatises that he was difficult to refute in debate.

At that time, the various brahmins within the city of Rājagṛha struck a great golden drum to summon eighteen billion people from the kingdom; they assembled at the site of debate and prepared four high seats.
At that time, Śāriputra was eight years old; attending the assembly at the site of debate, he asked the people, "For whom are these four high seats being prepared?"
The people replied, "First is the king;
second is the crown prince; third is the great minister; and fourth is the master of debate.
When Śāriputra heard these words, he immediately ascended the high seat of the master of debate and sat upon it.
At that time, all the venerable elders and brahmins, along with the entire assembly, were struck with wonder and thought to themselves:
"If we scholars defeat this young boy in debate, it will not be much cause for honor;
yet if we do not defeat him, it would be deeply shameful."
Having formed this thought, he immediately dispatched a junior Brahmin from the lower seats to debate with Śāriputra; they exchanged a few preliminary questions and answers.

At that time, the Brahmins found their words exhausted and their reasoning stumped; gradually passing the responsibility upward, they eventually reached the Elder. Within only a few rounds of discussion, they were all defeated.
At that time, Śāriputra, having emerged victorious in debate, became renowned throughout the sixteen great kingdoms; his wisdom was so vast and comprehensive that he stood alone without peer.
Later, on one occasion in Rājagṛha, he ascended a high tower and looked out in all directions. Seeing the people within the city gathered for a festive celebration, he reflected:
"These multitudes, though bustling about, will after a hundred years vanish utterly into nothingness."
Having formed this thought, he immediately descended from the high tower and left the household life to seek the Way within the teachings of the non-Buddhists.

At that time, the World-Honored One had only recently attained Buddhahood, and none of the sixteen great kingdoms had yet heard of him. Out of his great compassion and desire to transform beings, the Tathāgata dispatched the bhikṣu Abhiya to the city of Rājagṛha to wander for alms.
At that time, Śāriputra, seeing that his deportment was so dignified and orderly as to be worthy of admiration, had this thought:
"Who is this person, whose merit is such as this?"
"I have never before seen such a bhikṣu.
Having thought this, he immediately stepped forward and asked,
"Whom do you serve as your teacher, that your Dharma principles are such as these?"
Then the bhikṣu Abhi spoke in verse, answering:
“My Teacher is the God among Gods, the Supreme Honored One of the three realms;
his body, adorned with the marks and signs, is sixteen feet tall, and he travels through the void by means of supernormal powers.”
When the bhikṣu Abhi had spoken these verses, he remained silent.
Then Śāriputra said to Abhi:
"I have long heard of your teacher’s appearance and supernormal powers."
"By awakening to what path did you attain such [a state]?
At that time, the bhikṣu Abhi answered again in verse:
"The fragrance of flowers dispels the five aggregates; The twelve faculties are uprooted and severed."
"Not coveting the pleasures of heaven or the world, with a pure mind, one opens the gateway to the Dharma.
Then Śāriputra again asked the bhikṣu Abhiya:
"How long has it been since your teacher spoke these words?"
"What dharma have you studied?
The bhikṣu Abhi answered again in verse:
"My years are still young, and my days of study are but recently begun."
"How could one possibly proclaim the true and correct, the vast and great meaning of the Tathāgata?
Then Śāriputra spoke again to Abhiya:
"I would be grateful if you would kindly inform me of what your teacher has taught."
At that time, Abhi replied again in verse:
"Among all phenomena, causes and conditions are empty and without a master.
One who quiets the mind and realizes the fundamental source is therefore called a śramaṇa."
At that time, having heard these verses, Śāriputra’s mind was immediately awakened and he attained the fruit of *srotāpanna*.
Then Maudgalyāyana, seeing that Śāriputra’s countenance was serene and joyful, asked him:
“Formerly, you and I made a mutual vow that if either of us first attained the taste of the nectar of the Dharma, we would certainly inform the other.”
"I observe you now, and because you have attained something, your countenance is joyful.
At that time, Śāriputra recited the aforementioned verse three times for Maudgalyāyana.
Having heard this, Maudgalyāyana’s mind was opened and his understanding clarified; he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna.

At that time, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana, each having realized the traces of the Path, felt great joy in their hearts. They returned to their respective groups of disciples and recounted these matters in detail to them.
"I now wish to go to seek ordination under the Buddha; what do you think?
At that time, each of the disciples said to their teacher:
"Great Teacher, if you are now to practice and study what Gautama has taught, we, your disciples, shall likewise follow you."
When Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana heard these words, they each took two hundred and fifty disciples and followed the bhikṣu Aniruddha to the Bamboo Grove.

Beholding the Buddha, the World-Honored One, endowed with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like hundreds of thousands of suns, he felt great joy in his heart; he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and requested to leave the household life.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they became śramaṇas.

Through diligent and arduous cultivation, he attained the fruit of Arhatship, possessing the three knowledges and six supernormal powers, and was endowed with the eight liberations; he was revered and honored by all devas and worldly beings.
At that time, the brahmin Dīrghanakha, hearing that Śāriputra had left the household life to enter the Path, was filled with anger and distress, and spoke these words:

"This nephew of mine, Śāriputra, is by nature intelligent and wise, having mastered a vast array of scriptures; the veteran masters of debate from the sixteen great kingdoms all submit to his virtue. How could he suddenly abandon such a high reputation to serve the Gautama?"
He then came from South India to the place where the Buddha was and engaged in debate with him.
At that time, the World-Honored One said to the brahmin:
"What you have now perceived is not the path to ultimate nirvana."
When that brahmin heard these words, he remained silent and did not answer.
Though asked a second and a third time, he likewise remained silent.
Then Vajrapāṇi, from the midst of the sky, brandished his vajra toward the crown of the brahmin’s head.
"If you do not answer, I shall shatter your body with this mace.

At that time, the brahmin was seized by terror; his limbs were covered in sweat and filth, and he had nowhere to turn. Feeling deep remorse and finding no refuge for his countenance, he immediately humbled himself before the Buddha, seeking with a heart of reverent submission to leave the household life and become a disciple of the Buddha.
The Buddha immediately granted his permission,
saying, "Welcome, Bhikṣu!
Whereupon their hair and beards fell away of their own accord, dharma robes appeared upon their bodies, and they became śramaṇas.
Through diligent application in the practice of the path, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
When the bhikṣus witnessed this event, they addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
"What merit did this brahmin bhikṣu plant in past lives that he has abandoned error for the right, encountered the Buddha, the World-Honored One, left the household life, and attained the Way?
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the bhikṣus:
"Listen attentively!"
I shall now analyze and explain this for you.
In the past, immeasurable eons ago, there was a Pratyekabuddha in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī who sat in meditation and contemplation within the mountain forests.
At that time, there was a band of five hundred thieves who, having plundered the property of others, were about to enter those mountain forests and groves.
Then the leader of the thieves first dispatched one man to go and see whether there was anyone in the woods or not.

Seeing a pratyekabuddha sitting cross-legged beneath a tree in deep contemplation, he immediately went forward, seized him by force, and bound him, bringing him before the leader of the bandits with the intent to kill him together with his followers.
At that time, the Pratyekabuddha thought to himself:
"If I remain silent, I will be killed by him; this will increase his karmic offenses, causing him to fall into hell from which there will be no hope of escape."
"I shall now manifest supernatural transformations for them, so as to cause them to have faith and submit.

Having formed this thought, his body ascended into the void; he leaped up in the east and vanished in the west, leaped up in the south and vanished in the north; water and fire issued from his body; or he manifested a vast body that filled the entirety of space, and then again manifested a small one—thus proceeding in succession, he performed the eighteen transformations.
At that time, having witnessed this transformation, the bandits were filled with great terror; they immediately prostrated themselves on the ground with their five limbs and sincerely repented.
When the pratyekabuddha had accepted their repentance, they prepared various delicacies and invited him for a meal; thereafter, they made vows and departed.

By virtue of these merits, throughout immeasurable lifetimes, he did not fall into the realms of hell, animals, or hungry ghosts; instead, among devas and humans, he experienced celestial bliss, until now, having encountered me, he has left the household life and attained the Way.
The Buddha told the bhikṣus:
“If you wish to know who that leader of the bandits was at that time, it is this bhikṣu, the brahmin Dīrghanakha.
When the bhikṣus heard what the Buddha had said, they rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
100. The Story of Sundarī’s Beauty (100). The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha in the Kalandaka Bamboo Grove.

At that time, the queen of King Prasenajit became pregnant; when her ten months were complete, she gave birth to a son whose countenance was so upright and handsome that he was peerless in the world, his two eyes being as bright and clear as those of the *kūnāla* bird.
At that time, the king, whose name was Kuṇāla, adorned himself with various necklaces and exquisite garments; he had a person carry him as he traveled through all the villages, asking the people:
"Is there anyone in the world who can compare to my son in such handsome and upright features?"
At that time, there were several merchants in the village who addressed the Great King, saying:
"May Your Majesty grant us forgiveness!
Grant us fearlessness, and we shall venture to speak."
The king immediately replied, "Speak; do not fear.
Thereupon, the merchant addressed the great king, saying:

"In the village where I reside, there is a young boy named Sundarī; he is exceptionally handsome and marvelous, his appearance resembling that of a celestial being, surpassing the prince by hundreds of thousands of millions of times, beyond all comparison."
Furthermore, when the child was born, a spring spontaneously appeared within the house; its fragrant water was cool and delicious, and it was filled with various precious jewels.
When King Prasenajit heard the merchant’s words, he immediately dispatched a messenger to that village with these instructions:
"I shall go there myself to see Sundarī."
At that time, when the village headman heard that the king wished to come and see Sundarī, he consulted with the others, saying:
"If the king comes now, with what shall we entertain him?"
"It would be better to send her first.
Having reached this conclusion, they immediately adorned Sundarī with various necklaces and exquisite garments, and went to deliver her to the king.
When the king saw Sundarī, he perceived her to be so exceptionally beautiful and peerless in the world that he was struck with deep wonder and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
He then took the young child and went to the Buddha’s dwelling, wishing to ask the cause by which she had received such a body.

When the boy saw the Buddha, with his thirty-two major marks and eighty minor characteristics, his radiance shining everywhere like a hundred thousand suns, his heart was filled with joy; he stepped forward to prostrate at the Buddha’s feet and withdrew to sit to one side.
The Buddha then preached the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths for him; his mind was opened and his understanding awakened, and he attained the fruit of Srotāpanna. He then sought ordination.
The Buddha addressed him, saying:
"Welcome, Bhikṣu!"
His hair and beard fell away naturally, dharma robes appeared upon his body, and he immediately became a śramaṇa.
Through diligent and earnest cultivation, before long, he attained the fruit of arhatship.
At that time, King Prasenajit, having witnessed this event, addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One!

What merit did this bhikṣu Sundarī plant in his past lives, such that at the moment of his birth there were naturally these springs and various precious treasures filling them, and furthermore, he encountered the World-Honored One, left the household life, and attained the Way?”
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed King Prasenajit:
"Listen attentively now!
I shall analyze and explain it for you."

In this Bhadrakalpa, a Buddha appeared in the world in the kingdom of Vārāṇasī, named Kāśyapa; he had eighteen thousand bhikṣus who sat in meditation and practiced the Path within the mountain forests.

At that time, there was an elder who happened to encounter them while traveling; his heart was filled with joy, and he immediately returned home to prepare scented water for the monks to bathe. Having finished providing various delicacies as offerings, he further cast precious jewels into the water in the basin and presented it to the monks, making a vow before departing.
"By virtue of this merit, he shall not fall into the evil realms; among gods and humans, he will always have lotus ponds and precious treasures arise spontaneously alongside him.
The Buddha told the Great King:

"If you wish to know who that son of a great elder was at that time—who, because he bathed the assembly of monks and provided offerings, constantly attained such physical beauty—it is now the bhikṣu Sundarī."
At that time, the Great King, having heard what the Buddha had spoken, rejoiced and practiced accordingly.
*The Compendium of the One Hundred Karmic Conditions*, Scroll Ten, Chapter on the Brahmin.
